News.title: 'Vile' sex offender raped teen girl who was with his own son at house party
News.content:
'Vile' sex offender raped teen girl who was with his own son at house party

Richard Murphy, 48, attacked the 16-year-old after coming across her and his son in the garden of the house next door, where the pair had been socialising at a party

View Image Richard Murphy, 48, has been jailed (file) (Image: Collins Photo Agency)

A convicted sex offender has been jailed for raping a teenager who was with his son at a house party.

‌



Richard Murphy, described by a High Court judge in Dublin as a "danger to young girls", attacked the 16-year-old after coming across her and his son in the garden of the house next door to where he had been living as part of his bail conditions.

‌



The court heard Murphy's son had been socialising with the girl at the party and had engaged in consensual sexual activity in the property's garden.

‌



Murphy, 48, arrived and told his son to go inside before questioning the girl for details of who her parents were. The victim was in a state of partial undress and Murphy did not allow her to pull up her clothing.

He orally raped the injured party then raped her before leaving and telling her not to tell anyone. The girl told her friends and they then left the party.

The judge noted that in her evidence, the victim was terrified when she realised she was about to be raped.

‌



Ms Justice O'Connor said Murphy's defence was that he asked the girl for her details because he was concerned for his son, then left with his son.

But evidence during the trial was that Murphy's son returned to the party alone and that Murphy disappeared for a period of time, with his then-partner looking for him, reports the Irish Mirror.

Murphy, of Rectory Heights, Enniscorthy, Co. Wexford, was on bail at the time for other sexual offences involving young girls, for which he has since been convicted and is currently serving a sentence.

‌



He was convicted of rape and oral rape in October 2022 following a Central Criminal Court trial sitting in Waterford in June. Murphy was jailed for 11 years and six months, consecutive to the sentence he is currently serving.

The court was told that Angelique Schreuder was happy to waive her right to anonymity to allow Murphy to be named in reporting of the case.

Ms Justice Karen O'Connor said it was aggravating that Murphy was on bail for sexual offences at the time of this offence, and noted his previous convictions relating to three young girls, including sexual assault and making threats.

‌



The judge said the offending here was "of a more serious nature" and represented an "escalation". She said it was the court's view that he had demonstrated "predatory behaviour."

"This man, in the view of this court, is a danger to young girls," she said.

She said it was "egregious how this young girl was treated" and noted that the injured party was "particularly vulnerable" at the time.

‌



The judge said this was a "particularly disturbing case" and that Murphy "behaved in a vile and devious manner in the way he treated this young vulnerable girl". She noted the injured party's impact statement referred to Murphy's "sense of entitlement" in how he treated her that night.

Ms Justice O'Connor said the injured party made a "very coherent and powerful" victim impact statement, where she described wanting to rip her skin off and crawl out of her body to get away from the feeling of violation.

Ms Schreuder added that the attack continues to impact her life. Her mother encouraged her to attend counselling, which has helped her, the court heard.

‌



The judge said there was "limited mitigation" in the case, noting that Murphy does not accept the jury's verdicts, as is his right.

She said where there is no expression of remorse and the verdict is not accepted, there are "no conditions I can impose which are going to allay concerns of court". The judge noted that Murphy is entitled not to acknowledge guilt.

She said the court was aware of his background in training with the GAA and had considered testimonials provided by Murphy's two adult children and his parents.

Article continues below

Ms Justice O'Connor said the court would impose a consecutive sentence as these offences were committed while Murphy was on bail. She imposed a sentence of 11 years and six months in respect of the rape count and a concurrent eight-year sentence in relation to the count of oral rape.

The judge directed that the sentence of 11 years and six months should be consecutive to the sentence Murphy is currently serving, for which he has an earliest release date in October 2027. She also extended legal aid in the event of an appeal.

Addressing Ms Schreuder, Ms Justice O'Connor said: "You are very brave young woman and very courageous. Your mother would be very proud of you. Your sisters and friends are very proud of you."

News.title: Viral kids' toys could be confiscated at UK airport security - warning to parents
News.content:
Viral kids' toys could be confiscated at UK airport security - warning to parents

Airports have warned that kids could be forced to leave the items behind

View 2 Images Squishy toys could easily raise a red flag at airport security this summer (stock image) (Image: Getty)

Parents are being told to leave certain children's toys at home. If kids bring them to the airport, they may be taken from them at security. There is a high chance that items like NeeDoh cubes and other popular 'squishy' toys could be flagged and confiscated.

‌



Even at airports using advanced scanners, gel-filled toys look highly unusual on security screens. This frequently triggers a manual bag check, causing travel delays, and some staff will not take the risk with these items going any further into the airport.

‌



Travel specialist Kate Donnelly (@Thedonnelllyedit) said: "From my own personal experience, [squishy toys] do tend to come under closer scrutiny when passing through airport security. My top tip for parents this summer, pack these items in your whole luggage.

‌



"There is a high chance that if you put these in your hand luggage, they will get confiscated. There are absolutely no markings on them to let you know exactly how much liquid is contained within them, and therefore, they are very easily removed.

"This means that you have upset children and you will have to pay out for a whole new load of toys when you get to your destination." She suggested that the best thing to do is to pack toys safely in your main suitcase that gets checked into the hold, as this allows more liquids than hand luggage does, helping you avoid delays and reduce the risk of them being confiscated.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Posting online, Luton Airport confirms that any squishy toys, including NeeDoh cubes, that contain a gel or liquid must comply with the strict liquid rule when packed in hand luggage. The airport said: "As the quantity of gel contained within these items cannot be accurately verified during the screening process, they are not permitted through security in hand luggage."

Manchester Airport also said: "Things like squishy toys contain liquid - this includes NeeDohs, which use malt syrup. Smaller versions of the toy are under 100mls, but larger versions are not.

"The problem is that, as they don't have measurements printed on them, security staff have to estimate their size. Our advice is that all but very small squishy toys should be placed in hold baggage."

‌



View 2 Images People could be caught out at airport security over these rules

As a result, kids could be forced to bin their favourite toys before going on holiday. The issue is that there is often no way to verify exactly how much 'liquid' is inside one of these objects.

Not all UK airports follow the same rules about liquids in 2026 due to a staggered rollout of new high-tech 3D CT security scanners that allow the 100ml rule to be relaxed. Different locations are at different stages of upgrading, with a pause currently in effect this summer to avoid disruption over peak travel times.

‌



Below is a list of what airports are following the new (2000ml) rules. At the airports accepting two litres in hand luggage, the scanners also mean people do not need to empty their bags, as scanners are powerful enough to detect these items, as well as electronics:

News.title: Andy Burnham live: PM hits ground running with electricity bills VAT pledge to axe £45 off household bills
News.content:
Andy Burnham promised to deliver 'breathing space' for families during his maiden speech outside No 10, and has already helped millions of families in the UK by abolishing VAT on electricity bills

Andy Burnham has wasted no time in offering up potential solutions to the cost of living crisis, announcing on his second day in office that he will "bring back hope" for struggling families by cutting VAT on energy bills.

Burnham has started making good on his promise for “breathing space” for struggling households, a key plinth of his economic plans unveiled in his maiden speech outside No 10 on Monday. The move will see VAT removed from domestic electricity bills from October 1.

Burnham said: “Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living. That needs to change. I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that’s what I’m announcing on my second day as Prime Minister. We’re taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people’s pockets and bring back hope.”

It is estimated that the change will reduce the annual Ofgem price cap by around £45 from October, with companies expected to pass the reduction onto customers.

Chancellor John Healey said: “For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. Today’s energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills, and provide some reassurance this winter". He continued: “This measure is funded this year from cancelling the Digital ID programme, and it will help bring down inflation while supporting households in every postcode.”

The fully priced plan from Mr Healey comes as Burnham continues to pad out his cabinet, with a number of key appointments made since yesterday, including Ed Miliband receiving the FCDO brief, Angela Rayner returning as Housing Secretary, and Shabana Mahmood staying on as Home Secretary.

News.title: Barry Hearn gives clear verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight collapsing
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Barry Hearn gives clear verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight collapsing

Barry Hearn has delivered his verdict on whether Anthony Joshua's proposed fight against Tyson Fury could collapse, with both boxers in action this weekend

View 3 Images Barry Hearn has delivered his verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury collapsing (Image: Getty Images)

Anthony Joshua's proposed heavyweight fight against Tyson Fury is still expected to GO AHEAD later this year, according to Matchroom's Barry Hearn. Joshua and Fury are due to clash in an all-British boxing showdown in November, providing both win their warm-up bouts this weekend.

‌



Fury, 37, is scheduled to go up against Mariusz Wach on Friday, with Joshua, 36, facing Kristian Penga the following evening. Should both win - which is backed as short as 1/16 with the bookmakers – a mammoth multi-million pound fight is poised to take place, though a final venue is yet to be decided.

‌



Although there is still an outside chance of the fight collapsing, boxing promoter Hearn is confident that both Joshua and Fury will come through their warm-up bouts unscathed. This is despite Prenga's team claiming that Joshua has made a "big mistake" by fighting the Albanian in Saudi Arabia.

‌



Guide to the 2026 Commonwealth Games is on sale now READ MORE :

Anthony Joshua undercard finally revealed ahead of comeback fight READ MORE :

When asked if the fight might not go ahead, Hearn, 78, told Mirror Sport: "No. I don't know if you've ever been hit on the chin by someone who weighs 17st... I haven't, and I don't want to. There's always the potential of a banana skin in boxing. History tells us that. I think it's unlikely in both cases, of course.

"But Anthony Joshua, to his credit, he's not thinking beyond Saturday. He knows what's at stake here, a fight that he's wanted for 10 years has been signed for. All they have to do is deliver their respective victories, I believe that is a huge odds-on favourite.

"Kristian Prenga's team, of course, whilst they're entitled to their opinion, have absolutely no idea what they're talking about. They've never been in with an animal like Anthony Joshua, especially in his [Oleksandr] Usyk training regime that he's now adopted and embraced and realised that he thought he was doing the best training that he could ever do, and now he's seen another level, which has inspired him, which I like.

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Joshua is on "another level", according to Barry Hearn (Image: Getty Images)

"I like people that are ready to embrace something new. So no, if there's always a banana skin, it's unlikely, and I can't wait for Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua. It's been a long time in the making."

While the long-awaited mega-fight has been discussed for years, Joshua and Fury have never fought in a professional boxing match before. Should the clash go ahead as planned, it's poised to be one of the biggest boxing has EVER seen, according to Hearn, alongside the 'Rumble in the Jungle' and 'Thriller in Manila' where both were won by the legendary late Muhammed Ali.

‌



Hearn added: "Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua would be... I'm trying to think what would be bigger. You're at Muhammad Ali, the Rumble in the Jungle. You're at the thriller in Manila with Frazier and Ali. You're at that level, that sort of marketplace. It's creme de la creme, but in today's world, it's on Netflix, the Tyson Fury fight.

View 3 Images Tyson Fury is set to go up against Anthony Joshua later this year (Image: Richard Pelham/Getty Images for Netflix)

"It's just a massive global event. I mean, the big global events get bigger and bigger. We've just seen the World Cup possibly. Forget Argentina because they weren't my favourite team there. But there's a massive, massive commercial enterprise beyond their normal imagination, and Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua is exactly the same."

Article continues below

Watford-born Joshua, who last fought against YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in December 2025, has an imperious record of 29 wins and four losses across his professional. Meanwhile, Fury's most recent fight was against Arslanbek Makhmudov in April 2026 and has lost just ONCE across his 38 professional bouts.

Both Joshua and Fury as seen as two of Britain's greatest-ever heavyweight fighters, with both former world champions, making November's proposed fight a must-not-miss should it go ahead as scheduled.

News.title: New Aldi 40p summer reminder for thousands of shoppers using its car parks
News.content:
New Aldi 40p summer reminder for thousands of shoppers using its car parks

Shoppers have been issued a reminder when using the car parks this summer

View 3 Images Aldi has shared a reminder to shoppers in a new message issued on Tuesday (Image: Getty)

Aldi has issued a message to drivers across the UK who use its car parks, reminding them of something that may be useful to know this summer. Nearly all of Aldi's 1,086 stores in the UK come with their own car park. More than 550 of these car parks are managed by Parkingeye, a private car park management company, and over 250 now provide on-site electric vehicle (EV) charging stations.

‌



In a message to motorists with electric vehicles, shared on Tuesday, July 21, Aldi reminds drivers that they can charge their cars while they shop at hundreds of stores across the UK. The price for using an EV charger starts at 40p.

‌



Many families will be heading off on day trips, staycations and longer journeys over the summer holidays now that the majority of schools have closed. Aldi says its EV charging network lets drivers top up while stocking up on picnic food, drinks and other summer essentials.

‌



The supermarket has recently transitioned around 1,200 electric vehicle (EV) chargers at more than 250 stores across the UK over to Drax Electric Vehicles. The store says it is giving customers a quick and convenient way to top up during their shop.

Drax is a renewable energy company in the UK. It offers a wide range of fleet electrification services and electric vehicle charging solutions for businesses.

View 3 Images Aldi is reminding electric vehicle drivers they can charge their cars while they shop at hundreds of stores across the UK

‌



Stores with charging facilities include Aldi's Diss store in Norfolk, as well as locations in Eastbourne, Durham and Yate near Bristol. In addition to its existing charging network, Aldi says it will also install chargers at around 20 new stores each year as part of its ongoing expansion plans, "offering a mix of fast and rapid chargers so customers can choose the option that suits their journey".

Charging is priced at 40p per kWh for fast charging and 62p per kWh for rapid charging. Shoppers can check availability, view charging costs and pay through the Charge Assist app, or use contactless card payment, with no subscription needed.

Jonathan Neale, Managing Director of National Real Estate at Aldi UK, said: "We’re committed to making sustainable choices more accessible for our shoppers, and we know many are looking for affordable, reliable and convenient ways to charge their cars. By expanding EV charging at more of our stores, we’re helping to make that easier and offering great-value charging while they shop."

‌



View 3 Images Aldi says its EV charging network gives drivers a simple way to top up while stocking up on picnic food

When will the sale of new petrol and diesel vehicles be banned?

The expansion reinforces Aldi’s long-term commitment to sustainability and supports the UK’s transition to electric vehicles, with the government targeting the end of new petrol and diesel car sales by 2030. And, all new vehicles must be completely zero-emission by 2035.

The regulations for phasing out the sale of new combustion-engine vehicles include specific rules for drivers and buyers. After 2030, no new traditional petrol or diesel vehicles will be available for purchase. However, full hybrids and plug-in hybrids that have a substantial zero-emission range will still be permitted to be sold new until 2035.

Article continues below

Electric vehicles (EVs) can be classified into four primary types depending on their power source: BEVs (battery electric vehicles), PHEVs (plug-in hybrid electric vehicles), HEVs (hybrid electric vehicles that charge themselves), and FCEVs (fuel cell electric vehicles that use hydrogen).

News.title: World's longest undersea tunnel stretching 17 miles and costing £1.8bn gets major update
News.content:
World's longest undersea tunnel stretching 17 miles and costing £1.8bn gets major update

The Rogfast tunnel in Norway is set to become the world's longest and deepest underwater tunnel when it is completed in 2033 - and it has just received a major update

View 3 Images The project has received a funding boost (Image: SKANSA)

The Rogfast Tunnel in Norway is set to be a truly incredible feat of engineering. Not only will it be the world's deepest undersea tunnel, plunging 400m beneath the surface, but it will also be the longest, stretching an impressive 27km (roughly 17 miles).

‌



Now a significant development has emerged in the extraordinary scheme to keep the project on track.

‌



Work on the ambitious scheme, which will link the villages of Randaberg and Bokn, initially began in January 2018 but was suspended the next year amid soaring costs. Construction restarted in 2021 following revised plans, and now a significant development has been confirmed which will give the project a major boost.

‌



The remarkable tunnel forms part of a broader upgrade of the E39 road, a coastal route linking Trondheim and Kristiansand in Norway. At present, journeying between these two locations takes 21 hours and requires multiple ferry crossings.

The long-term goal is to replace all seven ferry crossings with tunnels and bridges, which would cut the 21-hour journey down to 11 hours. Authorities are aiming to complete the entire project by 2050.

View 3 Images The tunnel will be the longest undersea tunnel in the world (Image: Norwegian Public Roads Administration)

‌



This first tunnel will shave 40 minutes off the trip between Stavanger and Bergen while boosting transport reliability.

Earlier this month the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB) approved a NOK 4 billion loan (approximately £307m) to fund the scheme, with Norwegian toll operator Ferde AS serving as an intermediary, reports the Express.

"Reliable infrastructure is essential for regional development and efficient transport links. Rogfast will improve connectivity in wester Norway and support the long-term integration of labour and transport markets," said Carlos Rodriguez, senior bank at NIB.

‌



The overall cost is anticipated to reach NOK 25 billion (approximately £1.8billion), with around 4,000 vehicles expected to pass through each day.

The Rogfast Tunnel, also referred to as the Boknafjord Tunnel, will even feature a double roundabout deep beneath the sea, connecting to the island of Kvitsøy - and travellers will find themselves descending further underground than the height of the Empire State Building.

View 3 Images It is hoped the tunnel will be complete by 2033 (Image: Volvo Construction Equipment/Youtube)

‌



Construction giant Skanska, which is overseeing the northern section of the tunnel, has spoken openly about the challenges involved in drilling so far beneath the ocean.

Project manager Anne Brit Moen told Engineers Ireland: "Since we are going all the way down to 392m below sea level, we're focusing on finding the best methods to maintain safe and efficient working conditions for everyone. The tunnel will significantly improve connectivity along the Norwegian west coast."

Norwegian Public Roads Administration project manager Oddvar Kaarmo added: "About half a year after the last drill and blast, we have to deliver the project, so we have to get a lot of work done simultaneously. It's more about logistics than tunnelling," as reported by the Daily Telegraph.

Article continues below

An art installation will be placed inside the tunnel to "prevent monotony" and "alleviate tunnel anxiety", with those overseeing construction hopeful that this measure will reduce the number of accidents.

News.title: Dozens of tourists including Brits hospitalised in swimming pool poisoning near Marbella
News.content:
Dozens of tourists including Brits hospitalised in swimming pool poisoning near Marbella

At least 60 people needed hospital treatment for toxic gas poisoning after a problem with the pump for the swimming pool at a hotel in Benahavis near Marbella

View Image The hotel is in Benahavis near Marbella (Image: Getty Images)

Dozens of holidaymakers at a Costa del Sol hotel have been taken to hospital with toxic gas poisoning.

‌



At least 60 people needed hospital treatment due to the release of the gas after a pump problem at their swimming pool, while others received medical attention at the unnamed hotel in Benahavis near Marbella.

‌



An investigation into the scare was ongoing today. A regional government official told local press it appeared the circuit breaker on the pressure pump that injects chlorine and acid into the pool tripped and the system failed.

‌



He said the chlorine and PH systems stopped working as a result of the fault while other gases continued to be released.

Children and elderly people, including holidaymakers from the UK, were taken to Marbella’s Costa del Sol Hospital according to Malaga-based paper Sur.

Met Office verdict on August heatwave as weather maps show 37C scorcher READ MORE :

Iran-backed group declares another crucial strait closed as Middle East war widens READ MORE :

The pool was subsequently sealed off and closed “for maintenance reasons.” It was closed yesterday but it was not immediately clear this morning if it would reopen today.

‌



"All I heard was that there were problems with the water, but I don't know what happened," said a Polish tourist at the hotel.

Staff from a public health and clinical laboratory based in the Malaga TechPark, around 45 minutes from Marbella, were seen carrying out tests. As well as swimming pool and drinking water analysis, the firm also specialises in testing foods for E.coli and Salmonella.

A major chlorine leak at a hotel in Majorca in July 2022 left more than 20 people including children poisoned. The drama occurred at the Sea Club Hotel in the resort of Alcudia.

‌



A number of holidaymakers are said to have suffered symptoms including vomiting, skin irritation, and itching. Health workers administered oxygen to some of those affected in the hotel’s garden area.

Pool-related poisonings occur when chlorine concentrations and the pH are not kept at the proper levels. That leads to the formation of toxic substances that cause eye irritation, respiratory problems and gastrointestinal disorders.

And in August, 2024, a dozen people were hospitalised due to gases coming from the swimming pool storeroom area of a hotel in Menorca.

Article continues below

Seven ambulances, police, firefighters and paramedics rushed to the four-star Royal Son Bou Family Club Hotel following the incident. Staff kept around 400 guests from their rooms for nearly four hours as more than a dozen workers were rushed to the emergency room.

The incident was believed to have been caused by human error, with a gas cloud developing after hydrochloric acid was poured into one of the chlorine tanks in the pool’s machine room during a lorry delivery.

News.title: Dog with 1 eye who beat cancer just wants to know what it's like to be loved
News.content:
Dog with 1 eye who beat cancer just wants to know what it's like to be loved

Little Santa is searching for a new home in the UK after being dumped on the street and left for dead, and he just wants somebody to show him the love and kindness he craves

Meet Santa - he beat cancer but still nobody wants him

Meet Santa - an adorable dog who has endured surgery, pain and abandonment but doesn't let it stop him from showing kindness to everyone around him. But despite overcoming every obstacle life has thrown at him, there's one battle he still hasn't won - finding someone who wants him.

‌



While other rescue dogs are chosen and head off to start their new lives, Santa continues to wait, hoping each day that someone will finally see past his scars and give him the chance he's never had. The gentle dog was found abandoned on the streets of Nemea, Greece, with a devastating eye injury. The damage was beyond repair, leaving vets with no choice but to remove his eye.

‌



Just as Santa began recovering, he suffered another heartbreaking setback when he was diagnosed with penile cancer.

‌



View 2 Images Santa just wants a loving home (Image: Greek Stray ResQ)

Once again, he underwent major surgery and faced another long road to recovery.

Remarkably, Santa pulled through.

‌



Today, he is cancer-free, healthy and being cared for in a temporary foster home. But while his physical wounds have healed, he is still waiting for the one thing medicine can't provide - a forever family in the UK.

His rescuers say the sweetest part is that Santa has never stopped loving people.

Despite everything humans have put him through, he remains gentle, affectionate and calm. He adores company, loves other dogs and is happiest curled up beside someone who will simply let him be close.

‌



View 2 Images He has endured surgery, pain and abandonment (Image: Greek Stray ResQ)

Santa doesn't know he's missing an eye. He doesn't know he survived cancer. He only knows that each day ends the same way - without a family to call his own.

Greek Stray ResQ says Santa has shown incredible resilience throughout his life and believes it's finally time for his luck to change.

‌



After everything he has overcome, the charity hopes someone will look beyond his appearance and see the extraordinary, loving dog underneath.

Santa has already fought the hardest battles of his life - and now he just needs someone willing to fight for him.

Commenting on his rehoming post, one user said: "He’s gorgeous do hope someone out there can give this beautiful dog his forever home."

‌



Another user said: "What a cheeky face he has! Despite enduring so much, he still has a smile on his face! He’s hoping, he hasn’t given up."

A statement from Greek Stray ResQ reads: "Volunteers are crucial to Greek Stray ResQ and are the heartbeat of our group, providing essential support that makes our mission possible.

"We're reaching out to animal lovers across Greece, especially in the northern regions where the need is greatest, to join our cause.

‌



"Connect with like-minded individuals and be part of a community that values compassion and action. Your time can change lives!"

If you would like to re-home Santa, or any of the other dogs in Greek Stray ResQ & Support's care, visit the charity's website to find out more about the adoption process.

The plea comes after it was revealed that another two dogs who survived years in a dungeon also can't find loving homes.

Article continues below

Jimmy and Hector, two German Shepherd brothers who spent the first two years of their lives locked in a dark dungeon with no view of the outside world, are still waiting for their forever home three years on.

News.title: Chris Mason: New chancellor faces tough spending choices
News.content:
A government ends and a new government begins, determined to make a splash with its early policy announcements.

Andy Burnham has started his first full day in the job with a promise to cut VAT from household electricity bills from 1 October.

We can expect to see and hear plenty from the new prime minister and his senior ministers in the coming days, making arguments, travelling the country and trying to make an impact.

Burnham's new cabinet will meet for the first time at lunchtime.

Its appointment became something of a nocturnal affair.

At gone 22:00 BST on Monday night, there was still a minibus full of ministerial wannabes inside Downing Street waiting for their new positions to be confirmed.

One of the later posts to be filled was that of defence secretary, a role taken by Wes Streeting, whose resignation as health secretary two months ago contributed to the draining of Sir Keir Starmer's authority as prime minister.

The story of the reshuffle can best be summarised as neither of the two ministers most widely talked up as chancellor - Shabana Mahmood and Ed Miliband - getting that job, it instead going to John Healey.

And there being a pretty significant cull of the ministers closest to and most loyal to the now former prime minister: think David Lammy, Darren Jones, Peter Kyle, Lord Hermer, Steve Reed and Rachel Reeves â albeit Reeves, I am told, was offered a cabinet post but turned it down.

News.title: Man due in court charged with murder of Ann Widdecombe
News.content:
In a statement read outside New Scotland Yard, Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said: "I want to make it very clear that our investigation into [Kerry], determining his motivations and any wider activity he may have been involved in is continuing."

"As with all murder investigations, understanding the 'why' is a key part of our enquiries," he said, adding that it was "a particularly intensive and complex investigation".

Taylor said it remained the case that investigators were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

He added that counter terrorism teams have gathered "a huge amount of information" over the last week, leading to more than 800 lines of enquiry.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

Frank Ferguson, of the Crown Prosecution Service's (CPS) special crime and counter terrorism division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked closely with the police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses."

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial," Ferguson said.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

Widdecombe's career in politics spanned decades.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

She later represented South West England as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for the Brexit Party and in 2023 she joined Reform UK as a party spokeswoman.

Days after Widdecombe's death, mourners gathered in Haytor Vale to remember the 78-year-old.

News.title: Is UK facing drought for second summer in a row?
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995.

England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

Very little rainfall is forecast through this week for most places, with only a few light showers possible, mainly close to coasts.

As we head through the second half of summer, what are the longer range predictions, and are we heading into drought for the second summer in a row?

News.title: Watch: 'My flat was turned into a brothel,' landlord tells BBC Panorama
News.content:
A BBC Panorama investigation has uncovered how organised crime gangs are exploiting the UK's private rental market - targeting properties to take over and use for their operations.

Among those featured in a new documentary is landlord and property developer Craig Shepheard, who discovered his flat was being used by a prostitution ring, run by a network in Brazil.

BBC Panorama reporter Hazel Martin also found that criminals are using fake IDs to get rental agreements.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
A Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 40 nautical miles south of Plymouth on Monday.

The Royal Navy monitored the exercise and is continuing to "track the vessel's activity closely", a Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said.

The Russian frigate, Neustrashimy, was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

Prior to opening fire, the BBC was also told that the Russian warship informed the Royal Navy Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to conduct gunnery activity.

The Russian warship requested that that HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did. The Russian live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months. UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles (37km) off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they were "not on a collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling

News.title: Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble
News.content:
Argentina will face an investigation into the ugly scenes at the end of the World Cup final, Fifa has confirmed.

Fifa's disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at MetLife stadium.

Any player or coach involved in the fracas could face suspension, while the Argentine Football Association (AFA) may also be fined.

Following their 1-0 defeat on Sunday, members of the Argentina team and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players as they began to celebrate their World Cup success.

Nahuel Molina, Leandro Paredes, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all appeared to be involved.

It was incorrectly reported on Fifa's commentator information system that Paredes had been sent off by referee Slavko Vincic for pushing Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat.

Paredes' red card was deleted shortly afterwards and Fifa has confirmed to BBC Sport that no disciplinary action was taken at the time.

Argentina had already had one player dismissed, with Enzo Fernandez receiving a second yellow card in second-half stoppage time.

Fifa had already begun the process of potential disciplinary action against Argentina after their players held a banner in support of their country's claims to the Falkland Islands following the 2-1 semi-final win against England.

News.title: UK government borrowing lower than expected in June
News.content:
The UK government borrowed slightly less than expected in June, according to official figures published as new prime minister Andy Burnham began setting out measures to cut living costs for households.

Borrowing - the difference between spending and income from taxes - was Â£16bn last month, Â£7.9bn lower than June last year, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

Separate figures also showed the unemployment rate was unchanged between March and May, with the ONS saying the labour market was "relatively steady".

However while the borrowing figures were better than forecast the ONS said total debt remained near Â£3 trillion, which is close to the annual value of the entire UK economy.

Borrowing for June was slightly below the Â£16.3bn that had been predicted by the government's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said June's slightly lower than expected borrowing figure was "a rare piece of good news" for the new prime minister and his new chancellor John Healey.

However, she added: "Overall, there's no escaping the fact that the public finances are fragile and that there is limited scope for extra borrowing."

So far in the current financial year, borrowing has reached a total of Â£57.6bn. While this is down Â£3.7bn from the same period last year, it is Â£2.7bn above the OBR's forecast.

Burnham and Healey have both pledged to stick to former chancellor Rachel Reeves' fiscal rules on spending and borrowing. although the new prime minister said on Monday he would use "any flexibility within them" to help with policy changes.

In a statement released on Monday, Healey said "fiscal credibility is the bedrock for economic stability and for national security".

June's borrowing figure was helped by higher revenues from income tax and VAT, while interest payments on inflation-linked debt fell.

The government paid Â£11.8bn in debt interest payments in June, which was nearly a third lower than the same point last year.

However, it was still the fourth highest total for June on record, the ONS said.

Meanwhile, the latest survey of the labour market showed the unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.9%.

Growth in regular earnings - which excludes bonuses - remained unchanged, rising at an annual pace of 3.4% in the March to May period.

However, the ONS noted that regular wage growth in the private sector fell below 3% for the first time since 2020.

Yaelâ¯Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said the "subdued" wage growth made it more likely that the Bank of England would keep interest rates on hold at 3.75% when it meets next week.

"Weak hiring activity is continuing to weigh on workers' bargaining power, limiting upward pressure on wages," she added.

"Workers are also set to see a renewed squeeze on living standards during the second half of the year as higher energy costs feed through to household bills."

News.title: Northern Ireland's deputy first minster was 'floored' by news of Donaldson arrest
News.content:
Northern Ireland's deputy first minster says she was "completely floored" when she first heard of the arrest and charges of former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson over historical sex abuse.

In June, he was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

Emma Little-Pengelly said that people who worked alongside Donaldson over the past 20 years are "floored, shocked and utterly repulsed".

On Friday, it emerged Donaldson is to appeal his conviction.

After the former DUP leader was found guilty, a BBC Spotlight investigation reported on the double life of Donaldson.

The programme heard from former senior police officers and politicians who spoke about behaviour they described as hypocritical and which put Donaldson in danger of being compromised by his political opponents.

Speaking to the BBC's Red Lines podcast, Little-Pengelly said those reports should not take away from the scale of the crimes that he has been found guilty of.

"He's been convicted of being a paedophile and a rapist, and yes, there's all of these other allegations, but they absolutely pale into insignificance of that," she said.

"The focus should always be on the fact that he's been convicted of being a rapist and a paedophile, and that the victims of that have gone through a terrible ordeal to get justice."

News.title: Monkey abandoned in laundry bag on London bus
News.content:
A marmoset monkey has been rescued by animal welfare officers after being found abandoned inside a laundry bag on a bus in north-west London.

The female primate was discovered by a driver on the route 302 bus when it arrived at Kensal Rise on Friday morning, the RSPCA said.

A passenger with a buggy had been unable to move down the bus because the bag was blocking the luggage bay. When the driver moved it, the monkey began chirping and jumping inside.

A spokesperson for the charity said the marmoset was trapped inside a small, metal bird cage wrapped in a chequered plastic bag. She was left with a piece of apple but was stressed and dehydrated.

News.title: Does Scotland have the 'game changer' helicopters it needs to fight wildfires?
News.content:
A devastating wildfire burning in the Cairngorms has entered its seventh day, as helicopters battle to stop the spread of the flames.

Two specialist helicopters have been "invaluable" for waterbombing hard-to-reach areas, the Cairngorms National Park Authority says.

But the flames were allowed to torch the landscape for nearly two days before they arrived on the scene around Glenmore Forest Park.

There's been vocal frustration from some local people, who believe the wildfire might have been brought under control if specialist air support had been called in sooner.

Why the delay? Do Scotland's firefighters have the aerial resources they need to tackle the growing threat of wildfires?

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Tributes to Kevin Keegan 'will never be enough'
News.content:
Fans around Newcastle have paid tribute to Kevin Keegan after news broke of the former footballer's death at age 75.

Although not from the city, Geordies claim Keegan as one of their own thanks to the influential stints he had as both player and manager.

Even Sunderland fan, Eddie, whose wife Brenda supports Newcastle, said: "He's a legend isn't he? Red and white, black and white it doesn't matter."

Flowers have been laid at St James' Park as supporters flock to the ground to pay their respects.

Keegan first came to Newcastle as a player at the start of the 1982-83 season and helped the club towards promotion to the First Division.

He announced his retirement at the end of the following season and famously left St James' Park in a helicopter following his testimonial match.

News.title: Ofcom launches investigation into Married at First Sight UK
News.content:
Married at First Sight UK is facing renewed pressure after the broadcast regulator launched an official investigation into the hit Channel 4 reality TV show.

In a statement on Monday, Ofcom said it was investigating "a fairness and privacy complaint" about the prime-time show.

In May, a BBC Panorama investigation revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show - allegations the men involved deny.

An Ofcom fairness or privacy complaint can be lodged by individuals who participated in TV or radio programmes. Complaints like these usually relate to claims of being treated unfairly or having unwarranted infringements of privacy on programmes.

It is understood the watchdog is considering a complaint of unjust or unfair treatment from a cast member of Married at First Sight UK.

At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: 11 best proseccos for all budgets, taste tested by a wine expert
News.content:
Sign up to our free weekly newsletter for insider tips and product reviews from our shopping experts 

From the Veneto region of Italy, prosecco is one of the UK’s most popular wines. It gained attention in the late 2010s, thanks to its low price point, with the best proseccos consistently tasting fresh and fruity.

Traditionally, prosecco is made from the glera grape, which holds a bubble really well and always stays fizzy. Most of the prosecco we enjoy in the UK is made using the tank method, where wine is put into tanks to be carbonated, ensuring more control over the wines and preserving the fresh fruity flavours.

While this sounds fairly straightforward, things can become a little more confusing when consulting the labels. If you see spumante on a bottle, expect a high level of fizz. Frizzante, on the other hand, is lightly sparkling and is closer to a pet nat. It’s also worth noting that extra dry is sweeter than a brut, but you’ll get the most sweetness dry or demi-sec styles.

Prosecco has different appellations of quality too, with valdobbiadene being the highest and best quality. The quality is often reflected in the price, with bottles available for around £20.

The best proseccos for 2025 are:

How I tested

I tried and tested bottles across a range of price points to find the best fizz of the year ( Lily Thomas/The Independent )

Every bottle of prosecco was refrigerated before opening and tasted within a few minutes of opening, at around 6C. When testing, I sipped each prosecco out of the same glass (a large glass, not a flute, to best observe the aromas) and assessed the taste (flavour, balance and concentration), smell, appearance, and value for money.

The UK has seen a record-breaking summer so far, with the mercury breaking 30C for at least 12 days in a row this month as part of the latest heatwave.

While some stretches of Wales and the south west of England remain in a heatwave, temperatures appear to be cooling down for most parts of the country.

Temperatures have dropped to the low twenties and late teens further north, ending the third heatwave for many parts of England and Scotland.

Many Brits may already be asking when the next heatwave could be on the cards, whether they are preparing to bask in the sunshine or check how soon they need to invest in an air conditioning unit.

open image in gallery Parts of the UK are experiencing heatwave conditions still on Monday while temperatures have gone down for many ( Met Office )

Heatwave conditions are met when a location records a period of at least three consecutive days with daily maximum temperatures meeting or exceeding the heatwave temperature threshold, which varies by UK county between 25C and 28C.

ITV’s weather service has predicted that another heatwave could brew at the start of August, remarking on an area of high pressure building in the first weekend similar to the type of weather seen earlier this month.

The BBC weather service meanwhile remarked that a temperatures were expected to remain above average during late July and August, so further heatwaves could not be ruled out.

The Met Office told The Independent that there are no signs in their forecast at the moment of a widespread heatwave, but there was time for another one to develop.

open image in gallery The heatwave threshold varies across the country between 25 and 28C ( Met Office )

The forecaster’s midterm predictions for between 25 July and 3 August show that the weather could be changeable with some rain spreading southeast across part of the UK at the start, with sunny spells interspersed.

Towards the term of the month, the Met Office is already seeing hints of high pressure returning to resume the dry conditions much of England and Wales has seen.

“Winds will be mostly light or moderate, but occasionally fresh or strong around some coasts, mainly in the north. Temperatures will be near or above normal, warmest in the south, and perhaps becoming very warm again by the start of August,” the forecast read.

It comes after the forecaster warned last week that the extreme climate conditions seen by Brits this summer are set to become the new normal.

open image in gallery The Met Office has warned these extreme climate conditions could become the new norm ( Getty )

Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, said: “2025 was the UK’s warmest year on record, the sixth time this record has been broken in the 21st Century so far. The last four years are all in the top five warmest years.

“With warming at around 0.25C per decade since the 1980s, it seems likely this record will be broken again in a matter of years.”

There have already been 28 days in 2026, consecutive and non-consecutive, when 30C has been exceeded somewhere in the UK: seven in May, eight in June and 13 in July.

The record for the number of 30C-plus days in a calendar year is 34, which was set in 1995.

Met Office forecast for the next five days:

This Evening and Tonight:

Rather cloudy this evening and tonight in the north, with some light rain or drizzle towards windward coasts and hills. Dry elsewhere with clear spells and feeling a little warmer than the previous night.

Tuesday:

Largely dry with sunny spells for many, although there will be some showery light rain at times across northern coasts. Feeling warm in the sunshine, especially in the south.

Outlook for Wednesday to Friday:

Staying settled through the end of the week with patchy cloud and the odd shower in the north. Feeling warm or very warm in the sunshine and light winds.

News.content:

Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, recently announced plans to measure testosterone levels in US soldiers with a promise of “ensuring you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”. Soldiers found to have low testosterone would be offered treatment, although accepting it would remain voluntary.

The announcement has reignited debate about testosterone, masculinity and performance. Here’s what testosterone can – and can’t – tell us about men’s health.

Testosterone is one of the most useful indicators of men’s health, but it is not routinely checked during health screening. Although it is best known for its role in reproduction, testosterone also helps keep muscles and bones healthy and plays an important role in metabolism. Large studies have found that men with lower testosterone levels are more likely to develop obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease. They are also more likely to become frail, report a poorer quality of life and die earlier than men with “normal” testosterone levels.

Testosterone also declines gradually with age. However, this natural decline is usually small and, in otherwise healthy men, often does not cause medical problems until much later in life.

Far greater reductions are typically seen in men with obesity, type 2 diabetes and other chronic diseases, meaning testosterone deficiency often reflects unhealthy ageing rather than ageing alone – and the relationship runs both ways. Chronic disease can lower testosterone, while testosterone deficiency may itself contribute to poorer metabolic and physical health.

Testosterone replacement can improve lean muscle mass and bone density ( AP )

This is why testosterone is such a valuable biomarker. A low result may be a sign that something has changed in the body. But deciding what counts as a “normal” level is not simple. One man’s normal testosterone level may be much lower than another’s. So comparing a man’s current level with his previous results could be more useful than comparing it with a standard population range. This is one reason why checking testosterone more often could be useful.

The blood test itself is straightforward. The challenge is deciding what the result actually means. A testosterone test can provide useful information about a man’s health. But on its own, it cannot show how capable someone is as a soldier, who needs treatment or whether raising testosterone above an individual’s natural level would improve their performance.

Any screening programme would also need to consider female service personnel. Testosterone is important in women too, but levels are around tenfold lower than in men and cannot simply be interpreted using the same approach. Women’s testosterone levels need to be assessed differently, using their own reference ranges and medical guidelines.

The military – a different population

Active-duty military personnel are generally healthier than the wider population, with lower rates of obesity and metabolic disease. However, testosterone concentrations in this group may be influenced by factors specific to military life, including prolonged physical training, inadequate recovery, disrupted sleep and psychological stress. The important question is not simply whether testosterone is low, but why it is low.

Crucially, testosterone should not be viewed as a simple measure of military capability. A soldier’s performance depends on many factors, including physical fitness, decision-making, resilience, mental health and the conditions they are working in. Testosterone is only part of the picture.

This does not mean testosterone has no role in performance. In men with genuine testosterone deficiency, testosterone replacement therapy can improve lean muscle mass and bone density, and may improve aspects of muscle strength, physical function and quality of life.

However, evidence that raising testosterone above an individual’s natural range improves performance in otherwise healthy men remains weak. Treating a medical deficiency is very different from trying to boost performance.

About the author Daniel Kelly is a Senior Lecturer in Biochemistry at Sheffield Hallam University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

One of the most important distinctions in this debate is the difference between identifying low testosterone and treating it. Hegseth says any treatment would remain voluntary.

Some experts worry that testing soldiers could encourage the belief that a lower result requires correction – particularly in younger and otherwise healthy men. In an environment where physical capability and resilience are highly valued, simply being told they have lower testosterone could make some soldiers feel they should seek treatment, even when there is no clear medical reason.

Hegseth’s announcement also reflects a wider change in how people talk about testosterone, moving beyond its traditional medical role and into broader conversations around ageing, masculinity, performance and optimisation. This comes as regulatory views on testosterone therapy have also evolved.

Following a landmark study, the US Food and Drug Administration removed previous warnings on testosterone drugs about the risk of heart disease and stroke, while more recent proposed label updates have focused on updating advice about age-related testosterone decline and prostate health.

These changes should reassure men who genuinely need testosterone treatment. But they do not mean testosterone is a cure-all for better health or improved performance. Safe treatment is not the same as appropriate treatment. If low testosterone reflects poor sleep, excessive training, psychological stress or an underlying health problem, addressing those causes may be more beneficial than simply increasing testosterone levels.

Ultimately, Hegseth’s proposal highlights an important scientific question. Testosterone is a valuable indicator of men’s health and may deserve a bigger role in routine health checks. But it is only one piece of a much bigger picture. A blood test can show that something has changed, but it cannot explain why. It cannot, on its own, show how well someone will perform or whether they will need treatment. Those decisions require expert doctors to look at the whole person, not just a single test result.

Andy Burnham has scrapped VAT on household electricity bills from October in his first major measure to tackle the cost of living crisis since becoming prime minister.

The government said the cut will save the typical household £45 a year from 1 October by cutting VAT on domestic electricity from five per cent to zero.

Unveiling the policy on his first full day in office, Mr Burnham said the tax cut would give families “breathing space” after years of pressure from rising living costs.

For the latest updates as Andy Burnham becomes prime minister, follow The Independent’s live blog

“Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living,” he said.

“That needs to change. I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that's what I'm announcing on my second day as prime minister. We're taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people's pockets and bring back hope.”

The announcement marks the first major economic intervention by the new Labour government following Mr Burnham's arrival in Downing Street on Monday, when he pledged to tackle the cost of living crisis, bring key utilities back into public ownership and end rough sleeping.

Here’s what you need to know about Mr Burnham’s plan to cut energy bills:

What the energy bill VAT cut means for households

The measure is expected to cut £45 from Ofgem’s final energy price cap of the year, which comes into effect for October to December.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to cut VAT from energy bills from October ( PA Wire )

The cap is the maximum amount suppliers can charge for each unit of energy to households on a standard variable tariff. It is expressed as an annual bill for an average home.

This means that the savings passed on to households from the VAT cut to energy bills will vary. One of the key factors will be usage, with those using more energy actually set to save more on their bills due to paying proportionally more VAT.

The government has said energy suppliers will be required to pass the VAT reduction on to all domestic customers, including those on fixed-price tariffs, as happened when previous energy bill reductions were introduced.

The measure will apply across England, Scotland and Wales, while Northern Ireland, which has a separate energy market, will receive equivalent funding through the devolved administration.

How much will it cost the government?

The Treasury said the VAT cut would cost around £850m this financial year and would be funded by cancelling the government's planned Digital ID programme, which had been expected to cost £1.8bn over the next three years.

However, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) highlighted in November that the cost of the Digital ID scheme was “unfunded”, as it was based on savings from departmental budgets not yet identified.

New chancellor John Healey said the measure would offer immediate help ahead of the winter, commenting: “For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living”.

open image in gallery New chancellor John Healey said the measure would offer immediate help ahead of the winter ( PA Wire )

“Today's energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills, and provide some reassurance this winter.

“This measure is funded this year from cancelling the Digital ID programme, and it will help bring down inflation while supporting households in every postcode.”

Officials estimate removing VAT from electricity bills will shave around 0.10 percentage points off CPI inflation and around 0.14 percentage points from the Retail Prices Index.

Does the change apply to businesses?

Small businesses eligible for domestic energy VAT relief that are not VAT-registered, along with charities and residential care homes qualifying for the reduced rate, will also benefit.

Unlike targeted support schemes, removing VAT benefits all households, although larger electricity users will see the biggest cash savings because they consume more power. Ministers argued that many vulnerable households, including those relying on electricity-powered medical equipment, would also gain from the measure.

The announcement builds on last year's Budget, when ministers removed nearly £150 of costs from household energy bills as part of efforts to curb inflation.

Kevin Mountford, co-founder of savings platform Raisin UK, said the move would be welcomed by households seeking greater financial certainty.

“Our 2026 Money Confidence Index found that over half of Britons feel stressed about their finances, while nearly half are either not confident or only slightly confident when planning their financial future,” he said.

“Greater clarity around tax, public spending and the government's economic priorities will therefore be important. Prolonged uncertainty risks making it even harder for people to feel confident about their financial decisions.”

The VAT cut is expected to take effect in time for the next Ofgem energy price cap from October, with ministers indicating that any further cost-of-living measures will be considered in the autumn Budget alongside updated forecasts from the OBR.

Chinese astronomers are planning to crash a spacecraft into an asteroid by 2030 in a test of methods of defend the Earth from potentially cataclysmic space rocks.

Nasa’s 2022 Dart test successfully shifted the asteroid Dimorphos onto a slightly altered path around the Sun. The Chinese mission instead aims to directly alter the orbit of a 30m-wide asteroid and break apart its structure.

Researchers say such asteroids could potentially threaten our civilisation if they collide with the Earth.

The impact of a 1908 meteor in Tunguska flattened large swathes of Siberian forest, while the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor airburst injured some 1,500 people.

Chinese researchers intend to smash a spacecraft directly onto a small near-Earth asteroid, known as the 2015 XF261, which circles the Sun in an orbit similar to the Earth’s and is set to fly relatively close to the planet around 2030, making it an ideal candidate for the test.

If the collision is successful, they will monitor how much it changes the asteroid's orbit around the Sun.

open image in gallery A TV at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral shows the final images from the Dart test ( AFP/Getty )

The Chinese project, unlike the Dart mission, involves launching two spacecraft at once, according to a new study that is currently under review by the Journal of Deep Space Exploration. The Chinese would also attempt to strike a solid asteroid, again unlike the Dart mission, which hit a "rubble pile" space rock.

“Dart was the first to demonstrate asteroid deflection by kinetic impact in space but it did not directly change an asteroid’s orbit around the Sun relative to Earth, making it different from a real planetary defence scenario,” researchers from the China National Space Administration note in the new study.

One of the spacecraft will slam onto the asteroid at over 26 times the speed of sound while the other will observe the impact before, during and afterwards from a safe distance.

The second probe will monitor the asteroid for years afterwards and beam images back to the Earth.

It will carry cameras, spectrometers, and dust detectors to help crack long-standing mysteries about asteroids such as the nature of their surface rocks, gravity, density, internal layering, and any hidden minerals.

open image in gallery Artist’s impression of the aftermath of spacecraft crashing onto an asteroid ( Nasa )

The two spacecraft will be launched together and separate soon after leaving the Earth, scientists say.

The final impact manoeuvres of the spacecraft will happen autonomously, since relying on signals from the Earth would take too long.

The findings, researchers hope, will help create the most detailed picture ever made of a small asteroid.

“Such missions would provide an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the internal structure, composition, and mechanical properties of near-Earth asteroids,” the study notes.

One major challenge, according to the study, is finding the target asteroid. 2015 XF261 has been observed only 74 times in the past decade.

News.title: I tested Charlotte Tilbury vs Urban Decay setting sprays in a heatwave, here’s which is best
News.content:
If your make-up has a habit of sliding off by lunchtime, a good setting spray can make all the difference, especially in warmer weather. For more than a decade, Urban Decay’s all nighter setting spray has been a holy grail product that’s achieved cult status for its staying power, whilst Charlotte Tilbury’s airbrush flawless setting spray has quickly gained a similar reputation, with its ability to set, hydrate and blur.

With temperatures soaring this summer, I put both setting sprays to the test to see which one could keep my make-up intact through sweaty commutes, a full day at the office and evening plans.

Most make-up setting sprays, like these two, work through a polymer dissolved in a solvent. When you spray it on your face, the solvent evaporates, leaving behind a polymer “film” that locks in make-up and provides some water resistance. The ingredient can also diffuse your make-up slightly to make it look more blended.

So far, so similar. Both promise up to 16 hours of wear and waterproof performance, but which one actually delivers? I tested them side by side to find out.

If you’ve already got your eye on Charlotte Tilbury’s airbrush flawless setting spray, now’s an excellent time to try it with up to 45 per cent off Charlotte Tilbury icon kits, plus free gifts if you spend more than £200. The setting spray is included in a number of kits, including this duo that comes with full-size and mini products for £39 (worth £54, Charlottetilbury.com).
