Sports.title: A big red speaker, Louis Vuitton trophy trunks and a tattoo bet – how Spain celebrated World Cup win
Sports.content:
On the night that Spain won their first World Cup in 2010, Rodrigo Hernández was on camp somewhere lost in the woods of Connecticut. He had been canoeing when the selección beat Germany in the semi-final, upset to have missed it, and for the final he convinced one of the supervisors to let him watch, alone, on a mini-laptop in the hut where the staff slept. When Andrés Iniesta scored the winning goal in the 116th minute, he ran off screaming, doing laps of the lake. He was 14.

On the night that Spain won their second World Cup 16 years later, Rodrigo Hernández was back in the US, not so far from there. When Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the 106th minute, he ran off screaming in a straighter line and accompanied this time: towards the corner where his other family were. And then, when it ended, when the fighting finished too, he collected the trophy, pausing just long enough for Donald Trump to leave centre stage before lifting it, his timing perfect even here.

It wasn’t the only trophy he had, but those could be handed over and this could not. By the time Rodri departed at 9.38pm eastern time, the last man out of the dressing room at the New Jersey New York Stadium, he couldn’t carry them all: walking with him, just ahead, Ladis had to lend a hand. A football team is never just the players, nor even just the coaches. When he departed the dressing room nine minutes earlier, the same happened for Pau Cubarsí. Nuria helped him, their boy: just 19, looking like a kid down here in the stadium in real life but not on the pitch where he’s a leader. Luis de la Fuente was accompanied by Paloma.

Rodri came with the trophy for the tournament’s best player too. Cubarsí had the young player award, Unai Simón the Golden Glove. They also had two World Cups, every Spain player did: a replica of their own in a black Louis Vuitton trophy trunk, not easy to fit under an arm, and another in Lego. Rodri had three: both of those and the cup. They departed laden down, great big plastic bags full, pieces of the history they made. Shirts, in red and yellow and blue and white. Balls, boots. They had cut the net and taken pieces of that too. They had been given rings, NBA style.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Merino holds a replica of the trophy in the dressing room after Spain’s triumph. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Before the final began, Marc Cucurella had sneaked off towards the touchline and buried a coin in the pitch, like that other left-back Joan Capdevila had done in 2010. Iniesta had been out there, his name chanted, as he showed the cup to the stands. After it, Sergio Ramos brought it back again. Dashing out, excitedly kissing it, he placed it on the plinth for this new generation, achieving the impossible in emulating them, to go and collect. One by one they passed, Borja Iglesias and Lamine Yamal among the most evasive in shaking Trump’s hand, until Rodri took the trophy and lifted it to the sky.

Nico Williams went to find his mum in the front row and handed over his medal. Lamine Yamal had made his way across to Lionel Messi, who was sitting but who stood for him, embracing the boy in the bath, the successor: a rite of passage, an image that will be for ever. The actor Javier Bardem was hugging Iglesias, his new friend and idol. Ferran Torres was talking about a “great liberation”: he had suffered, felt how cruel this game could be, how people could be too, but he said: “Destiny is written: God gives to those who deserve.” And Keyne was, well, Keyne. In the dressing room – the same one, Cucurella noted, where he had been at last year’s Club World Cup – the champagne was cracked open.

It was brief – the flight to Spain was scheduled for 11pm and they wanted to get back – and soon they were on their way again. Behind the screen, along the corridor they came, way down in the depths and the half-light of the stadium. The president, the staff, all the players; the many, many people who made this so. Iglesias carried a bag so big it was like he was a student taking his washing home, and he was struggling to stop that box slipping. In the other hand he wheeled a big red speaker. Now playing: Dirty Cash (Money Talks) by PAWSA & Adventures of Stevie V. Lamine Yamal came, via the anti-doping room, in orange sunglasses, four chains, black cap on backwards. He didn’t wear his medal, but most did, thick discs round their necks. And commemorative shirts, ordered up in case.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Argentina’s Lionel Messi embrace after the match. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Back in Dallas, at a celebration after the semi-final victory, someone had joked to the federation president, Rafael Louzán, that the shirts should say world champions on one side and Finalissima winners on the other, two trophies in one. Tempting, but these bore just the one trophy, “Spain 26” on the back. The war in the Middle East had prevented the Finalissima from going ahead in Doha as scheduled in March and every time another option was offered, Argentina said no, the impression that of a team, a federation, running scared. “Good job we didn’t play,” Emi Martínez had said then, after they scraped past Mauritania in a hastily arranged friendly that filled the hole. “If we had played [Spain] like this …”

Something like this might have happened. Not just because Argentina played like this but because Spain made them play like this. “We gave them a battering,” came the verdict from one of those heading out of the dressing room. This wasn’t just a win; this was more. Has a 1-0 ever been as dominant? There was a moment late in the game, still at 0-0, when the Spain fans chanted: “Look at them! Look at them! How they shit themselves!” and they weren’t wrong. Argentina could not get out all game; as Spain turned the screw, still less, the goal seemingly inevitable; the surprise was that it hadn’t come yet, that there would be just one. When it did it came as a liberation but also an act of irresistible logic.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scores the only goal of the World Cup final. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

Torres’s shot was Spain’s 20th. Argentina didn’t manage one until the 115th minute. They didn’t manage any on target, all game. Across 900 World Cup games for which Opta has the stats, it is only the third time that a team has failed to shoot. And this in the final. They had done to Argentina what they did to France and to everyone, choking them. For the whole tournament Spain had an xG against of 0.3 per game. “If my gloves could talk, they would say they didn’t have much work to do,” Simón said. “Many teams depend too much on the back line,” Aymeric Laporte said, but not Spain.

This was the triumph of a collective, of a group; it ended in New York, but it was built in Chattanooga and beyond, over 51 days. It is the triumph of an idea, a conviction and of a coach too: a victory for De la Fuente and the system he leads and the system that made him. He began his coaching career at Deportivo Alavés in the third tier, where he lasted just 11 games. It was November 2011 when he left and he has not had a club job since. For months, no one returned his calls. He was on the dole for a year and a half until he saw an advert for a job: the Spanish federation was looking for a coach for the youth system. He started in the under-17s. He won the European Championship with the under-19s and the under-21s. Then he won it with the senior side; now he has won the World Cup.

“They asked me what there is left to win; we said the next game in September because they’re insatiable,” he insisted afterwards. Simón said: “The manager is outstanding; he has been our leader.” Cucurella, meanwhile, was in trouble. He had promised that if Spain won the World Cup, he would get a tattoo of De la Fuente’s face and now he had to decide where to put it to minimise the damage, the flight home an opportunity to think. Not least to think what a fool he had been.

View image in fullscreen Marc Cucurella is to have a tattoo of Luis de la Fuente’s face after Spain’s win. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

“I said: ‘You made a bad mistake’,” the coach joked. “But it’s not like I am so horrendously ugly that you have to put it somewhere it can’t be seen. And they are men of their word.” For all the laughs, that final line really mattered, and he knows: 10 of them played with him at junior level. The first title he ever won was the Under-19 Euros in 2015. In the middle of his midfield that day was Rodrigo Hernández.

Eleven years on, 16 since he watched Spain’s first World Cup win, motivation sought and identification found in what they achieved, Rodri was back in the US. The embodiment of that idea, a player who approached perfection here, no one played more passes nor made more tackles than him. No one had his weight either, the captain leading Spain out and leading them back too. Like so many of his teammates at a tournament that was an expression of justice and vindication too, he had suffered for this, a torn cruciate ligament overcome.

“It doesn’t matter if you fall, there’s always a reason to get up again,” he said and now he had it right here in his hands. It was 9.40pm when he boarded the bus bound for the airport, carrying the actual World Cup.

Sports.title: Argentina players face bans as Fifa opens investigation into World Cup final brawls
Sports.content:
Fifa has opened an investigation into the violent scenes that followed Spain’s World Cup final win on Sunday, with several Argentina players facing bans.

Nahuel Molina appeared to strike Spain’s captain Rodri in the stomach as he ran on to the pitch following the final whistle, while there was also a large melee on the halfway line, where Leandro Paredes appeared to grab Eric García by the throat before throwing Gavi to the ground.

Parades was subsequently shown a red card by the referee, Slavko Vincic, who had also sent off Enzo Fernández towards the end of normal time, as well as booking three other Argentina players and the head coach, Lionel Scaloni.

“Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the Fifa World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the Fifa Disciplinary Code (FDC), the Fifa Disciplinary Committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents,” Fifa said in a statement.

Fifa is also investigating Argentina’s conduct after their semi-final win over England, when their players celebrated with a banner proclaiming “Las Malvinas son Argentinas”, which was smuggled into the Atlanta Stadium by supporters.

Fifa prohibits players or teams making political statements, so those involved could be banned.

Sports.title: Gaza celebrates World Cup victory of Spanish team they took into their hearts
Sports.content:
The Spanish football team’s World Cup win has been celebrated in the streets of Gaza, where Spain’s support for Palestinian rights and Israel’s backing for the Argentinian team turned the competition into more than a football showdown.

Gathered at cafes and outdoor screenings, Palestinians defied the risk of Israeli attacks to cheer on a team they had taken to their hearts.

Many waving Spanish flags paid tribute to teenage star Lamine Yamal, who brought a Palestinian flag to celebrations for Barcelona’s La Liga win in May.

“Whoever raises the Palestinian flag deserves to raise the World Cup,” the Gaza al-Irada amputee football team wrote in a pre-game video message for the Spanish team.

Saadi al-Masri, 40 and captain of the amputee team in Gaza, watched the game with friends in a cafe. “I support Spain because we see it as a country that stands with the Palestinian cause and supports Palestinian rights,” he said.

View image in fullscreen Palestinians defied the risk of Israeli attacks to cheer on Spain. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

Spain has been among Europe’s most vocal critics of Israel’s war on Gaza and state-backed violence in the occupied West Bank. It is pushing for stronger European Union action over human rights violations, including suspension of a broad free trade pact.

When Israel’s defence minister attacked Yamal for raising the Palestinian flag, accusing him of “inciting hatred”, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, was quick to defend the young player.

“Lamine has only expressed the solidarity with Palestine that is felt by millions of us in Spain. Another reason to be proud of him,” he said in a social media post.

Israeli support for Argentina was led by Netanyahu, who has cultivated close ties with far-right president Javier Milei, and posted a good luck message for the team ahead of the final.

The Palestinian delegation to the United Nations responded with an image of the Spanish team, under the headline “world champions”.

Even keen fans in Gaza have struggled to keep up with matches during the World Cup. Most of the 2 million Palestinians in the territory live in tent camps after Israeli attacks destroyed their homes, with little access to power or internet connections.

Arkan al-Walaida, 23, went to internet cafes to seek out match highlights each morning during the tournament, looking for short videos on TikTok or Fifa’s official YouTube and Instagram pages.

When she found out on Monday that Spain had won, she was overwhelmed. “Honestly, I felt like I was about to cry from happiness,” she said. “We see their support as a sign of humanity.”

Al-Masri watched the match at a cafe, packed with an excited crowd. “We were very happy when the final whistle confirmed Spain’s victory,” he said, but fear of Israeli airstrikes meant there were no late-night parties.

In early July, an Israeli bomb killed Mohamed al-Wahidi, a Palestinian aid worker who organised screenings of World Cup matches in Gaza.

The strike, just before the game between Egypt and Argentina, also killed brothers aged eight and 10, and a second man. The Israeli military confirmed the attack but said it had not targeted al-Wahidi.

Sports.title: Nearly two million people join Spain’s World Cup celebrations in Madrid
Sports.content:
Almost two million Spaniards, many still bleary-eyed and feeling a little delicate after the country’s historic World Cup victory against Argentina, descended on central Madrid on Monday night to welcome the triumphant national team home.

La Roja, who beat Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey on Sunday night, were afforded the first of many heroes’ welcomes when they touched down at Madrid’s Barajas airport at 2.30pm local time on Monday.

Spain’s captain, Rodri, waved the trophy aloft as he emerged from the plane, his medal from the previous night around his neck. The team posed for a photo before heading into terminal four where hundreds of delighted fans, many in Spain strips and carrying the country’s red-and-yellow rojigualda flag, waited and hoped for a glimpse of the freshly minted champions.

Their first stop was an audience with King Felipe, Queen Letizia and their daughters, Princess Leonor and Princess Sofía, at the Zarzuela palace, northwest of Madrid, where the king paid tribute to their talent and determination.

“It’s been an epic triumph,” he said. “It’s been a privilege and a joy for the four of us to see you play in the final and to be able to celebrate with you that moment of lifting the cup, with immense thanks from all of Spain.”

Felipe also praised their fortitude, saying: “You’ve suffered, you’ve come home bruised and tired, you’ve endured some criticism, but what is all that compared with the joy of bringing the cup home?”

View image in fullscreen Thousands of Spain supporters gather at Plaza de Cibeles in Madrid on Monday. Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

The team’s next meeting was a visit to the Moncloa palace – the office and residence of the prime minister – to see Pedro Sánchez. The socialist prime minister offered the players and technical staff “massive thanks … for the game, for the effort and for the victory”.

Speaking at the Moncloa palace, Rodri said that “winning for you country is the most beautiful thing there is”. He added: “This generation grew up watching [Iker] Casillas and [Andrés] Iniesta lift the cup [in 2010] and having been able to do that today is the biggest thing you can do in football.”

The highlight for the fans – who braved the 34C evening heat – was the victory parade that wound its way from Moncloa to the Plaza de Cibeles just outside Madrid city hall. They crowded into the square, some sheltering from the sun under umbrellas, as the team approached in an open-topped bus. The central government’s delegate in Madrid put attendance along the route at around 1.8 million.

Madrid’s mayor, José Luis Martínez Almeida, told Radio Nacional de España that the capital had been working to give the team the homecoming they deserved. He also hailed the peaceful and joyous scenes that had greeted Spain’s victory on Sunday night.

View image in fullscreen Rodri carries the World Cup at Barajas airport on Monday. Photograph: Sergio R Moreno/GTRES/Shutterstock

“Even though there were thousands and thousands of people on the streets last night, there were practically no incidents in the city,” he said.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We’re getting everything ready for tonight … The thing we’re focusing on is how to celebrate and greet a team that will live for ever in our memory.”

The victory – Spain’s second men’s World Cup win after their triumph against the Netherlands in South Africa in 2010 – was seen by hundreds of thousand of Spaniards who followed the match in bars, parks, fairgrounds, bullrings, and on giant screens in the centre of Madrid. The Spanish press have hailed it as “a unique collective experience” made possible by a young team that reflects all that is best about a modern, diverse and determined country.

The win has also been enthusiastically hailed by the country’s political class.

“WE ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS!!” Sánchez wrote in a social media post. “What an amazing national squad. Thank you, team.”

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party, was equally free with the capital letters. “Well-deserved WORLD CHAMPIONS! Values, hard work, humility, and faith. You have made history. There are no limits for this team … Long live Spain!!!” he wrote on X.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, also offered his congratulations to the team for carrying “the flag of Spain so far and so high”.

The Spanish postal service, Correos, has announced the creation of a special stamp to commemorate what it called “one of the greatest achievements in the history of Spanish sport”. The red-coloured stamp will bear the word CAMPEONES and feature two stars – one for each of Spain’s World Cup victories.

Sports.title: Neuer to Neymar: 11 World Cup players who retired from international football
Sports.content:
Manuel Neuer (Germany, 40)

First participated in the World Cup in 2010 before winning the trophy four years later. Germany have had little success since and their penalty shootout defeat by Paraguay marked the end of Neuer’s international career. He initially retired after Euro 2024 but reversed that decision a few weeks before this tournament. “Despite the bitter end, I don’t regret this decision,” he said after his 23rd and final World Cup appearance. The former Germany defender Robert Huth criticised the decision to bring Neuer out of retirement: “I think the big one that really unsettles the squad was the Neuer inclusion. I think [it was] really unexpected, he came late to the table.”

Patrik Schick (Czechia, 30)

Made his World Cup debut this summer having left an impression at Euro 2020. Schick failed to score as Czechia went winless and were eliminated in the group stage. The striker announced his international retirement hours after the final group game. “Today, my national team chapter is coming to an end,” he said. The official Czechia statement paid tribute: “Thank you for every match, every goal, and the pride with which you represented the Czech Republic.”

Guillermo Ochoa (Mexico, 41)

Cemented himself as a fans’ favourite in 2014 when he kept a famous clean sheet against the World Cup hosts, Brazil. His playing time was limited this summer, but he got 12 minutes against Czechia, where he was celebrated by teammates. After full time the manager, Javier Aguirre, said: “The moment he stepped on to the pitch, it overshadowed everything else. He is a world-class legend, and I am incredibly proud of him.” Ochoa later posted: “It was the greatest privilege of my life. Thank you for believing, for always accompanying us. I love you Mexico.”

View image in fullscreen Guillermo Ochoa shows his emotions after Mexico’s exit against England. Photograph: Álex Cruz/EPA

Riyad Mahrez (Algeria, 35)

Having made one appearance at the 2014 finals, Mahrez had to wait 12 years to add to his tally. He scored two goals against Austria before Algeria were eliminated in the last 32 by Switzerland in his final game. Mahrez said: “Representing Algeria has been a dream of mine ever since I was young, to play for my country. It’s been an immense honour and a great source of pride.” A Confederation of African Football’s statement said: “You gave us memories that time can never take away. Thank you, Riyad Mahrez.”

Enner Valencia (Ecuador, 36)

The forward got six goals in as many matches across the 2014 and 2022 finals but was unable to add to that tally for an Ecuador team who lost to Mexico in the last 32. “I’ve played my last match with the national team,” he said in the tunnel after. Ecuador’s official X account showed appreciation to their record scorer: “The GOAT. Super Enner. Thank you for giving yourself to the country and representing it in the best way.”

Nicolás Otamendi (Argentina, 38)

The uncompromising defender played every minute as Argentina triumphed in Qatar, having made his World Cup debut in 2010. Playing time was harder to come by in North America, though he featured in every game bar one, having revealed his intention to retire in March. “It’s my last World Cup, from there I’ll be a fan,” he said. Otamendi’s final home match became a tribute, with Lionel Messi letting him score a penalty at La Bombonera.

Marko Arnautovic (Austria, 37)

This was the striker’s first and last World Cup. He scored twice as Austria reached the last 32, where they were defeated 3–0 by Spain. Arnautovic revealed his departure in an emotional post-match interview, saying: “Playing for Austria was the biggest highlight. It hits me that from now on I won’t see my second family any more.” In a social media post, the Austrian Football Association said: “What a career. What a character. Thank you for everything.”

Sadio Mané (Senegal, 34)

Participated in 2018 but injury ruled him out four years later. Following Senegal’s capitulation against Belgium, Mané released a statement regarding retirement via Senegalese outlet Le Quotidien – although there have been questions about its authenticity – saying: “Know that I sacrificed everything for this flag. I gave the very best of myself and I always fought fiercely for our homeland.” Pape Thiaw was asked about Mané’s retirement in January and replied: “We want to keep him as long as possible … when we say it’s his decision, it doesn’t just belong to him, he belongs to the people of Senegal, and they want to see him carry on.”

View image in fullscreen Sadio Mané has called time on his international career with Senegal. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/FIFA/Getty Images

Craig Gordon (Scotland, 43)

The goalkeeper amassed 84 caps, making his debut in 2004, but did not get off the bench at his first World Cup. “I’ve never wanted it to end, but it must,” Gordon said, calling time on his club and international career. Gordon’s spell was described as “a career unlike any other” by the Scotland national team’s social media account.

Jean Michaël Seri (Côte d’Ivoire, 35)

Made his World Cup debut in his side’s 2–0 victory over Curaçao, his 64th cap. In a social media post, the former Fulham midfielder later said: “After 11 years in the national team, and one World Cup played, I announce the end of my international career today.” Seri received a wealth of tributes below his post. “Congratulations on all that you’ve accomplished with the national team,” replied the captain, Franck Kessié. “Thank you for all these moments shared under our colors.”

Neymar (Brazil, 34)

Announced himself on the World Cup stage with two goals on debut in 2014. Restricted by injury at the current tournament, he managed 55 minutes before Brazil’s exit against Norway and announced his international retirement shortly after full time. “It started here at MetLife Stadium,” he said, referring to his debut against the US in August 2010, “and I finished here. It is now over.” Zlatan Ibrahimovic, working as a pundit for US television, said: “An amazing player, and the skill set he had was just crazy. So, sad moment for Brazilian football.”

Sports.title: Melvine Malard hungry for trophies after joining Chelsea from Manchester United
Sports.content:
Chelsea have announced the signing of the France forward Melvine Malard from Manchester United on a four-year contract. The Guardian revealed last week that a deal was close for the 26-year-old, who has left United after three seasons for about £850,000.

Malard had one year on her contract and United were keen to keep the forward. However, once it became clear Malard wanted a move United decided to sell rather than lose a high-value player on a free next summer.

It is believed United will reinvest the fee, which is a record sale for the club, into the squad, with the transfer window open until 3 September.

United have made one summer signing, the full-back Andrea Medina from Atlético Madrid, but more incomings are expected after the departures of Leah Galton, Hannah Blundell, Sienna Wareing, Millie Turner, Lisa Naalsund and Malard.

“I’m so happy because I have a plan for my life and my career, and Chelsea were a part of that plan,” Malard said. ”My objective is to become better every single day and to win trophies. I know Chelsea always have that as an objective.”

The France international played under Chelsea’s head coach, Sonia Bompastor, at Lyonnes (formerly Lyon) and was recruited to their academy by Bompastor. “I have known Sonia since I was 14 years old, so it is great to work with her again,” Malard said.

It is understood Chelsea have been tracking Malard for some time. They have lost a number of players across the forward line, with the club record-goalscorer Sam Kerr and Guro Reiten departing for Gotham FC, Catarina Macario joining San Diego Wave and Johanna Rytting Kaneryd signing for Lyonnes.

Malard is Chelsea’s third signing of the summer, after the former Arsenal full-back Katie McCabe and the forward Manaka Matsukubo, who was with North Carolina Courage.

Malard spent seven seasons at Lyonnes, winning four Champions Leagues, three league titles and two Coupes de France. Her first season with United was on loan.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Last season she scored four goals in United’s run to a first Champions League quarter-final and six times in 18 Women’s Super League games.

Liverpool have signed the Japanese attacking midfielder Mao Itamura from Feyenoord. The 19-year-old, who won the Under-20 Women’s Asian Cup in April, was the Eredivisie player of the year last season in the Netherlands. She scored eight times and provided six assists as Feyenoord qualified for European competition for the first time, their third-place finish earning a place in the Europa Cup.

Itamura is Liverpool’s fifth summer signing, after Vivien Endemann, Sara Agrez, Mari Ward and Khiara Keating.

Sports.title: Unseen footage of Lionel Messi's bizarre World Cup final pep talk goes viral as he tells upset Argentina stars to 'relax and forget everything' moments before kick-off
Sports.content:
Unseen footage of Lionel Messi's bizarre World Cup final pep talk goes viral as he tells upset Argentina stars to 'relax and forget everything' moments before kick-off

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Argentina captain Lionel Messi gave a curious message to his players just moments before their World Cup final defeat by Spain, new footage has revealed.

Spain beat the 2022 world champions 1-0 at the MetLife Stadium on Sunday, triumphing thanks to Ferran Torres' goal in extra time after dominating the ball in one of the most one-sided World Cup finals ever staged.

Argentina, who had controversially edged past Cape Verde, Egypt and Switzerland before knocking England out in the semi-finals, were heavily criticised for their aggressive tackling and dirty tactics throughout the tournament - and their World Cup campaign ended in disgrace as they became embroiled in a mass brawl with Spain's players after the final whistle.

Speculation that something was not quite right within Argentina's camp has been circulating on social media after new footage of Messi addressing his players before the final was shared to social media on Monday.

In the video, as Messi prepares to lead Argentina out holding his country's pennant flag, he turns to his players who appear strangely downbeat and gloomy and says: 'Come on, guys, stay calm, folks. Let's stay calm, guys. Let's just think about playing, stay calm. Let's forget about everything. Let's just think about playing, folks.'

The curious message has led many fans to speculate whether Argentina's camp were in the right frame of mind heading into the huge match.

Wait... what the hell , look at this vid, Enzo was crying before the game and Licha looked like he'd been crying too.Then Messi says, "Let's forget about everything." What the hell happened before the 2026 World Cup final?????????pic.twitter.com/C3RUOrKKPB — Arvin (@sozirv) July 20, 2026

Lionel Messi delivered a curious message to his Argentina stars before the World Cup final

Argentina's World Cup final defeat by Spain ended with a disgraceful brawl on the pitch

Some supporters have theorised whether Messi was telling his team-mates to forget about world football's negative perception of them throughout the tournament, amid claims that World Cup referees had favoured Argentina in decisions throughout the knockout stage.

After staging a late comeback to win 3-2 against Egypt in the last 16, opposition manager Hossam Hassan furiously accused FIFA of rigging the World Cup after a string of controversial refereeing decisions went against his side.

Switzerland were also furious at officials after their 3-1 defeat by Argentina in the quarter-finals, as forward Breel Embolo was shown a controversial second yellow card following a VAR review.

Other supporters have suggested that Argentina's stars were emotional about the prospect of playing with 39-year-old all-time great Messi for the final time at the World Cup, despite him not having officially retired yet.

Argentina reacted disgracefully to Spain's celebrations at the full-time whistle as Leandro Paredes was sent off for throttling Eric Garcia and throwing Gavi to the floor in shameful scenes.

Nahuel Molina also punched Rodri in the torso as he was running by, while Thiago Almada was involved, too.

Their emotional manager Lionel Scaloni then stormed out of his press conference in tears, saying: ‘We need time to reset and form another group like this one. It’ll be hard to recreate this one. It hurts my soul, I’m sorry.'

Responding to the video of Messi on social media, one fan posted: 'I know Spain are a quality team, but Argentina’s performance genuinely left me baffled. They looked nothing like the team we’ve come to know.

'There was no intensity, no urgency, no excitement completely different from the energy they showed in their previous games. Something felt off about that performance. I still can’t explain what I watched.'

A second fan said in a post: 'Argentina knew they couldn’t beat Spain so were trying to just make it to penalties.'

A third posted: 'Something weird is going on here. Very weird. Lionel's pep talk, Enzo's eyes, Licha's red nose… something VERY weird happened before the final.

'Neither Messi, nor De Paul, nor Paredes, nor Dibu, NO ONE is posting anything on social media. Minimally weird.'

Another conspiracy theorist added: 'At the Qatar final, they got off the bus totally unhinged, tearing through everything. Something happened, some argument with Scaloni, Tapia told them something, some FIFA sanction, I don't know.

'They were wrecked physically and mentally. I insist, something really shady went down there and we're gonna find out about it in 40 years.'

Messi was in tears at the end of the game and refused to watch Spain lift the World Cup trophy

Fans were not afraid to offer their speculative theories on social media in response to the video

Argentina also made headlines after the World Cup final defeat for refusing to watch Spain lift the trophy.

The defeated finalists collected their silver medals from FIFA supremo Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump on the stage at the MetLife Stadium but decided not to watch as Spain lifted the trophy - which is customary in finals of major tournaments.

Instead, the Argentina players, coaching team and staff walked over to the end where the majority of their fans were located and spent time gazing into the crowd with glossy eyes.

Sports.title: Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world: OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world: OLIVER HOLT

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Kevin Keegan, a kid from mining stock in South Yorkshire, a kid who started out at Scunthorpe United and went on to conquer Europe, was one of the greatest players English football has ever produced but it was the unquenchable passion that burned within him that won him such a prominent place in the hearts of the public.

Mighty Mouse, he was called as a player and it suited him. He was the little man who would never give up. He was the small guy who punched way above his weight. He was the lad who never bowed to anyone. He may have been slight of stature but he had the biggest heart that ever beat in the chest of an English footballer.

Sometimes, it feels as if time has dimmed the memory of quite what an outstanding footballer Keegan was and how he became a pioneer and a pathfinder, the first Englishman to play in a European Cup final with both English and foreign clubs, in his case Liverpool and Hamburger SV.

Sometimes it feels as if England’s mediocrity when he was at the peak of his playing career and the fame and affection he garnered in his managerial career, particularly at Newcastle United, have obscured the fact that he remains the only Englishman to have won the Ballon d’Or, the prize bestowed on the greatest player in the world each year, more than once.

Keegan won it in successive years during his time in Germany, in 1978 and 1979. For context, that puts him level with Franz Beckenbauer, Alfredo Di Stefano, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge and the Brazilian Ronaldo in the pantheon of the greats of the game. ‘I’m probably the most ordinary player to have won it twice,’ Keegan said in a recent interview.

But there was nothing ordinary about Kevin Keegan. Anybody who ever met him or ever watched him play or ever heard him giving a manager’s post-match press conference or ever saw him spending hours with fans desperate for a word or an autograph, knew that.

Liverpool, Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness

Keegan (pictured in 1977 after winning the European Cup with Liverpool) is one of the greatest players English football has ever produced

Once, after his playing career was over, I sat opposite him on a stage at Westminster Central Hall, asking him questions in an interview organised by the newspaper I worked for then. I don’t remember the questions I asked, or the answers he gave.

What I do remember is how Keegan held the audience in the palm of his hand. They were rapt. After it was over, Keegan stayed until he had fulfilled every autograph request and spoken to every man and woman who wanted a word, who wanted to say that they had talked to one of the legends of the English game.

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world. In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild and people loved him for it.

His public profile rose even more when he competed in the BBC programme Superstars, which aired in the 1970s and 80s, and featured sportsmen battling it out against each other in series of different disciplines.

‘Superstar’ has become an overused term now but if ever a man fitted that description, it was Keegan. He was box office, from head to toe. The combination of the reach of television and the dynamism of his personality made him one of football’s first new age icons.

Even in the midst of everything he achieved on the pitch, what endeared him to people, and a huge part of the gift he leaves behind for us, was his heart and soul. His passion lit up his life. He could not contain it and we loved him for it.

His passion gave us some of the landmarks we remember him for. The fight with Leeds United captain Billy Bremner at the 1974 Charity Shield that got both men sent off and saw Keegan ripping off his shirt as he left the pitch.

What a different world it was then. ‘That looked very much like a right hook by Johnny Giles,’ commentator Barry Davies said when Keegan was flattened by a sweet right hand. Keegan pleaded for leniency for Giles. A few moments later, he was trading punches with Bremner. ‘This is a side of English football we do not want to see,’ Davies opined.

Keegan was beloved in Germany after moving to Hamburger SV in 1977. He won the Ballon d'Or twice on the continent

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world

Keegan, who was born in Doncaster, had begun his career with Scunthorpe United before he was spotted and scouted by Liverpool manager Bill Shankly and established himself as the star player of the team that went on to win the European Cup, under Bob Paisley, in 1977.

That team was one of the great sides in the history of the English game. Let the names roll off your tongue: Ray Clemence, Phil Neal, Joey Jones, Tommy Smith, Ray Kennedy, Emlyn Hughes, Kevin Keegan, Jimmy Case, Steve Heighway, Ian Callaghan, Terry McDermott.

Keegan tormented the Borussia Monchengladbach captain Berti Vogts in that final in Rome and won the penalty in the 83rd minute that sealed a 3-1 victory for Liverpool and was the start of the club’s rise to being the most successful club in European competition in this country.

When Keegan moved to Hamburger SV that summer, many thought it would mark the end of Liverpool’s hegemony but they signed a player called Kenny Dalglish, who went on to emulate Keegan’s successes and more.

Then there was his bike crash in Superstars when he pedalled furiously down the main straight of an athletics track at the start of a race against Belgian footballer, Gilbert Van Binst, wobbling from side to side as he desperately tried to keep up, before crashing to the tarmac on the first bend.

It was a nasty accident. Keegan, who was close to the height of his powers as a footballer at that point, sustained cuts and grazes but he still refused to give up. The race was re-started and Keegan won. It was the show’s greatest moment.

Keegan became a hugely successful manager and is particularly adored by Newcastle fans

Keegan pictured in 1995 with famous entertainers Ant McPartlin (L) and Declan Donnelly (R)

Then there was the most famous diatribe in English football history when, feeling the hot despair of Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United closing in on the league title after they had overhauled his wonderful Newcastle United team, he snapped as he spoke to Sky Sports after an away win over Leeds United at Elland Road at the end of April 1996.

‘We’re still fighting for this title,’ Keegan almost shouted into the camera, his voice shaking with anger and his finger pointing and jabbing, ‘and he (Sir Alex Ferguson) has got to go to Middlesbrough and get something and I’ll tell you honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it.’

David Beckham has said since that when the United players watched Keegan’s rant, they knew they had won the league. They knew that Ferguson’s mind games had exploded in Keegan’s head and that the title was theirs.

But that only added to Keegan’s legend. There was something magnificently untameable about him, something beautifully unpredictable, something free and untrammelled. He was still Mighty Mouse.

And he is still adored in Newcastle. It may be, in fact, that he is adored there more than anywhere else. He is adored for the pride he brought to the city and the way he resurrected the club and for the thrill of the beautiful football the Geordies played under his management.

That team was made in his image and so it was brilliant and it was entertaining and it was breathtaking but it was also fragile. And it could not quite cope with the relentlessness of Manchester United. But every neutral was desperate for Newcastle to win the title that season. And that was mostly down to Keegan.

Keegan's 'I will love it' rant was a sign that he was cracking under the pressure of a title race with Manchester United - but it only added to his legend

In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild

There was no artifice about Keegan. He did not bother to try to hide what he was feeling. Or what he was. It was all out there, everything worn on his sleeve. He would have been the world’s worst poker player. He was not a man for keeping his counsel. Or for keeping his cool. Again, we loved him all the more for that.

Keegan always burned hot. At his unveiling as England manager in 1999, Daily Mirror journalist Nigel Clarke, who was sitting on the front row of the press conference, coughed while Keegan was speaking. Keegan became convinced that Clarke was mocking him and demanded to know why he was coughing. A long stand-off ensued.

Before a game against Sweden the same year, Keegan told Paul Scholes to ‘go out there and drop a few hand grenades’. Scholes promptly became the first England player to be sent off at Wembley after two horrendous challenges on opponents.

At the end of his short reign as England boss, Keegan was preparing his team for the final game at the old Wembley on October 7, 2000, a World Cup qualifier against Germany, and he decided he was going to play Gareth Southgate, a central defender in midfield.

On the Friday night before the game on the Saturday, the news began to leak out. I was on a Sky programme called Hold the Back Page, hosted by Brian Woolnough and Jimmy Hill, and we began the show by discussing the Southgate plan with varying degrees of scepticism.

Keegan was incandescent. He asked the FA to phone Sky to demand that the programme be taken off the air. Sky, obviously, could not accede to that request and the show continued as normal. To no one’s great surprise, the Southgate experiment did not go well.

Keegan managed England from February 1999 to October 2000 but resigned from his post

Keegan scored 40 goals in 113 games for Hamburg, between 1977 and 1980

England lost the game 1-0 and Keegan was booed by a section of England fans as he walked off the pitch. He stopped to remonstrate with some of them at the entrance to the tunnel. When he reached the dressing rooms, he summoned FA officials, retreated to the quiet of the toilets, and promptly resigned. The FA tried to talk him out of it but he would not reconsider.

Keegan had been a sublime player at Liverpool and Hamburger SV and then, in the late summer of his career with Southampton and Newcastle. I say late summer deliberately. There was never anything autumn about Keegan. His football did not yellow and fade. After his last game for Newcastle, a testimonial against Liverpool, he was lifted from the St James’s Park pitch in a helicopter.

‘Auf Wiedersehen, Kev,’ a message on the scoreboard at the Gallowgate End read that day in May 1984. And now, it is time to bid him farewell once more. Auf Wiedersehen, Kev, and thank you.

Sports.title: MICHAEL OWEN: I was nervous about Kevin Keegan's arrival at Newcastle in 2008 after our spell together with England, but I was so happy to be so wrong. He was the warmest, kindest, most genuine person I've known in football - and a head tennis master!
Sports.content:
MICHAEL OWEN: I was nervous about Kevin Keegan's arrival at Newcastle in 2008 after our spell together with England, but I was so happy to be so wrong. He was the warmest, kindest, most genuine person I've known in football - and a head tennis master!

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

There are some people in football you respect because of what they achieved. There are others you admire because of who they are. Kevin Keegan deserved both.

When I heard the news of his passing this week, my mind immediately went back to how our relationship changed over the years. I first played under Kevin for England in 1999. We had some enjoyable moments, but, if I'm honest, it wasn't the happiest period of my career. I'd just suffered my first serious injury and I wasn't quite the player I'd been a couple of years earlier. Kevin's England reign didn't really click, either for him or for me, and I never truly felt he believed in me in the same way Glenn Hoddle had. We got on perfectly well, but there wasn't a particularly close bond.

So when Newcastle announced Kevin was returning as manager in 2008, I had mixed emotions. Like everyone in the mid-90s, I'd watched from afar as he'd transformed the club during the Entertainers era. The football, the atmosphere, the connection with the supporters, it was iconic. But privately I wondered whether we'd be a good fit. I've never been so delighted to be so wrong.

From the moment he walked through the door, everything changed. He moved me into a different position slightly deeper, made me captain, trusted me and spoke to me constantly. I also knew he was pushing for me to sign a new contract because he wanted me to stay. I went from apprehension to outright love and admiration for the man and the manager. It made me understand why players would run through brick walls for him. He believed in me and I believed in myself under him. It was a happy period.

Michael Owen trains with his Newcastle United manager Kevin Keegan (right) in 2008

Owen wasn't sure about Keegan at first but was delighted to be proved wrong: 'He was one of the warmest, kindest and most genuine people I’ve been fortunate enough to work with'

Tributes and flowers are laid for Keegan at St James' Park after his death aged 75 on Monday

Everyone will rightly reflect on Kevin's football achievements this week. A two-time Ballon d'Or winner. A Liverpool and England legend. The player who conquered Germany with Hamburg. What he then did before retiring at Newcastle. He was a superstar. But that only tells half the story.

The Kevin I came to know was simply one of the warmest, kindest and most genuine people I’ve been fortunate enough to work with. There are plenty of people in the game who are polite with supporters because they know it's expected of them, and that’s fine. But Kevin was different. He genuinely loved people. It didn't matter whether you were the biggest celebrity in the country or someone waiting outside the training ground for an autograph. Everybody got the same smile, the same warmth and the same amount of time. I've honestly never known anyone who went so far out of their way for others.

He loved talking football. He loved talking horses. Him and I would talk for hours about both. But more than anything, he just loved life. He had an infectious enthusiasm that made people feel better simply by being around him. That is how he made me feel, and I was saddened to get off a flight from the Far East on Monday and learn of his death.

But then, the memories made me smile, and one in particular. One day at Newcastle's training ground, Kevin started telling everyone how he and Terry McDermott could beat anybody at the club in a game of head tennis. Me and Nicky Butt looked at each other thinking, “Is he serious?”.

Kevin was in his late fifties and Terry wasn't exactly sprinting around by then. We were both in our twenties, England internationals. We thought we'd absolutely wipe the floor with them. Eventually, after plenty of banter, we agreed to play for £100 a man. I've never had a £200 lesson delivered quite so brutally.

Keegan's relationship with Owen began when he was England boss between 1999 and 2000

To say they beat us comfortably would be putting it mildly. Kevin stood on the baseline and somehow got to absolutely everything. Wherever we hit the ball, he'd float it back perfectly onto the top of the net for Terry to head, every single time. Terry barely had to move. He'd head it away, glance it into space or dummy it altogether. They were like a perfectly rehearsed doubles partnership and we hadn't got a clue how to stop them. Kevin’s touch was unbelievable. They absolutely battered us.

For days afterwards, Kevin kept reminding us, "Where's our £200, lads?”. He’d ask every time he saw us. So we decided to get our own back. My dad was living with me in Newcastle at the time, so I asked him to spend a day visiting banks collecting £200 in one-penny coins. A few days later, once Kevin had left his office, it needed the two of us to tip the coins all over his desk. When he walked back in, he stopped dead, looked at the mountain of pennies and simply burst out laughing. That's when we jumped out. The debt had been paid.

I never did find out what he did with all those pennies, but I do know that's exactly how I'll remember Kevin - warm, kind, fun and infectious.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan dead at 75: Football legend passes away following battle with cancer as devastated family pay heartbreaking tribute to England icon
Sports.content:
Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness.

Keegan was diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January, having been admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

In a statement, his family said: 'It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

'The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

'Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support.

'This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.'

Keegan leaves behind his wife, Jean, who he met on the waltzers at Doncaster fair in 1970 – he was 19 and she was 16. They married four years later and had two daughters, Laura, 48, and Sarah, 44.

Kevin Keegan in the England strip in 1981 (left) and playing for Newcastle United in 1983

The former England manager was diagnosed with stomach cancer in January this year

Keegan, who played for Hamburger SV in the late 1970s (pictured), was a formidable footballer and twice won the Ballon d'Or - football's most prestigious individual prize - during his career

He won 63 caps for England and scored 21 goals across his ten-year international career

As a Liverpool player, Keegan delivered European glory for the Anfield club in 1977

In the 1970s, Keegan was renowned for his 'poodle perm' hair

Keegan pictured with his wife, Jean, who was by his side when he died on Monday

At Buckingham Palace with Jean and three-year-old Laura after being awarded an OBE in 1982

In a statement, Newcastle FC said: 'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

'As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

'As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

'Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

'Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

'At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him.

'Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev.'

Liverpool added: 'Liverpool FC is deeply saddened and mourning the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan. Our "Mighty Mouse", his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history. Rest in peace, Kevin Keegan.'

In January, Keegan was admitted to hospital due to 'ongoing abdominal symptoms', a statement from his family said.

'These investigations have revealed a diagnosis of cancer, for which Kevin will undergo treatment,' it added.

However, he looked sprightly when he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis in June, at An Audience With Kevin Keegan in Newcastle. He told fans at the Tyne Theatre that he was responding well to treatment after joking that he 'was still alive'. He also said, 'We have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got'.

'He [the doctor] was a Liverpool supporter, so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn't be walking alone, if you know what I mean.'

Keegan began his playing career at Scunthorpe in 1968, before moving to Liverpool to play for Bill Shankly three years later.

Keegan negotiated a contract worth £50 a week – Shankly had originally offered him £45.

It marked the beginning of a glorious playing career where he won 63 caps for England – captaining the Three Lions on 31 occasions.

The attacker won the First Division three times, the European Cup once and the UEFA Cup twice during a six-year stint at Liverpool.

Keegan even made the Charity Shield memorable after Leeds United midfielder John Giles punched him in the face and was shown a yellow card. Keegan's reaction, however, after a series of aggressive tackles from the other team, saw him sent off when it sparked a brawl with Billy Bremner and they came to blows. Liverpool won the game on penalties.

🗣️ "I WILL LOVE IT IF WE BEAT THEM, LOVE IT!"



We have lost an English football legend today 😢💔 pic.twitter.com/YWo87RCnUV — The 44 ⚽️ (@The_Forty_Four) July 20, 2026

After retiring from football in 1985, Keegan turned to management and was at the helm of his beloved Newcastle United for five years (pictured with famous Geordies Ant and Dec in 1995)

In 1996, in his post-match interview, Keegan accused Manchester United of being ‘slanderous’ and screamed ‘I will love it if we beat them, love it’, a meltdown that saw his team's Premier League title charge fall apart

Keegan also managed England but handed in his resignation in the Wembley tunnel following the drab defeat to Germany in October 2000

KEEGAN'S ILLUSTRIOUS CAREER Years Club Appearances Goals 1968–1971 Scunthorpe 124 18 1971–1977 Liverpool 230 68 1977–1980 Hamburg 90 32 1980–1982 Southampton 68 37 1982–1984 Newcastle United 78 48 1985 Blacktown City 2 1 Honours: Liverpool Football League First Division: 1972–73, 1975–76, 1976–77 FA Cup: 1973–74; runner-up: 1976–77 FA Charity Shield: 1974, 1976 European Cup: 1976–77 UEFA Cup: 1972–73, 1975–76 Hamburg Bundesliga: 1978–79 European Cup runner-up: 1979–80 Individual: Ballon d'Or: 1978, 1979 FWA Footballer of the Year: 1975–76 PFA Players' Player of the Year: 1981–82 Years Club Win% 1992-97 Newcastle United 55 1998-99 Fulham 62 1999-00 England 39 2001-05 Manchester City 44 2008 Newcastle 32 Honours: Newcastle United Football League First Division: 1992–93 Fulham Football League Second Division: 1998–99 Manchester City Football League First Division: 2001–02 Individual Premier League Manager of the Month: November 1993, August 1994, February 1995, August 1995, September 1995

He then moved to Germany to play for Hamburg and was named European Footballer of the Year in both 1978 and 1979. He added to the trophy cabinet in Germany, too, winning the Bundesliga and reaching the 1980 European Cup final.

After three years in Germany, Doncaster-born Keegan returned home and spent time at Southampton and Newcastle – who he would later go on to manage.

He rounded off his playing days with two appearances for Australian semi-professional side Blacktown City.

Keegan scored 204 goals in 592 career appearances across six clubs in a stellar career.

Alongside being iconic on the pitch, he produced his fair share of legendary moments off it too.

While Newcastle boss in 1996, Keegan launched a tirade on Manchester United during the heat of the Premier League title race.

Newcastle had let a 12-point lead slip at the top of the table, with Man Utd moving six points clear after beating ten-man Leeds United 1-0 in April 1996.

Leeds played the majority of the game with defender Lucas Radebe in goal, which prompted Sir Alex Ferguson to question the Yorkshire side's integrity and whether they would show the same grit against Keegan’s Newcastle.

Newcastle responded by beating Leeds 1-0 to move three points behind Man Utd with a match in hand, and only two left to play.

But Keegan let the pressure of the title race get to him in his post-match interview, accusing United of being ‘slanderous’ and screaming ‘I will love it if we beat them, love it’.

His managerial career produced its fair share of bizarre moments.

In 1999, Keegan succeeded Glenn Hoddle as England boss, but a year later famously resigned in the tunnel at Wembley following the drab defeat to Germany in October 2000.

After a brutal reception from the England fans, he told his players in the dressing room that he was stepping down before confirming his resignation to FA director David Davies in a nearby stadium toilet cubicle.

He guided Newcastle to the Football League First Division title during the first of two stints at St James' Park and came close to lifting the Premier League, only to be pipped by Manchester United.

He would go on to oversee promotions to the top flight for both Fulham and City.

Sports.title: Man United hold talks with representatives of France star Manu Kone as they look for third midfield signing after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans
Sports.content:
Man United hold talks with representatives of France star Manu Kone as they look for third midfield signing after Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United have held discussions with representatives of Roma star Manu Kone but have yet to agree on any terms with his club.

The 25-year-old, who made five appearances at the World Cup, is keen on a move to England and United have been evaluating various targets this month as they look for more energy in their midfield.

France legend Patrick Vieira was effusive in his praise of Kone while on punditry duty for ITV, outlining what he could bring to a new club.

'He had a really good season in Serie A with Roma. He came to the World Cup after a couple of injuries,' said the former Arsenal midfielder.

'He is for me today the best midfielder in France. He has mobility, he is aggressive, he is a ball-winner, and he has the technical ability to be part of the build-up, has the facility with the ball to break lines and move forward.'

Manu Kone's stock rose at the World Cup, with Patrick Vieira effusive in his praise

Daily Mail Sport reported last week that Atletico Madrid and Arsenal have previously spoken to his representatives.

United have already added to their midfield this summer with the £48m signing of Chelsea's Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, bought for £35m from Aston Villa. They want a third midfielder but cost will be key when it comes to which target they are able to secure.

They pulled the plug on a move for Brazil international Ederson after concerns over his medical, having agreed a deal before the World Cup. He has now signed a new deal at Atalanta.

Michael Carrick will be without Manuel Ugarte for a considerable period after he had surgery on a knee ligament injury suffered at the World Cup with Uruguay.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi breaks his silence on Argentina's World Cup heartbreak with emotional statement - after snubbing interviews in the wake of brutal loss to Spain
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi has taken to social media to speak following Argentina's World Cup final defeat by Spain that left the forward crying on the pitch.

Messi was bidding to lead his country to World Cup glory for the second time in as many tournaments on Sunday, but Argentina came up short on the night.

It was a game of intense controversy and drama, with an investigation underway into Argentina's conduct after the game, which saw the likes of Leandro Paredes lose their cool and get violent at the full-time whistle.

Messi himself drew attention too, as he tried to get Spain's Marc Cucurella sent off for covering his mouth in the second-half.

But his attempts failed and the star, who finished second behind France's Kylian Mbappe in the Golden Boot rankings, has now spoken on the ordeal.

'The pain is immense, and this wound will take time to heal,' he wrote on Instagram. 'But I also hold onto all the good things... The matches we turned around by giving it our all—moments that will remain in our memories forever—and the support of an entire country which, combined with this group's hard work and effort, brought us back among the world's elite once again.

Lionel Messi has broken his silence following Argentina's World Cup defeat against Spain

Messi was inconsolable shortly after receiving his runners-up medal from Donald Trump

'It is hard to fully appreciate our achievement right now, but this group reached two consecutive World Cup finals. Thank you from the bottom of my heart for every greeting and message.

'Once again, we managed to unite as a country and stand together, sharing the immense pride of being Argentine.

'I also want to congratulate Spain on winning the championship.'

The Argentina squad has also been slammed for standing with their backs to the winning team at MetLife Stadium as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy.

Instead, the Argentina players, coaching team and staff walked over to the end where the majority of their fans were sat and turned their backs as their rivals celebrated.

Footage shows Spain players holding the World Cup trophy aloft as gold confetti explodes behind them, with the Argentina team facing the other way.

Messi and his team also refused to face the music and speak to the media following their defeat.

Argentina only had two shots in the entire match, with the first coming in the 117th minute.

Sports.title: 'He showed how to lead by example and was a huge influence on me - I took so much from how he went about things': BRYAN ROBSON on KEVIN KEEGAN
Sports.content:
'He showed how to lead by example and was a huge influence on me - I took so much from how he went about things': BRYAN ROBSON on KEVIN KEEGAN

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

I'll never forget when I first walked into the England dressing room, it was Kevin Keegan who came over, gave me a hug and said 'enjoy this, son'.

He was the captain, the superstar and reigning European footballer of the year but there were no airs or graces, no front, just this fantastic footballer and man who was genuine in his support.

It was my debut against the Republic of Ireland at Wembley. We won 2-0 and Kevin scored both goals.

How to lead by example. This great No 7. That was Kevin all over. He was a huge influence on me.

He didn't have to go out of his way to make a fuss of me but he was really welcoming. This big star recognised I just needed a bit of encouragement and him adding normality by saying 'just enjoy it'. Playing for England.

I took so much from how he went about things. He had loads of energy and worked so hard. That always stood out. You didn't get to be European footballer of the year twice on talent alone.

Kevin Keegan led by example when Bryan Robson joined the England team. From left: Robson, Ray Wilkins, Keegan and Trevor Brooking at the England hotel for the 1982 Spain World Cup

He gave everything in training, not just the games.

I maintain to this day that if Kevin had been fit for the 1982 World Cup, we would have had a great chance of winning it. Instead, a back injury meant he could only play a small part as a substitute. But he was that good. He would have made the difference.

He retired at international level after that and I've always thought it would have been the most fitting way for him to end his England career to have won that World Cup.

Even when he went into management, his teams had his style. Always attacking, always wanting to entertain, reflecting his great enthusiasm for how to play the game.

As we got older, he moved round the corner from me in Hale and we used to meet up for a coffee. Reminiscing about the old days, mainly those with England, laughing about the characters we knew, the experiences we'd had. I used to see him on the after-dinner circuit and his stories were always so funny, a great raconteur. A genuine star, a terrific player but he could back it up as a terrific man.

To lose him is such a shock. It's a sad, sad day.

My condolences go to Jean and his daughters.

Sports.title: 'He became a superstar but never changed... to say he was a gentleman would be an understatement': GRAEME SOUNESS pays tribute to his friend KEVIN KEEGAN
Sports.content:
Graeme Souness faced Kevin Keegan as a player and manager - they later became friends and golfing partners. Here, after the news of Keegan's death at the age of 75, he pays tribute...

If you ever wanted an example of a man who became a superstar but never changed as a man, Kevin Keegan would be top of that list.

For everything he achieved in the game - the trophies, two Ballon d'Or - his greatest quality was the humility he carried with him through every waking moment. He treated every person he met in the same way: with utmost respect.

To say he was an absolute gentleman seems an understatement. He was a class act.

This was a genuine superstar. If only you could bottle the attitude he had and sell it to the players today.

I was in a restaurant not so long ago when I witnessed a young player, a so-called star, refuse to do a selfie with a fan. That was the absolute polar opposite to Kevin.

Kevin Keegan was a genuinely humble man who recognised he had got lucky in life, but boy did he make the most out of his talent and work hard at it.

He left nothing on the table. He got the absolute best out of himself every time he went out and played football whether training or in a game. His workrate was phenomenal and his enthusiasm lifted everyone around him.

Liverpool captain Graeme Souness shakes hands with Newcastle's Kevin Keegan before Keegan's testimonial at St James's Park in 1984

From an early age he became the biggest star in English football. When I faced him for Liverpool against Southampton, there was no legal way of stopping him. He didn't take kindly to that and gave me a right mouthful. But like all the greats, he didn't shy away, he just came back for more.

But afterwards we became friends. I got to know him even better in recent years.

We used to play golf in Portugal together and he'd always make it competitive. He was full of mischief. England v Scotland he'd say. He was a delight to be around and no matter who asked for a photograph, he'd always stop and make them feel special.

One Friday, a guest speaker for my charity DEBRA had let me down. The dinner was on the Sunday at Prestonfield House in Edinburgh. I rang Kevin and asked if he could step in. He said, 'give me five minutes'.

He rang back in three and said, 'I'll do it.' I said, 'how much do you want?' and he said 'just my travel expenses please', because he liked to drive everywhere.

He turned up, enchanted the room, then stayed and listened to the families' stories. When I went to pay him, he refused and said, 'put it in the pot'. It was a mark of the man.

He used to say, 'I wish for you and your family what you would wish for yourself'.

My heart goes out to Jean and his family.

Sports.title: Man Utd news: Marcus Rashford latest as transfer completed with Tottenham for star
Sports.content:
Man Utd news: Marcus Rashford latest as transfer completed with Tottenham for star

Manchester United are busy strengthening their squad in the transfer window while Marcus Rashford's future remains a topic of discussion

View 2 Images Marcus Rashford remains a Manchester United player after his loan spell at Barcelona (Image: Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Manchester United’s summer recruitment is underway as the club reshape their squad in the transfer market. Michael Carrick has already welcomed several new signings but will want to further strengthen before the start of the new campaign.

‌



United have begun rebuilding their midfield after losing Casemiro at the end of last season. Andrey Santos signed from Chelsea before the club completed a shock move for Aston Villa ’s Youri Tielemans.

‌



Former Leeds goalkeeper Karl Darlow has also arrived as experienced backup to Senne Lammens. However, United have shown a commitment to building for the long-term after sealing a move for highly-rated Tottenham prospect Tynan Thompson.

‌



Meanwhile, Marcus Rashford’s future remains a topic of discussion after his time with England at the World Cup recently came to an end. Here, Mirror Football takes a closer look at some of the stories surrounding United.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Marcus Rashford latest

Marcus Rashford is open to rejoining United training at the end of his summer break after collecting a bronze medal at the World Cup. The forward has not played for United since December 2024, though his next steps have seemed uncertain since Barcelona opted not to trigger their £26m buy option at the end of his loan deal this summer.

‌



Stormzy leaks Manchester United's new adidas away kit during World Cup final READ MORE :

A second clause that allowed clubs to sign Rashford for £40m also expired this month. BBC Sport reports that Rashford, who has two years left on his contract, is “relaxed” about the thought of linking back up with the United squad in training.

The 28-year-old is also claimed to have a more positive dynamic with his ex-teammate and new boss Carrick compared to his “confrontational relationship” with former United manager Ruben Amorim. In his latest spell away from Old Trafford, Rashford notched 14 goals and assists apiece for Barcelona last term, winning La Liga.

Upon completing his World Cup duties, Rahford wrote on social media: “Keep believing in us. Our time will come. Now it's time for me to rest, reflect, spend some quality time with family and friends, and come back a better version of myself."

‌



View 2 Images Tynan Thompson has completed a move to Manchester United (Image: Manchester United/Manchester United via Getty Images)

£8m transfer complete

United have completed the signing of Tottenham Hotspur prospect Tynan Thompason. The 18-year-old, who was named in Champions League matchday squads for Spurs last season, has arrived for an initial £4m, plus a further £4m in potential add-ons.

The winger is set to start his United career with the club’s U21s but could force his way into first team plans. The deal with Spurs also includes a 15 per cent sell-on clause.

‌



Announcing the transfer, a United statement said: " Manchester United have agreed the signing of exciting young winger Tynan Thompson, subject to registration. The England youth international has joined from Tottenham Hotspur.

"The 18-year-old scored 13 goals and contributed six assists last season across Under-18s to Under-21s level, including seven goals in seven UEFA Youth League games. His performances earned him opportunities within Spurs’ first-team matchday squads. Everyone at United would like to welcome Tynan to the club and wish him the very best of luck for the future."

Sports.title: Arsenal news: Tottenham beaten to signing as shock short-term transfer to save millions eyed
Sports.content:
Arsenal news: Tottenham beaten to signing as shock short-term transfer to save millions eyed

Mikel Arteta and Arsenal are gearing up for a busy pre-season and some transfer business is now taking centre-stage

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta is braced for more Arsenal arrivals (Image: Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

As Arsenal await the return of their World Cup stars, including newly crowned champions David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, attention will soon turn to transfer plans. There has already been some movement but we are expecting plenty more to follow.

‌



Piero Hincapie has now signed permanently for £34.5million after a successful season on loan from Bayer Leverkusen. Illan Meslier became the second new addition, with the goalkeeper joining from Leeds United on a free.

‌



Karl Hein, Jakub Kiwior and Leandro Trossard have all moved on to free up some funds. More could yet follow, with Fabio Vieira and Gabriel Jesus among those linked with summer exits.

‌



Mikel Arteta and his squad begin their pre-season campaign on August 1 and there's plenty of time to get business done before then. Here are our latest lines from the red half of north London.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Arsenal to receive millions in FIFA compensation after disastrous World Cup blow READ MORE :

Arsenal beat Spurs to the punch

Arsenal have agreed a deal for youngster Elijah Upson, son of their former defender Matt. The teenager was on Tottenham's books and Roberto De Zerbi's side reportedly offered him a new, pro contract, only for the Gunners to pounce.

‌



The centre-back, who turned 18 in March, played 23 times in all competitions for Spurs' age group teams last season. He started at the heart of the defence in a 4-1 north London derby win in the Under-18 Premier League, with Emerson Nwaneri scoring Arsenal's goal.

Elijah's father Matt, 47, was a Premier League champion with Arsenal in the 2001/02 season. He also played top-flight football for Birmingham, West Ham, Stoke and Leicester and played for England at the 2010 World Cup.

Shock Stones move eyed

View 2 Images John Stones is a free agent after leaving Manchester City (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



England and Manchester City defender John Stones is available on a free transfer this summer and Arsenal have emerged as a shock suitor. According to The Sun, the Gunners see him as a potential short-term, cheap fix after losing William Saliba for an extended period through injury.

Stones left City at the end of June after more than a decade at the Etihad Stadium. Mikel Arteta was part of the coaching staff for a section of that spell so he already knows all about the former Everton centre-back.

Arsenal are yet to determine how long they expect to be without Saliba, who aggravated a back injury at the World Cup. However, with French media suggesting he could be out for as long as five months, Stones - also a target for Inter Milan - could help plug a defensive hole.
