World.title: 10 things that wowed us at the 2026 World Cup
World.content:
10 things that wowed us at the 2026 World Cup

toggle caption Franck Fife/AFP via Getty Images

The 2026 World Cup has ended — after almost six weeks, 104 matches and games spread across three countries: the United States, Canada and Mexico.

Spain is the World Cup champion again, defeating the defending champion Argentina to claim its second title. With the win, Spain holds World Cup titles for both the men's and women's national teams — a first.

Here are the moments that stood out to NPR's team of journalists who covered the tournament:

All the drama before the tournament, and just pure enjoyment once underway

For the most part, the 2026 World Cup was a smooth, fun and safe one.

Sure, the mandatory hydration breaks added for all games (including those in domed stadiums with air conditioning) and a first-ever halftime show in the final were maddening for the soccer purists. But, still, the U.S., Mexico and Canada put on a great show for the world — with record viewership and attendance. And, wow, were people treated to some remarkable soccer games. Let's not forget the hand-wringing when the announcement was made about expanding the number of countries from 32 to 48. "The quality of play will be poor! There will be blowouts! It just won't be as fun!" And then we all saw what actually happened.

Sponsor Message

Those World Cup debutants — or those that hadn't been in decades — were just delightful. Scotland (and their wonderful fans), anyone? People from other countries enjoying and exploring the U.S. and posting the absolute best social media videos about it. And what about African countries powering into the knockout rounds? Soccer at its best.

— Russell Lewis

toggle caption Charlotte Wilson/Getty Images

The enthusiasm for the U.S. team is hopefully the start of something

I've been to a lot of sporting events, but I'm not sure I've heard a crowd pop like in Seattle when forward Folarin Balogun forced an own goal when the U.S. faced Australia, or like in Santa Clara, Calif., when midfielder Malik Tillman hit the free kick to put the U.S. up 2-0 despite being shorthanded after the Balogun red card. It's been a joy to see children all over the country, from L.A. to Kansas City to Atlanta to New York, wearing the team's red-and-white striped jerseys. I had friends and family who never normally watch the sport text me during the U.S. games.

Look, I'm not naive. The U.S. still has a long way to go to match the passion of, say, Argentina when it comes to our national soccer teams. But compared to the tiny crowds at other friendlies I've attended, or getting outnumbered by Mexico fans in the Gold Cup final in Houston, this was a great start. And I'm hopeful that come the next CONCACAF Nations League, which begins this fall, or even the possible Copa América that might be on deck here in the States in 2028, the passion will linger long enough that this story might change.

Sponsor Message

— Becky Sullivan

The Cape Verde-Argentina game

Cape Verde was an exciting team to watch in this tournament. The narrative was that they came out of nowhere, which is not quite true: yes, this was their first time qualifying for a World Cup, but in African tournaments, Cape Verde has been playing amazing soccer for years.

As someone who follows soccer closely, I think African soccer is having a moment, and we may see it come to full bloom in the 2030 World Cup (hosted in part by Morocco). Vozinha, Cape Verde's extraordinary goalie, was one of the breakout stars of this cup at age 40. On the other hand, Argentina is a relentless team; they were the defending champions. They have Lionel Messi, a living legend. The game, played in Miami, was a nail-biter: until the last moment, no one knew how it would end. The fans were wild (there was a moment in the press box when the stadium was shaking so hard, a local journalist turned to me and said, "It never shakes like this." I will never forget that game.

— Jasmine Garsd

toggle caption Patricia de Melo Moreira/AFP via Getty Images

The Argentina team working to decrease cardiac health globally

As someone who has followed the Argentina team for decades, this is nothing new: it is a team notorious for being slow starters, as if they needed to be up against the wall to find their motivation.

They started off the last World Cup, in 2022, with a shocking loss to Saudi Arabia, and then, just as everyone had discounted them, they went on to win the entire tournament.

The matches in this year's World Cup followed a similar pattern: Like against Cape Verde, Argentina seeming to be on standby during the first half, then coming to life in the second. Another example was Argentina-England, and yet another heart attack special. Argentina seemed to be getting its bearings in the first half of the game. It wasn't until after the 55th minute, when England scored a goal, that Argentina began to awaken and put up a fight. They equalized in the 85th minute, and then scored again in stoppage time to win and advance to the final. Argentina played the same way in the final, but unlike the previous games, could not find a way to bounce back.

Sponsor Message

— Jasmine Garsd

Unfortunately, the high ticket prices were justified

From the moment FIFA released the first tickets, our eyes collectively popped at the price of the tickets — what a cash grab! Hundreds of dollars for the seemingly low-demand group stage games, $1,000 or more for each U.S. game, and thousands for Sunday's final. But the fears of half-empty stadiums, of empty hotels, or visitors turned off by the high prices, never quite came to fruition. I'm sad to report it turns out FIFA was onto something. It turns out the World Cup is very fun and very cool, and many people are willing to pay those prices, whether diehard fans traveling from overseas or curious locals who wanted the experience. Soccer has long hung its hat on being the most accessible sport to play — all you need is a ball! — but a $10,000 entry price to the final, and hundreds for the cheapest games, are the latest proof that's changing.

— Becky Sullivan

toggle caption Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images

Kylian Mbappé's unbelievable speed

It's one thing to watch him play on TV, but when you see him in person, you really understand just how fast French captain Kylian Mbappé is. I did a little digging after the France-Morocco game near Boston, and found that Mbappé's fastest recorded sprint on a pitch was faster than Jamaican Olympic gold medalist Usain Bolt's average set in his 100m World Record in 2009. Mbappé's speed was 23.6 miles per hour, recorded in a 2019 match between Paris Saint-Germain and AS Monaco. And that speed helped him win yet another Golden Boot award. His ten goals were the most in the tournament, increasing his overall World Cup total to 22, the most all-time.

— Jasmine Garsd

The much-hated VAR

VAR, or video assistant referee, was first introduced at the World Cup in 2018. At the time, fans and teams appreciated it as a way to correct the occasional referee error or missed call. Fast-forward to 2026, and VAR is ubiquitous in almost every game.

Sponsor Message

At times, the decisions have been accused of being ludicrous: a Colombian goal against Portugal annulled because a toenail was found offside by the VAR.

An Iranian goal against Belgium was wiped away because the striker's butt was offside. There have also been controversial VAR calls, like the questionable foul that led to an Egyptian goal against Argentina being annulled. Argentina won that game and Egypt got knocked out. Fans also say it's slowing down the game and putting a damper on goal celebrations, lest the great VAR take the moment away.

— Jasmine Garsd

The continued politicizing of the Cup

It's nothing new: the 2018 Russia World Cup was rife with accusations of sportswashing of human rights abuses and FIFA corruption. The 2022 Qatar World Cup faced similar criticism. During this World Cup, there were critiques of the U.S. government's immigration policy as tens of thousands of foreign tourists tried to enter the country. The U.S.-led war against Iran trickled onto the soccer field too. Iran's soccer team had planned to base its training camp in Arizona. But it moved to Tijuana, Mexico, amid security fears and other worries. Then, the U.S. government only allowed Iran's team to enter the country a single day (and, later, two days) before each game, and the team had to depart immediately afterward. And, of course, the prohibitive cost of tickets, and President Trump's involvement in the tournament. He only attended one game, the final between Argentina and Spain, and was booed. There were also conversations about various teams and their colonial histories.

— Jasmine Garsd

toggle caption Odd Andersen/AFP via Getty Images

Trump's call to Infantino was an uncomfortable new frontier

The White House's involvement with the red card given to Balogun, the U.S. striker, was an uncomfortable new frontier for U.S. national teams. It wasn't a surprise, exactly — President Trump has often used sports as a way to score political points. But it was extraordinary for Trump to personally call FIFA president Gianni Infantino to ask for the red card to be reviewed. Whether his call made a difference in FIFA's decision to allow Balogun to play — FIFA insists it did not — the optics were terrible, and for many fans, it dimmed a summer's worth of enthusiasm for the team.

Sponsor Message

For days after Trump confirmed reports of his call to Infantino, U.S. Soccer remained silent on the president's involvement. That silence left some fans feeling as though the organization welcomed the White House's intervention. Then, when asked about it last week — after plenty of time had passed to issue a statement — the head of U.S. Soccer essentially shrugged.

"The president is able to do what the president wants to do. The president is the president of the United States," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson said. "Obviously we're incredibly grateful for all the support for all of our fans all across the country, wherever they are. And we're excited about that, and we know that that'll pay dividends going forward."

— Becky Sullivan

toggle caption Adam Gray/Getty Images

The World Cup that sparkled and thrilled

This is the fourth World Cup that I've covered for NPR, and, unlike at the Olympics, the pride in one's country at the World Cup is always so striking. Fans — young and old — attend the games or show up in the host cities to be around others to cheer on their team. The passion, the fervor and just the sheer love of home. Seeing tens of thousands of fans in a stadium, a bar, or a watch party, and watching them will their country forward believing that anything is possible on the pitch. And sometimes the fans aren't even from any of the countries playing that day. Soccer is a global sport and a global love. It truly is a treat to see in person.

— Russell Lewis

Want more fútbol in the United States? Major League Soccer has just resumed its season, and is working to capitalize on World Cup fever in the U.S. NWSL, the National Women's Soccer League and USL Championship are also underway. And the number-two-ranked U.S. Women's National Team is back in action this fall with a pair of tune-up matches against No. 1 Spain — ahead of next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

World.title: Court ruling freezes Paramount-Warner Bros. merger for now
World.content:
Court ruling freezes Paramount-Warner Bros. merger for now

toggle caption SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images



Paramount's owners were planning to have secured firm control of Hollywood rival Warner Bros. Discovery by the end of this week in a blockbuster deal that has the blessing of President Trump's Justice Department.

A federal judge has instead ground the process to a halt, at least for now. And her ruling on Monday in response to a lawsuit filed a week ago by a dozen states suggests Paramount may have some tough sledding ahead in order to get the deal through.

Sponsor Message

In the ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a 14-day temporary restraining order to pause the acquisition. The Democratic attorneys general allege that Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. would reduce competition, hurting filmgoers along with TV and news consumers and especially those who create entertainment programming and the news content that the public relies on.

The $111 billion deal would put under the same corporate roof Paramount's and Warner's movie and television studios, streamers Paramount+ and HBO Max, Paramount's CBS (the nation's most watched broadcast outlet), and 50 cable TV channels, not to mention both CBS News and CNN.

"This is a critical first win in our case to ensure this megamerger never sees the light of day," California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in a statement issued to the press.

"History tells the tale of what happens when a few people have great power over markets that are central to Americans' lives: fewer opportunities for more people, worse products and services for all people," said Bonta, who has taken the lead on the case for the states. "With our lawsuit, we're fighting for a free and fair market and a thriving film and television industry that serves creatives and audiences alike."

Sponsor Message

Paramount released a statement late Monday insisting it would prevail in the end.

"We are confident the evidence will demonstrate that the State AG's antitrust arguments are without merit," Paramount said in a statement. "This merger is lawful, pro-competitive and will benefit consumers, creators, workers and the entertainment industry."

The company also said it was grateful for the court's swift action. Paramount had hoped to complete the deal by Wednesday, July 22.

Lawsuit centers on movies and cable tv, not streaming

The legal challenge focuses on three markets: theatrical movie releases, blockbuster films and cable television channels.

In an episode of the Hollywood-industry podcast The Town released Monday hours before the ruling, Paramount Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim fought back against Bonta's claims that the consolidation would hurt consumers or producers. "You have to stick your head in the sand" to vast changes in consumer behavior in order to swallow the states' arguments, Delrahim said.

Paramount contends in its public statements and legal filings that competition in entertainment plays out not only among the five traditional Hollywood studios but also among tech giants Netflix, Apple and Amazon.

Those much bigger companies have drawn significant streaming audiences and have their own blockbuster hits. So, on occasion, have much smaller production houses, such as A24 and Lionsgate. Amazon also owns film studio MGM, which produced the hit Project Hail Mary. The Michael Jackson biopic, from Lionsgate, sold an estimated $1 billion in tickets globally.

The states' suit does not address the merger of streaming assets, in a sense seeking to sidestep the entry of the digital giants into the entertainment fray.

In her ruling, Judge Martínez-Olguín focused solely on the merger's consolidation of two of the remaining five major Hollywood studios, effectively as a test case for the states' other claims of antitrust behavior.

She found the states' case convincing, at least at first blush.

"Plaintiffs present compelling evidence that the combined firm resulting from the transaction will possess substantial market share in the wide-release theatrical distribution market," the judge wrote. "On this combined firm market share alone, the Court is persuaded that it can presume the proposed merger is likely to violate antitrust laws."

Sponsor Message

Martínez-Olguín also wrote that she did not consider the counterargument made by Paramount, invoking the arrival of the huge digital competitors, to be persuasive. In a footnote, she characterized the streaming market to be "ancillary" to the markets relevant to the litigation.

Longer delay would be costly

The states are also asking the judge to issue a preliminary injunction that could freeze the deal indefinitely, as the larger antitrust case plays out in court.

A longer delay would have huge financial costs for Paramount. Starting Oct. 1, Paramount has to pay Warner shareholders a "ticking consideration" of roughly $650 million for every 90 days the deal is set back. If the deal is not consummated by June 4, 2027, Paramount will have to pay Warner $7 billion.

Martínez-Olguín proposed a schedule that would have a full hearing on the preliminary injunction on Aug. 3.

Trump is a factor

The proposed deal has gotten a lot of scrutiny outside Hollywood for the relationship between Paramount's controlling family and President Trump — especially because two major newsrooms would be under that family's control.

The deal is largely bankrolled by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison and a close ally of Trump. Trump has long accused CNN of being "fake news" and has publicly mused about what he'd like to do to the cable news giant.

While the U.S. Department of Justice's antitrust regulators have signed off on the deal — Paramount's Delrahim used to run that division during Trump's first term in office — the Federal Communications Commission has not yet given its approval. The FCC's approval is needed because Paramount holds licenses granted by the agency to use the public airwaves for 28 local television stations. The merger anticipates a huge jump in foreign ownership of the new combined company. About 49% of the new Paramount-Warner would be held by Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds in nonvoting shares.

Sponsor Message

NPR's Mandalit del Barco contributed to this story.

World.title: India's Gen Z 'Cockroach People's Party' started as satire but is serious about change
World.content:
India's Gen Z 'Cockroach People's Party' started as satire but is serious about change

toggle caption Vipin/AP

NEW DELHI — Thousands of protesters marched to India's Parliament on Monday, facing a police crackdown as the demonstrators demanded the resignation of the country's education minister, in one of the biggest confrontations of an emerging, youth-led movement.

The demonstrators call themselves the Cockroach Janta Party ("Cockroach People's Party"), and they want to overhaul the way India is run, starting with an education system they say is corrupt. They are making their voices heard as they come up against the country's rising cost of living and a lack of quality jobs.

The protests mark a rare show of defiance against the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Critics say the 12-year rule of his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has marked a crackdown on civil society and jailing of political opponents. Despite rapid economic growth under Modi, analysts say, India's youth unemployment remains stubbornly high.

Sponsor Message

The Modi government has portrayed the demonstrators as villains. "These are people who want to make the country hollow," BJP chief Nitin Nabhi said in a speech last month.

But on Monday, the government appeared to make its first outreach to the protest group. Saurav Das, a spokesperson of the Cockroach Janta Party, said Indian Health Minister J.P. Nadda had met them for 10 minutes at the minister's residence. Another Cockroach spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, said the health minister asked for time to discuss the movement's demands, which include the release of a detained activist and the education minister's resignation.

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has so far refused to step down.

Pradhan did not respond to a list of NPR's questions. BJP spokespeople did not respond to requests for an interview.

Tear gas and wooden sticks

toggle caption Manish Swarup/AP

For more than a month, hundreds of Indian young people had camped at Jantar Mantar, one of the few open spaces in the Indian capital where the government allows mass protests. On Monday, they mobilized a major march to Parliament.

Authorities in New Delhi cut off mobile internet, put up barricades and shut off metro train stations near the protest site. Then, the riot police charged into protesters with batons and shields.

Sponsor Message

Protesters say police hit dozens of them with batons in their heads. While Delhi police denied using violence, NPR witnessed police fire tear gas to disperse the protests and hit the demonstrators with wooden sticks at several points in central Delhi.

Protester Mohammed Nasir, a high-school graduate, said tear gas shells fell near him and he witnessed officers hurting a protester. "I saw three to four personnel kicking a woman in her abdomen," he said. "She couldn't get up from the road after."

Many demonstrators retaliated by pelting stones at the police, injuring about 50 officers, according to local news reports.

Protesters were on New Delhi's streets until the evening, singing, sloganeering, waving the Indian tricolor flag.

"Whenever Modi is scared, he sends the police out," a group chanted near metal barricades. "Let's test the limits of your oppression," another group of men and women chanted as a dozen police hovered nearby. "Let's find out how much space you have in your jails."

The "cockroach" movement started as a parody

toggle caption Manish Swarup/AP

The "cockroaches" took their name as a mocking response to a pointed comment from India's top judge.

During a hearing in May, India's Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant compared the country's unemployed young adults to roaches while referring to criticism of judges on social media. "There are youngsters like cockroaches, they don't get any employment, they don't have any place in profession," the Indian Express newspaper reported him saying. He said some become social media creators, some become activists, and "they start attacking everyone." He later said he was misunderstood. But it was too late.

Days after the remarks, Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old with a master's in public relations from Boston University, launched the Cockroach Janta Party as a satirical online collective. Millions of people followed them on social media, drawing support from activists, movie stars and some opposition politicians.

toggle caption Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times via Getty Images

"In India, if you're rich, the system dances at your fingertips. If you're poor, nobody will be there for you," Dipke says. "We're frustrated because the government has stopped listening."

Sponsor Message

The Indian government banned the party's first X account, citing "threats to national security." So Dipke created another one, saying, "Cockroaches don't die." On Instagram, the group racked up nearly 22 million followers, more than twice that of India's ruling BJP. The satire had turned serious.

Dipke says he was born into a Dalit family. Considered the lowest of South Asia's hierarchical caste system, Dalits were once known as outcasts and many are still treated that way. Dipke says he spent his summers in his grandparents' village in central India. "We'd often share one roti among two people. If there was a drought, we'd travel miles on a bullock cart to fill water from a well."

In his 20s, he worked with an anti-corruption party's social media team.

Then, taking a cue from many of his peers, he applied to study in the U.S. in 2024. He didn't want to return — even when he says he experienced racism there. "It wasn't too different from the casteism I experienced in India," he says. "But at least in the U.S., you are able to feed your family."

But after his parody party went viral, Dipke returned and launched a sit-in in New Delhi.

Exam question leaks

The group's immediate demand is the resignation Education Minister Pradhan after a series of exam leaks. Every year, the Education Ministry conducts a set of screening exams for students seeking higher education, and for academics who want to teach in public schools and universities. With millions of candidates fighting for a highly limited pool of university seats and government jobs, a single exam can determine their entire economic future.

In the latest incident, a file allegedly containing test questions circulated on messaging apps ahead of a nationwide exam held in May. It affected more than 2 million aspiring doctors applying for a fraction of seats in India's medical colleges. Those students were informed about it two weeks after they took the exam. Local media reported at the time that at least a dozen students had died by suicide after hearing they'd have to re-sit an exam that many prepare for over years — and at great expense to their parents.

Sponsor Message

Dipke says it's why a chunk of those turning up for the protests are parents. "I have seen them come with their 10-year-olds. They tell me they want to make the system fairer by the time their kids appear for their medical college exams," he says.

Another of the movement's demands, according to spokesperson Ranka, is compensation for the families of the people who took their lives.

toggle caption Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times via Getty Images

Scant quality jobs

Dipke says it is getting harder to afford a decent education and find well-paying jobs in India and the ways to get them seem rigged.

India's economy has grown by more than 7% most years over the past decade. Even as it became the most populous country, it has reduced extreme poverty and improved education levels.

Yet, many of India's 300 million youth aren't seeing their lives improve, says Rosa Abraham, an economist at Azim Premji University. She says that's because "we're not creating enough jobs given the number of graduates we are producing."

Abraham says around 40% of India's university graduates under the age of 25 are unemployed: "It's among the highest rates in decades."

Even when they get a job, the entry-level salaries are lower than they used to be more than a decade ago, adjusting for inflation. The lack of options, she says, forces many to take up physical labor in agriculture or construction, where the pay is lower and there's no guarantee of income.

Bhanu Joshi, a political scientist and co-founder of Data Action Lab for Emerging Societies, says successive governments have struggled to create employment for Indian youth. But even as the problem became more acute under Prime Minister Modi, Joshi says the government has primarily addressed it using welfare or unemployment benefits. "It's like saying, unemployment is a huge issue but I cannot solve it. Let me give you 1,500 rupees [under $16] and take care of your grievance."

Sponsor Message

Economists say the concerns of young adults in India need structural solutions.

"We are sitting with a generation of the most educated group of youngsters we've ever had in the country," says Abraham, who heads Azim Premji's Centre for Sustainable Employment. "If they are not given the means to kind of utilize this education, fulfill at least some of their aspirations, that's going to lead to frustration, which can come out in different forms of unrest."

Unrest — like the ongoing protests in New Delhi's Jantar Mantar grounds.

Defying diktats

toggle caption Bilal Kuchay for NPR

Satire has been the bedrock of the Cockroach Janta Party's campaign. One evening, demonstrators invited people to sign diapers and mail them to the federal education minister to help plug exam paper "leaks."

On another occasion, they danced and banged plates while demanding the minister's resignation.

Two weeks ago, the prominent environmentalist and education activist Sonam Wangchuk joined them and launched a hunger strike. According to a Cockroach Janta Party press release, he lost more than 18 pounds in 18 days. Over the weekend, dozens of plain-clothes policemen entered the protest site and dragged Wangchuk into an ambulance.

Spokesperson Ranka said the party was demanding Wangchuk's release.

On Monday, local media reported that the police entered the protest site again, dismantled the stage and tents, and evacuated the protesters.

Even as the protesters accuse the education ministry of failing to prevent leaks, Education Minister Pradhan has refused to resign. In an interview with the news channel NDTV, he called the protesters "a B-team of terrorists" who were trying to "divide the country."

Dipke rejected the claim. Last week, Dipke also shared a montage of Pradhan's photos set to the lyrics of Taylor Swift's song "Anti-Hero." "It's me, hi, I'm the problem."

Students and professionals come to the protest site from across the city and neighboring states. Many speak of being let down by "the system."

toggle caption Bilal Kuchay for NPR

Twenty-year-old Mohammad Arshad says the medical exam paper leak in May destroyed his faith in the fairness of the system after spending two years preparing. "I appeared for the re-exam last month but I can no longer trust the process is fair." It has driven some of his friends to study medicine abroad, even in Russia. "They lost hope in India's education system," he says.

Sponsor Message

Kajal Singh, 22, says she traveled nearly three hours with her friend to join the protest. She wears a white mask, "because I haven't told my parents," and says she wants government accountability. "We are not anti-nationals," she says, referring to the term the ruling party uses for critics. "We are students. Listen to us."

World.title: Putin meets North Korean foreign minister in diplomatic push
World.content:
Putin meets North Korean foreign minister in diplomatic push

toggle caption Alexander Shcherbak/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — Russian President Vladimir Putin met with North Korea's foreign minister and thanked Pyongyang for supporting his war against Ukraine, in the latest high-level diplomacy between the countries, Russian state media reported.

The visit by North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui comes without an obvious occasion, such as a multilateral diplomatic event or state anniversary, and has raised speculation that she may be coordinating a possible visit to Russia by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. North Korean state media said Choe departed for Russia on Saturday at the invitation of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov but has yet to comment on the purpose of her visit.

Sponsor Message

Yoon Min Ho, spokesperson for South Korea's Unification Ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, said Monday that Seoul was closely monitoring the meetings but declined to assess whether Moscow and Pyongyang were discussing another summit between their leaders.

Russia's Tass news agency said Putin during his meeting with Choe at the Kremlin on Sunday praised the countries' bilateral relations and reiterated his "gratitude to the North Korean leadership and people" for supporting his military operations against Ukraine. Choe told Putin that Kim remains committed to the "comprehensive development" of relations with Russia, Tass said.

Kim traveled to Russia's Far East for summits with Putin in 2019 and 2023. Putin invited Kim to visit Russia again during their summit in Pyongyang in June 2024, where the leaders signed a strategic partnership agreement pledging mutual aid if either country faces aggression.

Kim in recent years has made Russia the priority of his foreign policy, sending thousands of troops and huge supplies of weapons to support Putin's war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for economic aid and technology transfers that some experts say are helping advance North Korea's military capabilities.

Kim has also been seeking stronger ties with China, including hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping for a June summit in Pyongyang, as he embraces the idea of a "new Cold War" and projecting Pyongyang as part of a united front against Washington.

Sponsor Message

Choe's visit to Moscow came shortly after North Korea and China exchanged high-level visits, with North Korean Cabinet premier, Pak Thae Song, Kim's top economic official, meeting Xi in Beijing and Wang Huning, a member of the Chinese Communist Party's powerful Politburo Standing Committee, visiting Kim in Pyongyang this month.

Kim has suspended all meaningful dialogue with the United States and South Korea since the collapse of his nuclear diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump in 2019. He has used Russia's war on Ukraine as a distraction to accelerate the advancement of his nuclear weapons and missile program, while demanding that Washington abandon its calls for North Korea's nuclear disarmament as a precondition for talks.

World.title: Why Trump is threatening new 50% tariffs on Canadian exports right now
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It may appear that U.S. President Donald Trump's move to hit many Canadian products with new tariffs of 50 per cent came out of the blue, but there are clear signs of what's driving the tactic.

Monday's announcement comes as the U.S. pushes for significant changes to the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), changes that would lock any Canadian trade concessions into the text of a trade deal.

The Trump administration wants to wipe out as much of Canada's leverage in those CUSMA talks as possible.

Some of that leverage comes from eight Canadian provinces banning the import and distribution of U.S. alcohol products — one of the trade irritants the White House said triggered the new 50 per cent tariff.

The U.S. escalation is a big deal but is not unexpected, says Brian Clow, who advised former prime minister Justin Trudeau on Canada-U.S. relations.

"It's not a surprise to the people in government and people who've been watching this closely because they've known for a while that the U.S. may turn up the heat on us," Clow told CBC's Power & Politics on Monday.

WATCH | What you need to know about the new tariffs announced by Donald Trump: Trump plans new 50% tariff on Canadian goods | Duration 4:30 U.S. President Donald Trump plans to slap 50 per cent retaliatory tariffs on a new list of Canadian products including wine, hockey sticks and dairy products.

Government should 'react calmly'

While Trump announced the new tariffs in presidential proclamations he issued on Monday, they aren't scheduled to take effect until Aug. 19.

That dangles a carrot to Prime Minister Mark Carney, suggesting Canada could escape the stick of the new tariffs if the government simply capitulates to the U.S. on its demands within the month.

Clow warns the government against responding rashly to the threat.

"They have 30 days, so they should take that time, react calmly, not rush into any quick judgments or decisions here and think about their next steps," he said.

The alcohol boycott has had a visible impact on the U.S. industry. According to U.S. Census Bureau figures, it has resulted in a $360 million US drop in wine exports to Canada in 2025 from the previous year, along with a $150 million US drop in spirit exports.

But retaliation for that boycott is just one of three ostensible reasons U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer gave for the new tariff threat.

"Canada has taken U.S. alcohol products off Canadian shelves, given better market access to dairy products from the European Union, and has put a cap on U.S. vehicle exports to Canada from companies reshoring to the United States," Greer said in a statement.

The tariffs would apply to nearly $20 billion US worth of Canadian goods, according to Greer's office. That's roughly five per cent of the value of Canada's exports to the U.S. in 2025.

WATCH | New tariffs likely a negotiating tactic, says Canadian auto parts official: 'We shouldn't panic' over Trump's new tariffs, says auto parts association head | Duration 13:59 U.S. President Donald Trump signed proclamations on Monday that impose new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports next month. Power & Politics speaks with president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association Flavio Volpe on how these tariffs would affect Canada.

Milk, wine, whisky … and wigs

The U.S. has listed nearly 500 product categories impacted by the new tariffs, some of which clearly relate directly to trade irritants with the Canadian dairy sector and the provincial alcohol boycotts.

Canadian milk products, wine and whisky are all targets for the 50 per cent duty.

But dozens of products seem chosen at random, with no clear link to the stated trade barriers. Circular saw blades, candles, envelopes, hammers, Christmas decorations, synthetic wigs and plastic cups are among the items that face the 50 per cent tariff.

Some appear to make the list for their status as quintessentially Canadian, including hockey equipment and down jackets.

The list of products facing tariffs to "offset Canadian discrimination against the commerce of the United States with respect to motor vehicles" does not include any motor vehicles or auto parts.

WATCH | What's behind Trump's new threat of 50% tariffs: What will this new wave of tariffs do to U.S.-Canada relations? | Duration 9:25 U.S. President Donald Trump is moving to impose 50 per cent tariffs on many Canadian exports. The rate is five times higher than the current tariff imposed on a limited selection of Canadian products. It's a move that deputy chief of staff to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Brian Clow, tells Power & Politics is going to continue to negatively affect the relationship between the two countries.

"When a country designs a list like this, they go after where they can inflict maximum pain but also suffer the least amount of damage on their own economy," said Clow.

Canadian exports of crude oil, potash and critical minerals are explicitly exempted from the tariff. That's a clear sign that the Trump administration doesn't want to trigger even more of a price increase at the gas pumps than was caused by the war with Iran, nor does it want to hamper U.S. farmers' access to fertilizer or the defence industry's access to military-grade material.

Still, the move would both broaden the scope and increase the size of existing U.S. tariffs on Canadian products.

Currently, the U.S. has a 10 per cent blanket tariff on all goods from Canada.

However, products that comply with the rules of origin in CUSMA are exempt, and that means the vast majority of Canadian exports enter the U.S. tariff-free.

The new tariff would be five times higher and CUSMA-compliant goods would not be exempt.

Never-before-used U.S. law

Trump is imposing the tariffs through a section of a 1930 trade law that has never before been used by a U.S. president.

John Veroneau, senior counsel with Washington, D.C.-based Covington and Burling law firm who also served as a trade official in the George W. Bush administration, says the section was intended to ensure trading partners don't give some countries preferential tariff rates that put the U.S. at a disadvantage.

"It is ironic, to say the least, to use this authority to impose tariffs to retaliate against tariffs that were imposed in response to actions taken by the U.S.," Veroneau told Reuters.

WATCH | Assessing the potential impact of Trump's newly threatened tariff: Trump to impose new 50% tariff on some Canadian exports | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 14:55 U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday imposing 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian exports. The tariff is in response to Canada's 'retaliation and discrimination' against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol, according to a senior Trump administration official.

Trump has threatened to impose new or increased tariffs on Canadian products several times over the past year, but hasn't actually followed through.

He threatened unspecified tariffs on Canada last week over smoke from wildfires, 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian-made aircraft in January, a 100 per cent tariff on all Canadian goods if Canada made "a deal with China" that same month, and an additional 10 per cent tariff on Canadian goods last October in response to a TV ad by the Ontario government.

For those who think Trump will once again chicken out, take note that he issued all those threats on social media or in comments to reporters. This time, he's formalized the threat in official White House proclamations.

He also announced the new tariff plan one day after appearing alongside Carney at the FIFA World Cup final.

Perhaps the timing is a coincidence, or perhaps Trump and his officials realized that slapping high tariffs on the U.S.'s second-largest trading partner while jointly hosting a soccer tournament watched by billions around the globe would be bad optics.

World.title: Trump's escalating trade war puts pressure on premiers with U.S. booze bans as they gather in P.E.I.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump's surprise escalation in his trade war with Canada puts renewed pressure on the premiers — most of whom have pulled American booze from liquor stores — as they descend on Charlottetown for their annual summer meeting.

The White House announced on Monday that it will impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of goods in response to what a senior administration official described as Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy and its discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol.

It all but certainly changes the tone and focus when the Council of the Federation gathers along the harbourfront starting Tuesday — not far from where the Fathers of Confederation discussed uniting th e colonies in the face of American threats some 160 years ago.

Speaking Monday to reporters following a dinner with his counterpars, B.C. Premier David Eby suggested nobody is talking about putting booze back on the shelves. Every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan has banned the sale of U.S. alcohol in retaliation to his previous tariffs on things like the auto sector, steel and aluminium.

The boycotts have been seen as a bargaining chip in the ongoing trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S. and have become an irritant for the Americans as U.S. exports of wine, beer and spirits to Canada plummeting.

"At this point I just feel sorry for Americans. You know, if you're picking fights with Canadians, then you don't have a friend in the world," Eby said.

"I can't make sense of what the president is doing, nobody can."

He also said he has asked staff to contact the U.S. Embassy to have his government's statement marking the two countries' friendship removed from the U.S. 250th birthday website.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Canada should hit back against the latest measures.

"I'll never stop fighting to protect Ontario. If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," he posted on social media Monday.

Premiers will first hear from Indigenous leaders before their own meeting on Wednesday. Prime Minister Mark Carney is joining the table later in the week.

American products were pulled off the shelves of the LCBO, one of the largest purchasers of alcohol in the world, last year in response to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

The new tariffs, set to come into place in 30 days, would apply to a variety of Canadian imports, "ranging from wine to hockey sticks to cement," the official said. Energy, potash, critical minerals and fish would be exempt, but other products that until now have been allowed into the U.S. tariff-free under terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) would be hit.

This follows the White House's announcement earlier this month declining to extend CUSMA, triggering what are expected to be tough negotiations on amending the continental pact.

Before Monday's news, premiers had listed health care transfers, energy development, economic growth and the wildfires destroying swaths of northern Ontario as priorities for their meetings.

In 2023 the federal government, under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, hiked the annual Canada Health Transfer by five per cent for five years. With the transfers reverting back to three per cent increases come March 2028, the provinces are beating the drum for more federal funding.

"It's very important that before we expand responsibilities, for example, do more on dental care or do more defence spending, that we do honour our commitments to Canadian citizens of providing quality public health care," Quebec Finance Minister Eric Girard told CBC's Power & Politics last week.

Referendums off the official agenda

The meetings also come ahead of what could be internal tests to Canadian unity.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is going ahead with a series of referendum questions in October — including whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or commence the legal process of holding a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

The question of Quebec independence has also been resurrected, with Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon promising to hold a referendum on separation if he secures a mandate in the fall provincial election. While St-Pierre Plamondon's party has been dominating in the polls over the last year, recent surveys suggest the race is tightening.

In an interview late last week, New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the referendums aren't on the official agenda, "but there are also conversations that we have around the coffee pot or as we're moving in and out of different discussions.

"We were one of the four that set Canada up and I believe very firmly in the beauty of this nation from coast to coast to coast and New Brunswick will do whatever we can to keep our country strong and united," said Holt.

World.title: How the outbreak of an intestinal parasite in the U.S. unfolded
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Federal and state authorities in the U.S. have been investigating cases of illness from an intestinal parasite.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that contaminates food that has come into contact with human feces, such as when produce is irrigated or washed with contaminated water.

Cyclosporiasis, the infection caused by the parasite, most commonly causes diarrhea, but some people can experience other gastrointestinal symptoms and dehydration. Symptoms usually start within a week of ingesting the parasite, doctors say.

The illness usually does not spread from person to person.

As of July 20, more than 30 states have reported illnesses, with about 100 hospitalizations to date and no deaths. The true number of infections is likely much higher given that many people recover without seeking medical treatment and that there is lag between when symptoms start and reporting.

Public health officials say they are not currently investiagting any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

The parasite can stick in the nooks and crannies of berries, food scientists say. (Frannyanne/Shutterstock)

Foods imported to Canada that have been linked to the Cyclospora parasite include:

Basil.

Cilantro.

Raspberries.

Blackberries.

Mesclun lettuce.

Snow and snap peas.

Pre-packaged salad mix.

This is how the current outbreak south of the border unfolded and how Canadian health officials reacted.

May 13, 2026

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says this is when the first illnesses from the C yclospora parasite started.

June 30

Michigan state health officials say as of this date, more than 170 cases have been reported across several counties compared with around 50 cyclosporiasis cases per year typically.

July 8

The Public Health Agency of Canada says it is not investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada and tells CBCNews the parasite is not commonly found on food and is not in drinking water here.

"In the spring and summer, there is usually an increase in Cyclospora infections linked to consuming fresh fruit and vegetables imported from other countries," a spokesperson for PHAC said in an email.

July 16

The FDA and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with state and local partners, investigate a multi-state outbreak of Cyclospora illnesses linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.

WATCH | A food scientist explains Cyclospora: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

Illnesses start occurring between May 13, 2026, and July 13, 2026. Michigan analyzes food exposure details from 190 of the cases of people who reported eating at Taco Bell and shared these findings with CDC.

The FDA says its traceback investigation to try to find the source converged on a single supplier of iceberg lettuce from Mexico used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill.

Meanwhile, health officials in Alberta say they're investigating an uptick in cyclosporiasis. But the province said no connection has been made between the Alberta illnesses and the American outbreak.

July 17

Taylor Farms de Mexico, which provided shredded iceberg lettuce used by Taco Bell locations where sick people ate before becoming ill, is flagged by the FDA as a supplier. The company announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

Health officials in Quebec say that since the beginning of the year, 85 cases of cyclosporiasis have been reported, compared to 30 cases in 2025 for the same period (average of 32 cases annually between 2022 and 2025).

"As in previous years, most Quebec cases are thought to be linked to travel exposure, primarily in Mexico," a spokesperson for Quebec's Ministry of Health and Social Services said in an email.

No Quebec cases appear to be associated with the outbreak in Michigan, they said.

July 18

On July 17, the FDA said Taylor Farms de Mexico, based in Guanajuato and also known as Taylor Fresh Foods, announces that it is voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

A recall notice put out by Taylor Fresh Foods includes Marketside-brand iceberg lettuce products available at Walmart in the U.S.

July 19

The FDA points to the complexity of detecting Cyclospora, saying its laboratory experts concluded a new sample of shredded lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico tested positive for Cyclospora during import examination at the U.S.-Mexico border. This ended up being a false positive, the FDA said.

July 20

On social media, FDA officials clarify there is still "overwhelming epidemiological data" supporting a large voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.

The Public Health Agency of Canada says is still not currently investigating any Cyclospora outbreaks in Canada.

World.title: The pyramid is back: Dance Moms is getting an unauthorized parody musical
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A trip to the Abby Lee Dance Company meant tears, tutus and grown women fighting over whose eight-year-old deserved the front row.

The 2010s reality show Dance Moms followed an elite group of young dancers — and their dramatic mothers — as they trained and competed under intense pressure.

But the real main event of the Lifetime reality hit was always Abby Lee Miller: a woman who built a career out of ripping apart little girls' chassés and ranking them best-to-worst on a pyramid every single week.

Some of Miller's chastising lines included "save your tears for the pillow" and "I wasn't put on this Earth to make her feel special," among many others.

Now, nearly seven years after the show ended, the show is getting the parody musical treatment

Titled The Pyramid: An Unauthorized 'Dance Moms' Musical, the show now in development all started with a simple question: What if Dance Moms was made into a musical?

That's what college friends James Stryska and Isabelle Grace Blankenship asked each other while wandering through a Goodwill thrift store in Greensboro, N.C., several years ago.

Now they're the show's music and lyrics team, alongside a crew of fellow Dance Moms fans to help them bring the show to life.

What started as a college project turned into their first original song, My Little Kendall, which they posted in 2023 on TikTok. The video racked up more than five million views. The huge response wasn't just coming from fans. Former Dance Moms cast members showed up in the comments with their support.

"It was a really great feeling," Blankenship said. "We were like, 'Oh my gosh, Christi's reaching out, Jill's reaching out.'"

The viral moment also caught the attention of L.A.-based producer Logan Clark, who worked on Dance Moms during its original run. Tye Blue, director and co-creator of Titaníque, another hit parody musical built around Céline Dion, joined as creative producer.

Abby Lee Miller, centre, and dancers Kendall Vertes, left, and Jojo Siwa, right, walk onstage to accept the favourite reality award for Dance Moms during Nickelodeon's 28th annual Kids' Choice Awards on March 28, 2015, in Inglewood, Calif. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Scrolling through TikTok, Clark said he stumbled across the video and immediately saw the potential.

"I kind of sat up and I was like, 'Oh my God ... this could actually happen.'" he said, describing himself as the Dance Moms' "pseudo-husband" back in the day.

As the show's talent co-ordinator, he'd often help get the girls where they needed to be, manage schedules and even handle day-to-day emergencies around their homes — like clogged toilets.

For him, a musical made sense. Dance Moms was supertheatrical — a group of talented young dancers, a whole lot of drama and of course, Abby Lee Miller's pyramid. Miller herself even showed up to an early showcase to offer support.

"Dance Moms was introduced right when social media was taking off," Clark said. "It kind of ran so everybody else could walk. I think for generations it will stay in pop culture."

Craving 'that old school ridiculousness'

And that staying power is real. Long after the cameras stopped rolling, Dance Moms never disappeared. Miller's jabs became viral sounds on TikTok. Old arguments between moms and kids became clips and new audiences became obsessed with the chaos years after it originally aired. Search for the show on TikTok and you'll find more than one million videos.

"It's the perfect kind of show to be clipped for TikTok," comedian and pop culture critic Ashley Ray said. "You see one weird moment and suddenly you're asking, 'Why is this woman yelling at children?'

"I think people sort of crave that old school ridiculousness, that level of drama."

Dancers Maddie Ziegler, left, and Siwa attend Nickelodeon's 2016 Kids' Choice Awards at The Forum on March 12, 2016, in Inglewood, Calif. The two went on to have breakout careers after Dance Moms wrapped. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)

The show's stars continue to make headlines, too.

Maddie Ziegler went from Sia's breakout music-video muse to Hollywood actor, starring in films like My Old Ass and Fitting In.

JoJo Siwa went from a kid-pop star with a multimillion-dollar hair bow empire to a viral personality, shocking fans with her "bad girl" rebrand, claims of originating gay pop and later nabbing a spot on Celebrity Big Brother, where she fell for a Love Island alum.

And Miller stayed in the headlines, too. In 2016, she pleaded guilty to bankruptcy fraud in Pittsburgh, Pa., and spent eight months in federal prison.

Back to the top of the pyramid

Ray says the show stuck around because it captured something that feels familiar to younger generations on social media: constant competition.

"Every week now, everyone gets to create their own pyramid."

Whether it's ranking celebrities, debating who is "flopping" or deciding who deserves the spotlight, Ray said the internet has taken on the same culture of public scrutiny that made Dance Moms so compelling.

The creators behind the new parody musical know audiences will come for the quotes and chaos — and promise them. But they also want to showcase the relationships behind the scenes.

"It's a love letter," Blankenship said. "The show is centred around … mother-daughter relationships and the intricacies."

"We're not trying to make a show that's just all jokes," Stryska added. "These are real people with real experiences."

The team is documenting their progress on social media and crowdfunding the project, with the goal of taking Dance Moms back to the top of the pyramid and onto the stage.

World.title: Sask. Roughrider in fatal crash was driving on wrong side of divided highway: RCMP
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan RCMP say Roughriders player and captain Jayden Dalke was driving the wrong way down a highway when he crashed into another SUV. Both drivers died. Police also said Dalke's vehicle was tied to a reported gas-and-dash half an hour earlier.

Saskatchewan Roughriders linebacker Jayden Dalke was driving the wrong way on the highway with alcohol and cannabis in his vehicle before the crash that killed him and another driver, RCMP say.

Saskatchewan RCMP sent a news release Monday morning saying officers responded to a crash Saturday night at 9 p.m. CST.

RCMP say investigation found Dalke had been driving a silver SUV northbound in the southbound lane on Highway 11 between Regina and Lumsden. The entire stretch of Highway 11 between Regina and Lumsden is divided, with two lanes in each direction.

Dalke's SUV collided with a black SUV about nine kilometres southeast of Lumsden.

Both drivers died in the crash and both were the only ones in their vehicles.

Bhishma Rajyaguru, 22, of Regina was identified as the driver of the other vehicle.

The families of Rajyaguru and Dalke, 30, who was from Leduc, Alta., have both been notified.

Sask. RCMP say 22-year-old Bhishma Rajyaguru died in a fatal crash near Lumsden, Sask., on Saturday night. (Submitted by Dakshesh Raval)

At a news conference Monday, RCMP spokeswoman Mandy Maier asked people to be kind in their online comments out of respect for the grieving families.

"There's a lot of people who are hurting right now," Maier said. "There are two people deceased. This is extremely tragic."

Rajyaguru​'s friends have started an online fundraiser in the wake of his death.

"His parents in India are currently facing the nightmare that no parent should ever have to endure: the loss of their chil​d," the page for the campaign says.

​"We, his friends here in Canada, are coming together to ensure that Bhishma is transported back home so his family can hold him one last time and lay him to rest​."

The fundraiser organizers described Rajyaguru as a "beautiful soul, a best friend, and a beacon of light," and called the crash as "a senseless tragedy that has shattered the hearts of everyone who knew him.​"

Police have identified 22-year-old Bhishma Rajyaguru as a victim of the fatal crash near Lumsden, Sask., on Saturday night. In an online fundraiser, his friends say they have 'lost a beautiful soul, a best friend, and a beacon of light.' (Submitted by Dakshesh Raval)

At the news conference, Maier told reporters that no more details were available about the alcohol and cannabis found in Dalke's vehicle.

Maier said RCMP did not receive any reports about a vehicle travelling the wrong way on the highway prior to the crash.

However, she revealed that RCMP received a report at 8:27 p.m. CST about a silver SUV having left a gas station in Lumsden without paying for fuel, and that further investigation found it was Dalke's SUV.

She also acknowledged the RCMP could have released information about the crash earlier. The information released was determined after "extensive consultation" to ensure the details were accurate.

"News travels fast on social media," Maier said. "And we realize that the RCMP is an official source of information."

Flowers have been placed near Highway 11 southeast of Lumsden where the crash that killed Saskatchewan Roughriders linebacker Jayden Dalke, 30, of Leduc, Alta., and Bhishma Rajyaguru, 22, of Regina happened Saturday night. This photo was taken on Monday, July 20, 2026. (Kirk Fraser/CBC)

Maier said she could not provide an estimate of when autopsies and toxicology tests will be completed. She said collision reconstruction investigations can take months.

RCMP do not usually reveal the names of those killed in crashes, Maier said, pointing to the public interest in this case.

She added that because both occupants were killed and there will be no court proceedings, some questions about the incident may remain unanswered.

"We may never know, right, we have no one surviving from this collision," Maier said. "But the reality is we may never know the answers to many of the questions we all have."

The Riders drafted Dalke in the sixth round of the CFL draft in 2022. Information on the Roughriders website says Dalke was returning to Regina after spending the team's bye week in Leduc.

Roughriders general manager Jeremy O'Day spoke to media about Dalke on Monday morning, before RCMP had released details of the crash.

"In football he was tough and reliable, accountable. Never wanted to let anyone down. He was someone that always wanted to do good for his teammates."

Sask. Roughrider in fatal crash was driving on wrong side of highway: RCMP | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 4:01 Saskatchewan Roughriders' linebacker and captain Jayden Dalke was driving on the wrong side of Highway 11 before the fatal crash, police confirmed Monday. Officers responded to the crash late Saturday, and located alcohol and cannabis inside the SUV.

O'Day offered condolences on behalf of the CFL.

"To Jayden's family, his friends, anyone that that has come in touch with Jayden. You know, we're deeply saddened by this tragic event," said O'Day.

The Lumsden RCMP detachment is investigating the crash with the help of an RCMP collision reconstructionist.

World.title: Trump tells Carney to take action on wildfire smoke during World Cup chat
World.content: U.S. President Donald Trump personally told Prime Minister Mark Carney to stop poisoning American air and take action to put out wildfires burning across the country. Trump said he raised the issue of wildfire management with Carney when the two leaders appeared together to watch the World Cup Final between Argentina and Spain in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. "I told him, I mean, 'You got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air. Our air has been poisoned,'" Trump said at Joint Base Andrews after the game. The U.S. president said he has a "good relationship" with Carney before reiterating his threat to impose financial penalties on his northern neighbour for the wildfires' impact on U.S. air quality. "If we can help them, we'll help them. But maybe they should pay some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs. But it was terrible," Trump said. "I mean you had businesses closing in particular Michigan." WATCH | Carney explains what he told Trump about Canada's wildfires: Carney says he told Trump that Canada is 'managing' the wildfires | Duration 1:52 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he 'made very clear' the scale of investments and resources Canada is putting on the front lines to fight wildfires across the country when he spoke to U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend. On Sunday, Trump said he might 'do some tariffs' on Canada if wildfire smoke drifting into U.S. states didn't abate. Carney said Monday he had "made very clear" to Trump that Canada was doing its utmost to control the wildfires. During recent conversations with the U.S. president, Carney told CBC News that he had conveyed the size of the problem, including "the scale of the forest that Canada is blessed with — eight times the size of Texas — [and] the fact that we have effectively drought conditions that have extended from the equivalent of Texas all the way to Minnesota, to put it in American terms." Carney also said he had highlighted Canada's investments in firefighting: "$12 billion in recent years, but fundamentally more than 5,000 brave women and men — firefighters — on those front lines." The prime minister also said he underscored Canada's contributions during American disasters. Managing the situation was "a complex issue," Carney acknowledged. "It's one we're managing and we'll continue to do that." Last week, cities in Michigan shut down beaches, splash pads, the Red Oaks water park and even indoor pools because of the toxic smoke that blanketed Michigan and other northern U.S. states. The Detroit Free Press reported that dozens of workers at Ford's Michigan assembly plant were taken to hospital after inhaling wildfire smoke inside non-air-conditioned plants. Trump's threats over wildfires Trump first threatened to make Canada pay for the cost of U.S. air quality in a Friday social media post when he joined some Republican House representatives' broad criticism of Canada's forest management practices calling them "wilful negligence." "We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air," the president wrote in a social media post on Friday. "This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying." This morning, I met with federal workers in Ottawa who are supporting the wildfire response efforts in Northwestern Ontario and across the country. This is one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history due to extreme heat waves and record-breaking dry conditions.… pic.twitter.com/ubS7Gupgam —MarkJCarney Canadians "prefer to focus on helping one another," Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson said during a media conference in Prince George, B.C., on Monday, referring to past assistance Canada has provided to fighting wildfires in the United States. "We want to focus on being good neighbours and good allies." The federal government is doing "what we can do" to combat wildfires, he said, outlining measures to train new firefighters, procure more water bombers, support the provinces in delivering emergency services and develop new firefighting technologies. "Extreme weather is a global challenge and we have to recognize that we're doing our part by trying to be a clean and conventional energy superpower," he said. "The world will be better off if we all work together as opposed to pointing fingers at one another." During a wildfire briefing in Toronto on Monday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford described Trump's comments as "disappointing to say the least." Smoke from wildfires in northwestern Ontario blanketed Toronto last week. (Cole Burston/The Canadian Press) "With all the assets the U.S. has, he's sitting there complaining," Ford said. "Why don't you send up some water bombers? Why don't you start helping us, like we would help you in a heartbeat? "You should support your neighbours. That's my message to the president." On Friday, Ford reminded the U.S. president, and other Republican legislators, it was time to repay the efforts Canada undertook to restore electricity in the U.S. after Hurricane Helene in 2024 and the California wildfires last year. "If there's some politicians out there chirping away, well maybe what you should do rather than complain is send support, send help, because we have done the exact same thing for our American friends. That's what you're supposed to do," Ford said. The premier said he thinks Americans are good neighbours but need to start acting that way. U.S. senator proposes sanctions Last week, Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno promised to introduce new legislation to sanction Canada for what his office called the "wildfire pollution emergency." The text of that bill, the Canada Fire Act, posted on Moreno's website, gives Trump the power to declare if smoke originating from Canada over the last 12 months found its way into the U.S. WATCH | Ford on wildfire comments from U.S. officials: 'Rubbish': Ontario premier responds to Trump's wildfire tariff threat | Duration 3:51 U.S. President Donald Trump raised the possibility of imposing punitive tariffs over Canadian wildfire smoke crossing the border. Ontario Premier Doug Ford called Trump's words a 'bunch of rubbish,' and pointed to wildfires burning in the U.S. If so declared, the bill, which has yet to be introduced to the Senate, sets out stiff financial penalties for any Canadian official, from the prime minister to lower-level officials, involved in wildfire management. Those penalties include halting loans to entities owned or controlled by the Canadian government, stopping any imports to the U.S. of anything produced by a Canadian government-owned entity and banning any officials from entering the U.S. if they have a hand in the wildfire response. As an interim measure, the legislation asks U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to consider kicking out Canada's ambassador, chief of mission and more than a dozen other officials right down to the embassy spokesperson.

World.title: Scale of Calgary-wide search for missing 11-year-old boy 'very rare,' police say, as search enters 5th day
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. As the search for a missing 11-year-old boy entered its fifth day on Monday, Calgary police said the scale of the city-wide search is "very rare," with hundreds of officers and volunteers involved. At a news conference on Monday, police said roughly 500 people have assisted with the search, covering approximately 6,500 kilometres. "This is absolutely not typical for a missing person file," Calgary police acting Staff Sgt. Scott Guterson said. "Searches of this degree are very, very rare in Calgary." Guterson asked the public to continue checking their yards, garages, open vehicles, RVs, sheds, pools or anywhere else a child would go. "We're going to keep hoping that he is alive, and we're going to keep acting as if he is alive, to bring him home as soon as humanly possible." Police released new CCTV footage of the boy they say was captured Thursday at 12:34 p.m. from a business adjacent to McKnight Boulevard and Centre Street N.W. The video was captured prior to previously released footage, Guterson said, in hopes that it will aid with the search. WATCH | Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy: Police release new CCTV footage of missing 11-year-old Calgary boy | Duration 2:26 On the fifth day searching for Parker, police released a video of the boy recorded Thursday at a business in the area of Centre Street N.W. and McKnight Boulevard. Investigators also gave an update on the scope of the search. As of Monday, police have received and assessed 150 tips from the public, and are reviewing more than 100 hours of CCTV, residential security camera and dashcam footage. Police are asking anyone with information about Parker's location, or who may have CCTV or dashcam footage, to call 403-266-1234 or reach the police's evidence submission portal. When he went missing on Thursday, Parker was seen shirtless, wearing grey shorts, black Skechers shoes and black noise-cancelling headphones. He’s four feet 11 inches tall and weighs approximately 90 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Guterson said Parker is autistic and functions at a two- or three-year-old level. An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) Police ask that any Calgarians choosing to search on their own do not interfere with police operations. They also ask any volunteer searchers to be mindful of the heat, so they do not end up requiring attention that could divert first responders from the search for Parker. Guterson advised the public that if they come across Parker, they should not engage him, but instead call police. He said they believe the boy is non-verbal, and gets agitated when strangers approach him. Police say Parker's family has expressed that he loves Disney music, so officers have been playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles driving in search areas. We know Parker loves Disney music, so officers are playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles in the search area in the hope that it may help draw his attention and encourage him to come out if he is nearby.

This search remains our highest priority. We'll continue… pic.twitter.com/kGAw6R7uMI —CalgaryPolice Child last seen on Thursday After Parker was seen Thursday at his day home in the 0 to 100 block of Connaught Drive N.W. between 11:08 and 11:41 a.m., the boy was seen in the Thorncliffe neighbourhood between 12:30 and 1 p.m., Guterson said. Clothing that’s believed to belong to Parker was found at noon Thursday in the 0 to 100 block of Northmount Drive N.W., police said. An emergency alert was broadcast on Saturday afternoon for Parker. Although police previously said the case did not meet the threshold for an Amber Alert, as foul play is not suspected, Calgary police said the provincial government made an exception in this case. "We are hopeful that expanding the awareness through the Alberta emergency system will generate new information that may help us locate him," said acting Insp. Rod MacNeil . On Saturday, police released a CCTV photo of the boy, captured when he was last seen on Thursday on the 5000-6000 block of Travis Crescent N.E., in hopes it might aid in the search. WATCH | More CCTV footage of Parker: CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary | Duration 0:27 Footage released by the Calgary Police Service on July 19, shows missing 11-year-old, Parker, walking past a home on Travis Crescent N.E. on Thursday, July 16, 2026. On Sunday, police released additional CCTV footage of the boy taken at 12:52 p.m. Thursday in the 5500 block of Travis Crescent N.E. They had released a similar photo the day prior, in hopes it might help the search. Police also said Sunday that search efforts are being increasingly focused on areas connected to Parker's last known movements. Guterson said police know the boy likes water and part of their search has been to check whether he's near bodies of water. He said Parker tends to lock doors behind him, meaning people searching their properties should take the time to check behind doors even if they're locked. Family issues statement In a statement, Parker's family said they have been living "every parent's worst nightmare" since he went missing. "Every hour that passes without knowing where he is or whether he is safe has been incredibly difficult for us," the family said in its statement, sent out by CPS on their behalf shortly after Saturday afternoon's emergency alert. The family implored people to continue searching their properties for Parker. "Parker experiences the world in his own way. He may not respond when his name is called, and he can become frightened when approached by people he does not know," the family said. "Parker is deeply loved, and he is missed immensely. We just want our son home." An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) CPS said it is aware of AI-generated, altered and unverified images of Parker or his whereabouts circulating online, and cautioned the public against viewing or sharing the content. "Unverified images, videos and claims can create confusion, spread misinformation and divert investigative resources away from credible leads that may assist in locating Parker," CPS said in a social media post on Monday. Situations like this warrant emergency alert, advocate says For Calgary mom Stephanie Karas, Saturday afternoon's emergency alert came far too late. "We've gotten alerts for tornadoes that have not touched down. We've gotten alerts for less, so I don't know why there wasn't," she said. Karas, a mother of two children with autism, says she's lobbying the municipal and provincial governments to create an emergency alert protocol specifically for situations like this. "Why isn't there something for vulnerable youth and adults that aren't equipped?" Karas said. WATCH | Why there are calls to expand Amber Alerts as police search for autistic Calgary boy: "It's long overdue, so somebody's got to start it," she said. "And if the people of Calgary have to start it and are motivated behind Parker, then that's what we'll do." MacNeil said Calgary police indicated to the province that "it may not be a true Amber Alert, but we need to reach as many Calgarians as we can in such a short amount of time." "The government stepped up right away, made that exception and we were able to get that alert out," he said. In a statement to CBC News, the provincial government said it "worked closely with CPS to assess the situation and determined that this measure to increase the public’s awareness of this missing child in these extremely particular circumstances was important."
