World.title: Joey Salceda joins Marcos Cabinet as Presidential Legislative Liaison Office chief
World.content:
Salceda, who holds the rank of secretary, will lead the office that bridges the gap between the executive and legislative

MANILA, Philippines – Veteran legislator and former Albay governor Joey Salceda is set to join the Marcos Cabinet as head of the Presidential Legislative Liaison Office (PLLO), Malacañang confirmed Tuesday, July 21.

As chief of the office that bridges the gap between the executive and legislative, Salceda will also hold the rank of secretary. The previous head of the PLLO, Adrian Bersamin, was an undersecretary. Bersamin left his post in November 2025 after he was accused of involvement in flood control corruption.

Salceda was a long-time representative of the 2nd District of Albay, and former governor of the province. In the 2025 midterm elections, the administration-backed Salceda lost to former Albay governor Noel Rosal. The one-year ban on appointing losing 2025 candidates lapsed on May 13.

Salceda had chaired several committees in the House, including those on appropriations, ways and means, economic affairs, and trade and industry.

Marcos’ appointment is Salceda’s comeback to the executive. Back in 2007, he served as then-president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s chief of staff for just over a month. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] Ivana Alawi, a promised iPhone, and the siren call of online gambling
World.content:
Betting on 'responsible gaming' as an innocuous way to entertain oneself is a fool's exercise, and content creators pushing for it may drive vulnerable people to ruin

Ivana Alawi is a powerhouse Philippine content creator with currently over 51 million Facebook followers, more than 24 million TikTok followers, and nearly 21 million subscribers on YouTube.

She has made a name for herself for friendliness and authenticity, and while that may be the case, she is now in the spotlight following a brand ambassadorship with Casino Plus to promote responsible gaming — or responsible gambling, as it were.

The premise is simple: Alawi purchases P4.28 million in iPhone 17 Pro Max units — 100 in all — and has a promotion to give them away for free. All you have to do is follow her “CP Fam” at Casino Plus, and comment in the right post to be part of the eventual drawing of the iPhone winners.

As of writing, there were over 24 million comments on that particular video post, getting Alawi a lot of engagement, and some 432,000 comments on the Casino Plus post asking people what color iPhone they want.

The number of comments would indicate that Casino Plus has garnered a following as a result, and at 2.8 million Facebook followers at present, they’ve certainly made a dent.

It’ll only cost you potentially constant exposure to gambling ads after the follow as a result.

Getting you on board was the easy part

The insidious nature of the onboarding process to get people gambling is simple, but takes time to complete.

It starts with a seemingly risk-free attempt to get you to join a promotion. That promotion, where you follow Casino Plus or some other gambling app’s social media account, will gradually introduce online gambling ads into your social media feed — whether it’s Facebook or a different sort of social media platform — and eventually get you to try online gambling.

The idea is that once you’re exposed to or eventually trying out gambling online, you’re more easily influenced into doing it again (and again, and again, repeat ad nauseam) at a later time.

The algorithms of social media platforms, such as Facebook or YouTube, will handle the erosion of your personal mental defenses. Since you followed Casino Plus as part of Alawi’s giveaway, maybe you’ll start seeing or expecting gambling-adjacent content to populate your Facebook feed, and that drip-feed of gambling content — which casinos try to neuter as “responsible gaming” — aims to wear you down through repeated exposure.

Leading the vulnerable to ruin

Content creators seeking a happy financial outcome might be buoyed by the online casino boom, but the business itself stinks, in the same way that Philippine offshore gaming operators did back in the day.

It’s just repurposing the same kind of stink to appear more fragrant, and masking the scent may make people who are vulnerable, whether through desperation or a predilection towards risk, want to strike out at online slots. I worry about this because while people can “gamble responsibly,” not everyone does, and not everyone can.

I say this as someone who avoids playing even videogames with paid randomization mechanics for acquiring loot (also known as gacha mechanics) because I am one of those vulnerable folks and I actively avoid paid games of chance when I can.

If I followed Casino Plus and their posts (or whatever gambling ad content social media might impress upon me) wore me down to try an online casino, I might spend an unsafe amount of money vying for a significant win, because my brain can obsess about winning in that manner.

Betting on “responsible gaming” as an innocuous way to entertain oneself is a fool’s exercise, and content creators pushing for it may drive vulnerable people to ruin.

Pagcor offers help, but is also part of the problem

In May, the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (Pagcor) announced it had set up the 24/7 National Problem Gambling Helpline to connect troubled gamblers and their families with counselors who may be able to help them navigate the treachery of gambling unabated.

Pagcor is part of the problem though, because while it regulates gambling, it still advertises it as “responsible gaming” while also acknowledging the problems of irresponsible gambling all the same.

As Pagcor Chairman and CEO Alexander Tengco said in a keynote speech for the helpline, “This National Problem Gambling Helpline that we are launching today reflects Pagcor’s commitment to ensure that the gaming industry remains productive, well-governed, humane, and accountable.”

“Pagcor is aware that for many, gaming is just a form of leisure and recreation, but for some, what may start as entertainment can gradually lead to financial strain and ruin, emotional distress, damaged relationships, and isolation,” he added.

Unfortunately, it aims to provide psychological support, assistance, and referrals to people they’ve infected with the gambling bug. This triaging of people with problems is itself a problem, and one that would be more adequately addressed if the country had a better social safety net.

That said, Pagcor and any regulatory frameworks — whether it be the Department of Trade and Industry, the self-regulating Ad Standards Council, or even the National Privacy Commission (Can you imagine the data privacy problems of online giveaways?) — that oversee paid online s would certainly be better served if they took influencers aside and told them, “No,” instead of allowing said content creators to be the gateway to a world of chance and circumstance where the house always wins. – Rappler.com

World.title: Chel Diokno: Legal expertise in the impeachment spotlight
World.content:
Prosecution counsel Rep. Chel Diokno makes a manifestation during day six of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 15, 2026.

'I've been in practice for almost 36 years, I am used to court proceedings,' Chel Diokno says a day after his impeachment court performance that led to an approved request for Duterte's financial records

Congressman Jose Manuel “Chel” Diokno was calm, cool, and collected amid persistent questioning from senator-siblings Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano on Tuesday, July 21, during the seventh day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Diokno articulated the importance of the prosecution’s motions to subpoena Duterte’s financial records and rebutted claims that their request amounted to a fishing expedition. At the end of the proceedings, the court ruled in their favor.

“This is a big step forward insofar as the presentation of Article 2 (unexplained wealth) is concerned,” Diokno said on Wednesday, July 22.

Play Video

The impeachment court is a familiar ground for Diokno, who also served as one of the private prosecutors in the unfinished impeachment trial of then-president Joseph Estrada from 2000 to 2001. That proceeding was aborted after the second People Power uprising forced Estrada out of Malacañang.

Today, Diokno is one of the 11 public prosecutors in Duterte’s trial. It’s a role that became increasingly likely as early as May 2025, after the victory of his party-list group, Akbayan, became certain. That trial, though, did not push through after the Supreme Court declared the House’s impeachment of Duterte as unconstitutional.

Since then, he has expressed readiness to prosecute Vice President Duterte.

“We have long called for accountability of our top officials. We all know that impeachment is the only way we can hold an incumbent high-ranking official accountable,” he said in a Rappler interview in July last year.

He was elected to the same prosecutor role in May this year, after the House impeached Duterte for a second time.

Diokno carries forward a family legacy rooted in law and public service. He is the son of the late statesman Jose Diokno, widely regarded as the father of human rights advocacy in the Philippines, and the grandson of former Supreme Court justice Ramon Diokno.

A philosophy graduate from the University of the Philippines, he pursued his law degree in Northern Illinois University and qualified for the Illinois Bar in 1986. His father’s death later brought him back to the Philippines, where he went on to pass the Philippine Bar in 1988.

Early in his legal career, he practiced at the Diokno Law Office and later took on the role of litigation head and partner at Moncupa, Diokno & De Los Reyes Law Firm.

In 2003, Diokno became chairman of the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), the Philippines’ oldest network of human rights lawyers. Six years later, he served as the founding dean of the De La Salle University College of Law, now called the Tañada-Diokno School of Law.

Diokno dedicated much of his legal work to providing free legal representation to marginalized sectors and victims of state abuses. These include:

MV Doña Paz disaster: Diokno was one of the lawyers who fought for justice for more than 4,000 lives claimed after the passenger ferry collided with oil tanker MT Vector, making it the biggest maritime disaster in the Philippines. Together with US counterparts, they pursued a class-action civil suit that took nearly three decades to resolve.

Manalo brothers: He successfully petitioned the Supreme Court to issue a landmark Writ of Amparo for Raymond and Reynaldo Manalo, who were abducted in Bulacan for being suspected members of the New People’s Army.

Maria Ressa cyber libel case: He served as counsel of the Nobel Peace Prize laureate. He argued that the case posed a threat to press freedom and the country’s justice system.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Diokno had also established his Free Legal Helpdesk which sought to provide pro-bono legal assistance to those who could not afford them. He was also elected chairperson of the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation in 2022.

He held advisory positions in the government. He was part of the Presidential Human Rights Committee under presidents Corazon Aquino and Fidel Ramos, and was presidential adviser on human rights to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines from 2017 to 2019.

Diokno has drawn the ire of the Vice President’s father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, who in 2020 mocked his appearance and accused him and the opposition of spreading black propaganda amid the COVID-19 pandemic.

Third time’s the charm for Diokno in elective politics. He mounted unsuccessful Senate campaigns in 2019 and 2022, before finally winning a House seat in 2025, representing party-list race topnotcher Akbayan.

His advocacies include labor and economic rights, gender equality, youth education, and anti-corruption. He has been opposed to the death penalty and political dynasties.

On days 6 and 7 of the trial, Diokno spoke on behalf of the prosecution and asserted that the impeachment court has the constitutional authority over the Vice President’s bank and tax records.

Diokno didn’t fluster, even when Senator Pia Cayetano invoked a 1967 Supreme Court ruling on a case whose respondent was his father. Diokno said a subpoena is not intrusive, as opposed to a search warrant, which was the subject of that landmark decision.

Play Video

Diokno, after the crucial win, said his years of litigation experience proved to be beneficial in the impeachment court.

“That’s a big challenge. It’s tiring to stand (at the court) for hours. But I can say I have some experience arguing in front of the Supreme Court and other courts. That probably helps me a lot,” Diokno said.

“I’ve been in practice for almost 36 years, I am used to court proceedings,” he added. – Rappler.com

Patricia Fontilar is a journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman and the managing editor of Tinig ng Plaridel, the official student publication of the UP College of Media and Communication. She is currently a Rappler intern.

World.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] An open letter to the Philippine Senate
World.content:
IMPEACHMENT COURT. Senators wear crimson robes as the upper chamber convenes as an impeachment court for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on May 18, 2026.

We deserve leaders who inspire trust instead of division, confidence instead of exhaustion, and hope instead of cynicism

Dear Senate President Gatchalian and Honorable Members of the Senate,

I write this letter not as a tax expert, but simply as a Filipino citizen and taxpayer who still believes in the dignity of public service.

Many of us grew up believing that the Senate is the highest deliberative body in the country—a place where wisdom, civility, and statesmanship rise above anger, pride, and political theater. Sadly, many Filipinos no longer see it that way.

Over the past several weeks, I have traveled from Australia to Canada, the United States, and now Europe, promoting the Philippines as an investment destination. Yet almost everywhere I go—even in China—the same question comes up: “What is happening in your Senate?” Instead of talking about our economic reforms, investment opportunities, and the potential of the Filipino people, I often find myself explaining the political turmoil back home. That is a burden no Filipino should have to carry while representing our country abroad.

While our people struggle with rising prices, recover from natural disasters, and endure one corruption controversy after another, many have watched—some even entertained—by the endless livestreams, public feuds, grandstanding, and political drama that increasingly define our national discourse. The Senate should never become a stage for performance when the nation is crying out for leadership.

Regardless of political affiliation, majority or minority, every senator has the solemn duty to protect not only the Constitution but also the dignity and credibility of the Senate itself. Passion is welcome. Accountability is essential. But respect, humility, professionalism, and self-restraint must never be sacrificed.

The world is watching. Investors, development partners, and millions of Filipinos around the globe look to the Philippine Senate as a reflection of our democracy. Let us give them a reason to admire our institutions—not question them.

The Filipino people deserve a Senate that spends more time solving national problems than creating political spectacles. We deserve leaders who inspire trust instead of division, confidence instead of exhaustion, and hope instead of cynicism.

We expect more from our senators because the Philippines deserves better.

Respectfully,

Mon Abrea

A Filipino citizen and taxpayer

Mon Abrea is a Global Tax Policy Expert and Chief Tax Advisor of the Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal), the Philippines’ premier international tax advisory and investment consulting tirm. A graduate of Harvard, with executive education at Oxford and advanced tax policy studies at Duke, he is known as “The Philippine Tax Whiz” and a leading advocate of genuine tax reform, advising multinational corporations, foreign investors, and policymakers. Follow him @askthetaxwhiz

World.title: For experts, blanket phone ban in schools is not the way to go
World.content:
Currently, the Department of Education prohibits the use of phones and other electronic gadgets during class time, except for academic purposes and emergencies. Students can still use their devices during recess or breaks.

MANILA, Philippines – Instead of an outright ban on mobile phones and other gadgets in schools, local medical experts are recommending age-based regulation.

The Philippine Mental Health Association (PMHA) and the Philippine Psychiatric Association (PPA) raised the suggeston as the House committees on basic education and health held a joint hearing on six bills seeking to either ban or regulate on-campus gadget usage on Monday, July 20.

Dr. Carolina Uno-Rayco, PMHA national executive director, laid out what’s at stake: “Excessive screen time is fueling a youth mental health crisis. More than three hours of social media daily doubles depression and anxiety risks, while more than four hours links to ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) symptoms, sleep loss, and reduced focus.”

According to the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment, around 41% of Filipino students said they get distracted using digital devices, which has affected learning of mathematics lessons. (READ: PH still among lowest in math, science, reading in global student assessment)

Currently, the Department of Education (DepEd) prohibits the use of phones and other electronic gadgets during class time, except for academic purposes and emergencies. Students can still use their devices during recess or breaks.

Pasig City Representative Roman Romulo, chairman of the House basic education panel, described the DepEd’s policy on gadgets as unclear and ineffective, urging education officials to rethink the protocol.

Romulo said he wants to ensure that students would be more focused on lessons, following the DepEd’s assessment that around 87% of Grade 11 students were non-independent readers.

For the PMHA, the policy requires stronger legislation for uniform enforcement across schools.

Play Video

Rayco also explained that it is crucial to provide alternative activities to students instead of just enforcing a gadget ban. These activities include sports, physical and social interactions, and other group activities that hone social skills.

While aiming to primarily address the health effects of gadget use, the renewed push for a ban or regulation came following the deadly school shooting in Tacloban City.

Authorities have been looking into the influence of online extremism on two minors who carried out the June 22 shooting, where three students were killed and 20 others injured.

On June 29, the municipal government of Dumanjug in Cebu province enforced a total ban on mobile phones in schools to encourage students to read and interact with their classmates, SunStar Cebu reported.

What experts propose

PMHA’s Rayco suggested the prohibition of gadget use for children aged zero to two years old, then a one-hour cap for children two to five years old. She said this is in line with the recommendation of the World Health Organization.

Meanwhile, the PPA recommended “developmentally-tiered regulation,” which would entail prohibiting gadgets during class time for kindergarten to Grade 3 students, then a shift to “supervised, graduated, and increasingly self-directed use” for older students.

Play Video

Dr. Joan Mae Perez-Rifareal, the PPA’s immediate past president, said the age group of kindergarten to Grade 3 has “the least capacity for self-regulation and the most to lose developmentally from gadget displaced learning and play.”

“Adolescence in particular is the stage in which digital literacy and self-regulation must be actively practiced under guidance and not simply deferred until adulthood,” Rifareal said.

“So, clearly defined exceptions for instructional, health, and emergency use together with due process safeguards such as parental notification and chain of custody protection in cases of gadget confiscation are consistent with clinical evidence…and therefore, visible, supervised, rule-governed use is safer for a child’s development than use driven underground by blanket bans,” she added.

For its part, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) also backs having a “differentiated model” that is determined by age and key stage.

EDCOM 2 Executive Director Karol Mark Yee recommended a “strict no personal device in school policy” for kindergarten to Grade 6, as well as a “managed access policy” for Grades 7 to 12, where devices are used only for purposes of instruction.

Yee said schools must set guidelines on how to store gadgets outside class hours.

The Teachers’ Dignity Coalition told lawmakers that it supports regulation of gadget use, and not an outright ban, as teachers and students alike have to use devices amid a shortage of textbooks.

What House bills say

Two out of the six bills being tackled have the same framework as the experts’ recommendations. However, the measure filed by Asenso Pinoy Representative Henry Oaminal Jr. seeks to regulate screen time of children even outside school premises.

Under House Bill No. 7887, Oaminal proposed prohibiting screen time for children two years old and younger, a one-hour cap for kids two to five years old, and a two-hour cap for those six to 12 years old.

For those 13 years old and above, the bill emphasizes regulation focusing on digital literacy, responsible use, and supervised independence, including measures to discourage excessive or unsupervised gadget use, particularly during nighttime.

Oaminal suggested tapping barangay health workers to help in regulating gadget use of children in home and community settings. In schools, devices would only be allowed for academic purposes during class hours, or in cases where students have health conditions that require the use of gadgets.

EDCOM 2’s Yee said other aspects of the proposals also need to be further studied, including the role of various government agencies in regulation of children’s gadget usage and parallel legislation to protect children from online harms. – Rappler.com

World.title: Army soldier killed in Abra clash gets hero’s welcome in Kalinga
World.content:
The remains of Private First Class Drexler Gumayat, placed in a coffin and draped with a Philippine flag, received a hero’s welcome at the 503rd Infantry Brigade headquarters in Calanan, Tabuk City, Kalinga on July 21, 2026. (Photo Courtesy of the Tabuk CIO)

CAMP MELCHOR DELA CRUZ, Gamu, Isabela- The remains of Army Private First Class Drexler Gumayat received military honors when his flag-draped casket arrived at the 503rd Infantry Brigade headquarters in Tabuk City on Tuesday.

The 34-year-old soldier belonging to the 50th Infantry Battalion was killed in an encounter with 10 armed men in Barangay Apao in Abra’s Tineg town on Monday. The armed group is believed to be members of the communist New People’s Army operating in the Cordillera.

READ: Army troops engage in second clash with communist rebels in Abra

Article continues after this 

After military honors in Abra, Gumayat’s remains were transported by a military helicopter to the 503rd Infantry Brigade headquarters.

Gumayat was given a hero’s welcome before his remains were turned over to his widow and his three children. Gumayat’s coffin was later escorted by soldiers to his home in San Pablo, Bulo, also in Tabuk.

Brig. Gen. Rhenante Salvador, 503rd Infantry Battalion commander, saluted Gumayat’s casket and lauded him for his sacrifice.

“He is not a native of Abra but of Kalinga. He chose to stay there and help in achieving peace. He is our hero,” he said during the military honors.

The battle that cost Gumayat his life was a second encounter with suspected rebels by the Army in Abra.

The first Abra clash took place in Sitio Ambalag, Barangay Lan-ag, in Abra’s Lacub town on July 19. The firefight that started at 12:15 p.m. left two soldiers injured, among them Private First Class Jake Awingan, who was identified in reports. They were airlifted to a government hospital for treatment./coa

World.title: Palace confirms Duterte on approved foreign trip until July 31
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte file photo

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte is out of the country until the end of the month while her impeachment trial is ongoing, Malacanang confirmed Tuesday.

At a press briefing, Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., through the Office of the Executive Secretary, approved Duterte’s foreign trip in several countries from July 16 to 31.

READ: Sara Duterte in The Hague as impeachment trial enters 8th day

Article continues after this 

Castro said Duterte’s “personal trip” itinerary includes Qatar, Germany, the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland, and the Netherlands.

Duterte is currently in The Hague, where his father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, has been detained since March last year while awaiting his trial by the International Criminal Court on Nov. 30.

In March 2025, the former president was arrested by Philippine authorities following an order from the ICC over crimes against humanity charges for being an indirect co-perpetrator in the extrajudicial killings during the anti-drug and anti-criminal campaigns from 2011 to 2019, when he served as Davao City mayor and later on as President.

Defense spokesperson lawyer Michael Poa shared Duterte’s current whereabouts during a press conference before Tuesday’s trial proper.

“As far as I know, she is in the Hague,” Poa said. “But she’ll be back soon.” /dp

World.title: Cash aid, not aerial spraying needed to fight Negros sugarcane pest
World.content:
GROUND BATTLE VS RSSI. Spraying operations continue against the red-striped soft-scale insect (RSSI) in sugarcane farms in Bukidnon province. On Negros Island, sugarcane farmers are seekingwider and faster efforts to fight the pest through aerial spraying, although the governor of Negros Occidental prefers an environment-friendly solution.

BACOLOD CITY — A labor group has urged government officials in Negros Island to stop what it described as “wasteful” aerial spraying against the red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI) infestation and instead provide direct cash assistance to thousands of affected sugar farmers and workers.

In an open letter released to the media on Monday, Roland de la Cruz, president of the National Congress of Unions in the Sugar Industry of the Philippines–Trade Union Congress of the Philippines (NACUSIP–TUCP), raised alarm over the rapid spread of the pest, which has infested more than 78,000 hectares of sugarcane plantations in Negros Occidental and Negros Oriental.

READ: Negros gov seeks ‘green’ solution to sugarcane pest

Article continues after this 

Citing data from the Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA), the labor group said the infestation has reached “catastrophic” levels.

According to NACUSIP–TUCP, the pest has affected 61,242 hectares in Negros Occidental, or 32.18 percent of the province’s total sugarcane area, while 16,970 hectares, or about 34.7 percent of sugar lands in Negros Oriental, have also been infested.

With crop losses estimated at up to 50 percent, the group warned that thousands of farmworkers, sugar mill employees, and agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs) face severe economic hardship.

NACUSIP–TUCP commended Negros Occidental Governor Eugenio Jose Lacson and the Sangguniang Panlalawigan for placing the province under a state of calamity, allowing the release of emergency funds through the provincial Quick Response Fund.

It also praised Negros Oriental Governor Manuel Sagarbarria for creating a provincial task force to address the infestation, while urging the provincial board to declare a state of calamity immediately to unlock additional resources.

Article continues after this 

However, the union said the effectiveness of the government’s response would depend on how emergency funds are spent.

“Our farmworkers cannot afford to let local emergency funds get tied up in bureaucratic red tape,” the group said, urging officials to release financial assistance directly to affected workers and farmers.

Article continues after this 

“Deliver emergency calamity funds directly into the hands of the individuals working the soil,” it added.

The labor group also questioned the SRA’s aerial and drone-based chemical spraying campaign, claiming field experts and sugar workers have documented its failure.

READ: Pest attack in Negros sugar farms worsens

According to NACUSIP–TUCP, the RSSI feeds and reproduces on the underside of sugarcane leaves, making overhead spraying largely ineffective because chemicals reach the upper canopy only while the insects survive and spread to nearby farms.

The group acknowledged that aerial spraying conducted by the SRA in 2025 temporarily slowed the spread of the pest after it first emerged in 2024, but argued that the widespread infestation this year shows the strategy is not a long-term solution.

READ: Labor group asks gov’t to help stop sugar farm infestation

NACUSIP–TUCP called on the SRA and local government units to discontinue costly aerial spraying operations and instead redirect funds to direct crop subsidies and science-based, environmentally sustainable pest management, including biological control measures and targeted ground spraying./coa

World.title: Cebu cops in hot water over alleged car scams
World.content:
INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — Several individuals from Cebu have accused some police officers of victimizing them in car scams.

The complainants filed an administrative case against the implicated officers before the National Police Commission (Napolcom) at the latter’s office in Quezon City on Tuesday, July 21.

In a press briefing after the filing, one of the complainants, businessman Ronald Elpa, alleged purchasing several vehicles from the group of police officers last August.

Article continues after this 

READ: Motorists warned vs scams from messages on traffic violation fines

“They first bring up the relationship, that they’re friends, acquaintances… They said they had special discounts,” Elpa told reporters.

“There were some vehicles that they delivered, some that they didn’t… Until now, they haven’t given us the documents,” he added.

Also at the briefing, co-complainant Baby Villaspin claimed he and a police colonel agreed to evenly split a P260,000 downpayment to purchase a vehicle from the same group.

However, according to Villaspin, the police colonel’s check “bounced,” which meant the bank could not process it, forcing Villaspin to cover the entire P260,000.

Article continues after this 

He further claimed that the vehicle was later taken from his residence and has not been returned despite repeated assurances.

At the presser, Napolcom Commissioner Rafael Calinisan said the commission will conduct a thorough investigation into the allegations.

Article continues after this 

“We’ll be looking at whether there is a connection between these allegations, if there is a larger scheme or a syndicate behind this. We really have to dive deep and check,” Calinisan said. — Written by Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /mr

World.title: ICYMI: Padilla objects to ruling to subpoena Duterte’s financial records
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judge Robin Padilla rose to voice his objection to the ruling of presiding officer Francis Escudero to have the financial records of the vice president subpoenaed during the seventh day of the Vice President Sara Duterte impeahcment trial on Monday, July 20. “If this is our standard,” Padilla said in Filipino, “let’s all just open our bank records, so we can show that we’re not biased.” / dp

World.title: DOH: 1M NCR children vaccinated vs measles-rubella
World.content:
File photo of child vaccination. NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) has vaccinated over one million children aged 6 to 59 months against measles-rubella in the National Capital Region (NCR), obtaining an 87.1% vaccination coverage, the agency said on Tuesday.

The DOH said it recently concluded its Measles-Rubella Supplemental Immunization Activity. The agency kicked off its supplemental immunization activity last January in Mindanao.

READ: DOH eyeing to vaccinate 11 million Filipino children vs measles

Article continues after this 

“As of the end of the campaign on June 30, 2026, NCR achieved an 87.1% vaccination coverage, with 1,045,889 of the targeted 1,200,428 children aged 6 to 59 months receiving the measles-rubella vaccine,” the DOH said in a press release.

“The total also includes 6,100 children whose vaccinations were initially deferred or declined but who were eventually vaccinated, reflecting the success of continued engagement with parents and communities,” the DOH added.

The agency noted that Parañaque, Makati, Manila, Pasay, Navotas, Mandaluyong, Pasig, and Quezon City surpassed the 95% coverage target for providing protection among communities, with Quezon City recording the highest number of vaccinated children at 262,720. It added that 1,092 of 1,715 barangays (64%) in Metro Manila achieved the recommended 95% vaccination coverage.

The DOH then emphasized the importance of routine childhood immunization as it “remains the best way to ensure children are fully protected as they grow.”

It cited that as of May 2026, the NCR leads among all regions in routine measles-rubella vaccination, with 32.32% coverage for the first dose and 32.57% for the second dose. It also said that Quezon City, Pasig, and Makati logged at least 40% coverage, which was “the highest” across the country.

Article continues after this 

“However, these accomplishments are still below the regional target of 54% for May, meaning many children have yet to receive their scheduled vaccinations,” the DOH pointed out.

With this, it called on the parents and guardians with children who missed their routine immunization to visit the nearest health centers. It added that it will continue to coordinate with local government units and partners to ensure that Filipino children are well protected against measles-rubella.

Article continues after this 

“Vaccines provided through the government’s National Immunization Program are safe, effective, and available free of charge,” it added. /mr

World.title: Prosecution presents video of Sara Duterte punching sheriff in Davao
World.content:
Then-Davao City Mayor Sara Duterte confronts sheriff Abe Andres, whom she punched four times for serving a demolition order on houses inside a contested property in Barangay Soliman, Agdao district, Davao City, on July 1, 2011. (Contributed photo)

MANILA, Philippines – The video footage of Vice President Sara Duterte when she was Davao City mayor punching a sheriff was presented at the impeachment trial as the Senate impeachment court tackles Duterte’s alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.

In its line of questioning of National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag, House prosecution lead counsel Rep. Gerville Luistro on Tuesday asked Matibag to state the considerations the NBI uses when investigating threats.

Matibag told the court that “pattern of violence” is among the five factors the NBI uses to determine whether the threat is serious, in accordance with those used by the United States Secret Service.

Article continues after this 

READ: Duterte impeachment trial day 8: NBI’s Matibag to testify on threats

Luistro later asked Matibag what the NBI had assessed about Duterte’s pattern of violence, to which Matibag cited the findings of its task force based on open-source intelligence.

“There we saw an event when our Vice President Sara Duterte was still mayor, where there was a sheriff who wanted to carry out his duty, which was a legal court order for a demolition order, but the then mayor and now vice president did not like it, she called the sheriff and punched the him in the face.” Matibag recounted in Filipino.

The video footage of the incident Matibag referred to was then shown to the court, where Duterte was seen punching the sheriff’s head at least four times.

Matibag is testifying before the impeachment court as the prosecution proves Duterte’s alleged betrayal of public trust after she claimed hiring a hitman to take down Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez. /gsg

World.title: Free eat-all-you-can fruits at Kidapawan’s Timpupo Festival
World.content:
In this 2025 photo, visitors from different provinces flood the two-kilometer stretch of the Cotabato-Davao national highway, where makeshift bamboo tables were laden with fruits offered for free to the public as part of Kidapawan City’s Timpupo Festival. WILLIAMOR A. MAGBANUA

KIDAPAWAN CITY — A fruit galore awaits visitors during the Timpupo (harvest) Festival next month, with the eat-all-you-can fruits on August 18 capping the merrymaking, the city government said.

But instead of a weeklong celebration, this year’s iteration will be held for only two days.

The first day on August 17 will be a celebration of the tri-people (Muslim, Christian, and Indigenous People) and interfaith, highlighting the Somaya Pokiyyab, a traditional ritual of the Obo Manuvu ethnic group to express gratitude and blessing for the success of the occasion.

Article continues after this 

READ: 18 metric tons of free fruits dished out in Timpupo festival

During Somaya Pokiyyab, city officials wear the traditional Obo Manuvu dress and join the IPs, also called Lumads, in the rituals that are usually done in front of the city hall.

These rituals will be followed by the Holy Eucharist in gratitude to the bountiful harvest and blessings bestowed to the farmers of Kidapawan. At night, an interfaith celebration to recognize various denominations will also be held.

On August 18, which is the culmination of the festivity, there will be no more parade, but it will be highlighted by the fruit-eat-all-you-can on the road.

A 2.5-kilometer table made from bamboo will be assembled along the Davao-Cotabato highway, where fruits such as marang, rambutan, banana, lanzones, and durian will be served free to visitors.

Article continues after this 

READ: In Kidapawan City, durians are not just eaten raw, they are grilled

The city government explained that the budget intended for various Timpupo Festival activities had been diverted to support at least 3,000 tricycle drivers and operators in the form of fuel subsidies.

Article continues after this 

By cutting the activities from one week to two days, the city government could save at least P64 million that can be used as additional funds for fuel as well as ensuring food security during the anticipated El Niño devastation expected to hit next month.

The city government is now preparing for the purchase of 15, 000 food packs to assist Kidapawenos once the El Niño phenomenon starts to affect the city./coa

World.title: China Eastern Plans Direct Astana-Shanghai Flights, FlyArystan Adds Chongqing Route
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is set to expand its air connectivity with China as China Eastern Airlines plans to launch direct flights between Astana and Shanghai this autumn, while FlyArystan will open a new route between Almaty and Chongqing in September.

Chair of the Civil Aviation Committee of Kazakhstan’s Transport Ministry Saltanat Tompiyeva met with China Eastern Airlines Senior Vice President for Marketing and Sales Jin Chenhua during a working visit to China, reported the ministry’s press service on July 20.

The officials discussed the launch of direct Astana-Shanghai flights. The airline confirmed strong commercial interest in the route and said it plans to begin operations this autumn after completing the necessary preparations.

The service will initially operate three times a week, with plans to increase frequency to daily flights.

The meeting also covered opportunities to expand air links between Kazakhstan and China. China Eastern expressed interest in increasing the number of flights to Kazakhstan and strengthening cooperation with Kazakh airlines.

China Eastern Airlines is one of China’s three largest state-owned carriers and the country’s second-largest airline. Based in Shanghai, it operates a fleet of 834 aircraft and carried around 150 million passengers in 2025.

FlyArystan launches Chongqing route

Also, low-cost carrier FlyArystan announced the launch of a new international route between Almaty and Chongqing.

The inaugural flight is scheduled for Sept. 23, with services operating twice a week. Flights will depart Almaty on Wednesdays and Saturdays, with return flights from Chongqing on Thursdays and Sundays.

The new service will become FlyArystan’s fifth destination in China, complementing its existing routes to Urumqi, Yining (Kulja) and Xi’an.

The flight time between Almaty and Chongqing will be approximately five hours.

World.title: Kazakhstan Holds Off Global Fertility Decline, For Now
World.content:
ASTANA – As fertility rates continue to fall across much of the world, Kazakhstan is among the countries where births are still above the population replacement level. New data, however, indicate that the country is beginning to mirror the broader global demographic slowdown.

According to the United Nations, the global fertility rate has dropped from around five children per woman half a century ago to roughly 2.2 today, reshaping population structures and creating long-term economic and social challenges for many countries. Much of Europe and East Asia has fallen well below the replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.

Kazakhstan, however, remains above that threshold at 2.57. A continuous belt of countries stretching from Pakistan to Mongolia still records fertility above the replacement level, and Kazakhstan is part of that group.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the country’s population has reached 20.58 million, an increase of more than 76,000 since the start of 2026.

Kazakhstan remains a regional demographic leader

Kazakhstan continues to rank among the region’s demographic leaders. According to available estimates, Uzbekistan records one of the region’s highest fertility rates at around 3.45 children per woman, while the Kyrgyz Republic stands at 2.75. Kazakhstan, at 2.57, remains well above Russia’s 1.46, Armenia’s 1.71, and Belarus’s roughly 1.2.

At the same time, birth numbers in Kazakhstan have started to decline from the unusually high levels recorded during and immediately after the COVID-19 period. According to an analysis by Finprom.kz, 74,100 children were born in Kazakhstan in the first quarter of 2026, down from 77,300 in the same period last year, a decline of 4.2%, or around 3,200 fewer births.

The decline affected both urban and rural areas, though it was sharper in the countryside. Urban births fell by 2.3%, from 46,700 to 45,600, while rural births dropped by 7.2%, from 30,700 to 28,500. No major gender imbalance was recorded. In the first quarter of 2026, 38,000 boys and 36,100 girls were born, compared with 39,600 boys and 37,700 girls a year earlier.

Regionally, the largest number of births was recorded in the Turkistan Region with 10,400 newborns, followed by Almaty city with 7,200, Shymkent city with 6,300, and the Almaty Region and Astana city with 6,200 each. The lowest totals were in the Ulytau Region with 738 births, the North Kazakhstan Region with 1,100, the East Kazakhstan Region with 1,600, and the Abai and Kostanai regions with 1,800 each.

Part of a broader global shift

Experts say Kazakhstan’s recent decline should not be viewed as a demographic crisis, but rather as part of the so-called second demographic transition seen in many countries as education levels rise, urbanization accelerates, women’s labor force participation expands, and the cost of raising children increases.

For years, Kazakhstan stood out from that global pattern by maintaining comparatively high fertility even as many countries saw sustained declines.

According to Aslan Temirkhanov, a medical doctor, specialist in molecular medicine and cell biology, and expert in youth reproductive health, the current decline is not critical and should be interpreted in context.

“We know that during the COVID-19 period, many countries saw a temporary spike in births because people were staying at home and their lifestyles changed. What we are seeing now is partly an adjustment after that peak,” Temirkhanov told The Astana Times.

In other words, Kazakhstan’s recent decline may say less about a sudden demographic breakdown than about normalization after an exceptional period. The more important measure, he suggests, is not the quarterly number of births alone but the country’s broader fertility trajectory over time.

“If we look not just at the absolute number of births but at broader demographic indicators, Kazakhstan still has a high fertility rate. In Russia, for example, the fertility rate is around 1.3. In the European Union it is roughly 1.5. In South Korea it is below 0.8,” he said.

Temirkhanov noted that economic uncertainty is one of the factors shaping reproductive decisions worldwide. In cities, especially Astana and Almaty, the cost of housing, childcare and everyday life can encourage couples to postpone having children or to have fewer children than earlier generations. Women’s educational attainment and labor force participation have also risen, which is generally associated with later family formation and smaller family size unless strong family support policies are in place.

However, that does not mean Kazakhstan is destined to follow the same path as East Asia or southern Europe. But it does suggest that the country’s demographic future will depend increasingly on how well it manages the social and economic conditions surrounding family life.

Education and healthcare as demographic investments

Temirkhanov said Kazakhstan’s relatively strong fertility rate reflects a combination of factors, including state support for families, cultural norms and the availability of reproductive health education and services. He also pointed to cultural expectations around family, but emphasized that one of the most important factors is comprehensive sexuality education.

“Education affects the quality of family planning, knowledge about contraception, understanding when to see a doctor and awareness of reproductive health services,” he said.

According to Temirkhanov, many young people in Kazakhstan are still unaware that the country has youth health centers offering free counseling and services related to reproductive and mental health.

Kazakhstan has more than 100 youth health centers that provide medical, preventive, psychosocial and legal services to adolescents ages 10 to 18 and young adults ages 18 to 29 on issues related to reproductive and mental health. He cited a 2025 UNFPA study on adolescents and youth ages 15-19 and 20-24, which found low levels of reproductive health knowledge. According to the report, only 11.7% of respondents demonstrated awareness of HIV, including 8.1% of adolescents ages 15-19 and 19.1% of young people ages 20-24.

“Awareness of sexually transmitted infections and their consequences, including infertility if left untreated, was also low. More than 60% of young people do not know enough about these infections, why they need to be diagnosed and treated, or what the consequences can be if they are ignored,” Temirkhanov said.

That matters because untreated infections, misinformation and delayed access to specialist care can all affect fertility outcomes later in life.

Temirkhanov highlighted that Kazakhstan has made notable progress in reproductive healthcare and infertility treatment, particularly through the presidential Ansagan Sabi (long-awaited child) program launched in 2021. The program allocates 7,000 In vitro fertilization (IVF) quotas annually for married couples, with services provided by around 20 clinics nationwide. Over five years, specialists have conducted 28,000 IVF programs, resulting in the birth of 12,000 children, while another 10,000 women are currently pregnant, according to available data. The program’s success rate stands at around 30%, which experts consider high by international standards.

Temirkhanov noted that reproductive health challenges vary significantly between urban and rural areas. In cities, infertility is more often linked to endocrine disorders, stress and physical inactivity. In rural areas, doctors more frequently see advanced inflammatory conditions and untreated pelvic diseases, often due to weaker access to specialized care.

“There is a serious shortage of primary healthcare personnel in villages. Access to specialized care and laboratory testing is generally better in cities,” he said.

Reproductive health myths

Temirkhanov noted that one of the most persistent myths in Kazakhstan is that comprehensive sex education encourages teenagers to become sexually active earlier.

“That is absolutely false. International research consistently shows the opposite: the more informed young people are about reproductive health, infections and consequences, the later their sexual debut tends to be,” he said.

He said Kazakhstan’s average age of sexual debut is currently around 16.8 years, underscoring the need for better education rather than less. Temirkhanov also pointed to misconceptions around HPV vaccination, calling it one of the most important issues in reproductive health.

“The human papillomavirus is a leading cause of cervical cancer, one of the deadliest cancers affecting women. Countries that introduced human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programs more than a decade ago, including Australia and Denmark, have dramatically reduced cervical cancer rates,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s demographic advantage remains intact, but it can no longer be taken for granted. Sustaining it will require a more deliberate strategy that treats reproductive health, family well-being, education and regional healthcare disparities as part of the same policy challenge.

World.title: What Drives Kazakhstan’s Economic Lead in Central Asia?
World.content:
ASTANA — Chinese business publication All China Review on July 16 placed Kazakhstan at the center of Central Asia’s economic growth, citing its output, investment stock, banking system and transit role. Kazakh economists said the country’s position rests on the combined weight of these factors.

Published on the day President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shanghai, the article compares the five Central Asian economies through their scale, structure, financial capacity and links with China.

The structure behind the scale

According to All China Review, Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) reached $306 billion in 2025, accounting for 53.7% of Central Asia’s combined output.

Uzbekistan recorded $147.1 billion, followed by Turkmenistan at $77.4 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic at $21.6 billion and Tajikistan at $17.5 billion.

The gap was also reflected in GDP per capita, which stood at approximately $15,000 in Kazakhstan, compared with $11,600 in Turkmenistan, $3,800 in Uzbekistan, $3,000 in the Kyrgyz Republic and $1,700 in Tajikistan.

The publication links Kazakhstan’s regional position to the structure of its economy, highlighting the contributions of trade, manufacturing and mining, as well as the overall scale of its economy. Trade accounts for close to 20% of gross value added, while manufacturing contributes 13% and mining 11.9%.

It also points to the expansion of manufacturing, digital industries, logistics, financial services and innovation-driven sectors as part of efforts to reduce reliance on commodity exports.

Financial analyst Andrey Chebotarev offered a brief reflection on the article in a post on his Finance.kz Telegram channel.

“Sometimes it is useful to see ourselves through someone else’s eyes,” he wrote.

Capital and financial capacity

Foreign direct investment (FDI) provides one of the widest gaps in the comparison.

Citing United Nations Trade and Development data, All China Review reported that Central Asia’s accumulated inward FDI reached $220.5 billion in 2024. Kazakhstan accounted for $151.3 billion, or 68.6% of the total. Turkmenistan held $44.6 billion, Uzbekistan $16.7 billion, while the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan each accounted for approximately $4 billion.

The figures cover investment accumulated over time, reflecting Kazakhstan’s longer history of attracting projects in energy, mining, infrastructure and other sectors. The publication links this concentration to the size of its market, its location between Europe and Asia, and its financial infrastructure and investment framework.

Kazakhstan also has the region’s largest banking system. Banking-sector assets reached $140 billion as of January 2026, while deposits totaled $96.4 billion.

According to the All China Review, the larger deposit base provides more stable funding for private-sector lending and long-term investment. The figures establish Kazakhstan’s lead in financial scale, though they do not address lending costs, access to credit or competition within the sector.

China ties extend beyond trade

Kazakhstan’s economic relationship with China forms a central part of the article. Bilateral trade reached a record $48 billion in 2025, according to Kazakh government data cited by the publication. The two countries aim to increase that figure to $100 billion by 2030.

Accumulated Chinese direct investment in Kazakhstan stood at approximately $11.4 billion by mid-2025, according to Eurasian Development Bank figures included in the article. All China Review described it as the largest amount among the five Central Asian states and close to one-third of Chinese capital invested in the region.

Transport adds another dimension to the relationship. More than 85% of overland cargo between China and Europe passes through Kazakhstan, while bilateral rail freight reached 35.6 million tons in 2025, up 11% from the previous year.

Kazakhstan has invested more than $35 billion in transport and transit infrastructure over the past seven years, according to the publication. Projects include the Aktau container hub, Kazakhstan’s dry port in Xi’an and the second track on the Dostyk-Moyynty railway.

They support routes connecting China with the Caspian Sea and Europe, including the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

Industrial cooperation is developing alongside trade and transit. Kazakhstan and China have completed 62 joint projects worth $8.7 billion, creating approximately 11,000 jobs.

Another 55 projects valued at $13.5 billion are under development, while a wider portfolio includes 222 proposed projects worth more than $60.5 billion. The sectors range from agricultural processing and metallurgy to unmanned aerial vehicle manufacturing.

Economist Ruslan Sultanov wrote on his Tengenomika Telegram channel that Kazakhstan’s position cannot be attributed solely to territory or natural resources.

“Kazakhstan’s competitive advantage is based not only on its large territory or rich natural resources. It is based on a combination of economic scale, a developed banking system, the region’s largest volume of foreign investment, modern transport corridors and close economic ties with China,” he wrote.

World.title: Kazakhstan Monitors CPC Exports After New Drone Attack on Oil Tanker
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh Energy Ministry is closely monitoring operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) after another drone strike targeted an oil tanker loading Kazakh crude at the consortium’s Black Sea marine terminal overnight on July 20, reported the Kazinform news agency.

The attack came after CPC resumed loading operations following an earlier drone strike on two civilian tankers at the terminal on July 19. According to CPC, the tanker NELSA was loading oil at Single Point Mooring (SPM)-1 when it was struck by an unmanned aerial vehicle. The drone hit the vessel’s starboard stern, triggering a fire on deck and in several compartments.

The fire was extinguished within several hours by the vessel’s loading crew and CPC emergency response teams. CPC tugboats evacuated the ship’s 22-member multinational crew, while the captain and chief officer remained on board. The tanker remained afloat.

Oil loading operations have been suspended while authorities assess the vessel’s condition. No oil spill or ignition of crude in the cargo tanks was reported.

In a statement, the Kazakh Energy Ministry said it remains in constant contact with the CPC regarding the incident.

“According to available information, a UAV attacked the tanker NELSA while it was loading at the CPC marine terminal. The resulting fire was promptly extinguished. There were no casualties, and no oil spill occurred. An assessment of the vessel’s technical condition and the consequences of the incident is currently underway,” reads the ministry’s statement.

The consortium urged its shareholder countries to condemn the repeated attacks and work together to prevent further strikes on critical export infrastructure.

“We expect the CPC participating states to condemn these attacks and, in strict accordance with international law, develop practical measures to stop attacks against infrastructure used to export hydrocarbons produced by international consortia in Kazakhstan,” reads the consortium’s statement.

The latest incident follows Kazakhstan’s earlier condemnation of drone attacks on July 17 and 19 targeting civilian vessels transporting oil through CPC infrastructure in the Black Sea. Both the Foreign Ministry and Energy Ministry described attacks on civilian energy infrastructure as unacceptable and warned that they threaten international energy trade and Kazakhstan’s economic interests.

World.title: Four Parties Complete Candidate Registration for Kurultai Elections as Kazakhstan Advances Preparations
World.content:
ALMATY – Four of the seven political parties approved to contest Kazakhstan’s Aug. 23 Kurultai elections have officially registered their candidate lists with the Central Election Commission (CEC), while the remaining parties continue submitting documents for registration. The CEC also announced that 76 international observers have been accredited to monitor the vote.

The parties that have completed registration are the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Ak Zhol (White Way) Democratic Party, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (OSDP) and the Respublica Party, while the Adilet (Justice) Party, the Auyl (Village) Party and the Baytaq (Vast) Green Party of Kazakhstan are still in the process of registering their candidate lists.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan registered a list of 72 candidates. Having secured more than 5% of the vote in the previous parliamentary elections, it was exempt from paying the election deposit.

The Ak Zhol Democratic Party registered 63 candidates, including 22 women, youth and persons with disabilities, representing 34.9% of the list and exceeding the legally required 30% quota. The party was also exempt from the election deposit after winning 8.41% of the vote in the 2023 Mazhilis elections.

The OSDP submitted a list of 33 candidates, of whom 14 belong to the quota categories of women, youth and persons with disabilities.

The Respublica Party registered the largest list among the four parties, nominating 75 candidates. Women, youth and persons with disabilities account for 38 candidates, or 50.7% of the list, well above the statutory quota.

International observation mission expands

The CEC also accredited 76 international observers representing four foreign countries and three international organizations.

According to Deputy CEC Chair Mukhtar Yerman, the observers include representatives of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights election observation mission.

CEC Chair Nurlan Abdirov said the accreditation of international observers remains open upon nominations submitted through Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and will continue until 6 p.m. on Aug. 17, in accordance with the election calendar.

Earlier, experts gathered to discuss expectations, party roles and participation on July 17 ahead of Aug. 23 Kurultai elections under the new Constitution.

World.title: What Kazakhstan’s Voters Want Beyond Campaign Promises
World.content:
ASTANA — Raising incomes and curbing inflation were priorities for 62.3% and 48.9% of 1,200 respondents, respectively, according to the findings presented at the July 17 Sapar Expert Club meeting in Astana. Experts discussed expectations, party roles and participation ahead of Aug. 23 Kurultai elections under the new Constitution.

Fighting corruption ranked third among respondents’ expectations at 30.3%, followed by the creation of new jobs at 29.8%. The same survey recorded potential electoral participation at 75.1%. This included 37.6% of respondents who expressed a firm intention to vote and 37.5% who said they were likely to participate.

Readiness increased with age, from 69.4% among respondents aged 18-28 to 80.7% among those aged 61 and older. The share of rural respondents certain they would vote was approximately four percentage points higher than the corresponding urban figure.

“Overall, citizens expect parties to participate professionally in resolving specific socioeconomic issues. They view the upcoming elections as an instrument for ensuring quality of life and achieving pressing goals,” said Azamat Baigaliyev, the deputy chair of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development’s (KIPD) management board.

Surveys capture public mood and electoral expectations

The meeting brought together political analysts, academics, leaders of think tanks and research institutes, and doctoral and master’s students.

The institute presented two independent nationwide surveys conducted face-to-face in May. One covered 2,400 respondents and examined perceptions of Kazakhstan’s socio-political and economic situation in the second quarter of 2026. The other surveyed 1,200 people about their political attitudes, intended electoral participation and expectations of parties.

Both studies covered every region of Kazakhstan, including major cities and rural communities. Baigaliyev said their results reflected similar overall trends in public sentiment.

Among the 2,400 respondents, 84.1% considered the socio-political situation favorable or stable, up from 70.4% in the first quarter. A further 76.6% assessed the economy positively, and trust in the president stood at 86.9%.

Trust is built through everyday experience

Political scientist and PhD candidate Nayla Mukhtarova said electoral attitudes should be considered within a broader competition for public trust.

“In today’s world, countries are competing not for votes but for people’s trust in political and state institutions. Public trust does not appear in one day, on voting day or during the campaign period. It is formed every day, when a person receives public services and sees that justice and the law work equally for everyone,” she told The Astana Times.

Mukhtarova said trust in the president and public assessments of individual state institutions should be examined separately.

“Trust in the president and trust in state institutions are, unfortunately, different things today. People do not always perceive a state institution and the president as one and the same. They may trust him but remain dissatisfied with the work of particular institutions, including health care and education bodies or employment services,” she said.

Asked what could strengthen public confidence in the survey findings, Mukhtarova linked their credibility to citizens’ everyday experiences with the state.

“Improving the quality of public services, which citizens encounter every day. The judicial system must also be fair and equal for everyone, because these factors strongly influence citizens’ trust in the state,” she said.

Parties need distinct values and sustained engagement

Political scientist, publicist and interethnic relations expert Talgat Kaliyev questioned whether general party-preference surveys always capture the depth of voters’ political choices.

“When people are asked which party they would vote for, there is a high proportion of socially desirable answers. But when they are asked which specific figures they trust or which initiatives they remember and support, they begin to struggle. Parties should be based not on platforms, which change from election to election, but on values,” said Kaliyev.

He noted that overlapping positions make it difficult for voters to understand what would change if a particular party gained greater influence.

Mukhtarova and Kaliyev shared the view that political engagement should continue beyond election campaigns. Mukhtarova connected sustained engagement with public trust, and Kaliyev said parties should demonstrate their values through consistent responses to major events and policy problems.

“If something happens, a party should speak and explain what systemic changes are needed to prevent it from happening again. Parties should state their position on every major issue and every high-profile event. This is how they increase their visibility and act in accordance with their values,” he said.

He also highlighted parties’ continued reliance on prominent athletes and entertainers to attract public attention, describing this approach as one developed when television played a larger role in political communication.

“Most parties have tried to use the old model by attracting celebrities and athletes. But now, when television is not as popular, completely different and more creative approaches are needed,” he said.

Kaliyev said parties should instead participate in debates where they offer competing responses to specific problems, allowing voters to compare their positions.

Young voters look beyond campaign promises

Among respondents aged 18-28, 65.6% expected their lives to improve over the next year. Mukhtarova and Kaliyev shared the view that younger voters’ optimism and political interest would not translate automatically into support based on campaign messages alone.

“They will not vote simply because there is a good program or a good promise. They will look at what the party has already done and what it is prepared to do next,” she said. “They will demand dialogue from the state, and they will demand concrete results.”

Kaliyev said researchers are still examining how Generation Z’s electoral behavior is formed.

“Generation Z is an entirely unpredictable category. We are still studying how its electoral behavior is formed. They will be politically active in any case, but where that activity is directed depends on how political actors behave today,” he said.

Parties that secure their attention could channel that interest into constructive electoral participation, he said. If they fail to do so, young people will pursue other forms of political expression.

Kaliyev also described public criticism of party lists and candidates on social media as a sign of political involvement rather than a purely negative reaction.

“Discontent expressed on social media about party lists and their composition should not be viewed negatively. On the contrary, it demonstrates that people are not indifferent and are engaged in the reform. (…) They are paying attention to the choice, are informed about the elections and want to express their point of view, so ignoring this discontent would be unwise,” said Kaliyev.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Assaubayeva Nominated for Inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh chess player Bibisara Assaubayeva has been shortlisted for the inaugural FIDE Excellence Awards, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) announced on July 16, as Kazakhstan marks International Chess Day on July 20 with one of the world’s fastest-growing chess communities.

The 22-year-old grandmaster was nominated in the Best Chess Player (Female) category alongside reigning world champion Ju Wenjun, Aleksandra Goryachkina, Koneru Humpy, Tan Zhongyi, Lei Tingjie, Anna Muzychuk, Divya Deshmukh, Vaishali Rameshbabu and Zhu Jiner.

Kazakhstan also received nominations in two additional categories. The Kazakhstan Chess Federation (KazChess) was shortlisted for Best Federation, while Kazakhstan’s men’s and women’s national teams were nominated for Best Team.

Established this year, the biennial FIDE Excellence Awards recognize outstanding achievements across the global chess community over a two-year cycle. Winners will be selected by an expert panel and announced during the awards ceremony in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, in September alongside the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad.

Chess continues to grow in Kazakhstan

The nominations coincide with International Chess Day, celebrated annually on July 20. According to the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, more than 278,000 people play chess regularly across the country, including approximately 128,000 in rural areas. Kazakhstan has more than 7,000 specialized chess clubs, while chess is taught as a compulsory or elective subject in 1,500 schools, reaching over 50,000 children.

More than 5,500 Kazakh players hold official FIDE ratings, which is the highest number in Central Asia, and participate regularly in international competitions. The country also hosts more than 3,800 domestic tournaments annually, attracting around 118,000 registered competitors. Experts estimate that more than 400,000 accounts from Kazakhstan are registered on the online chess platforms Chess.com and Lichess.

World.title: Jackie Chan’s ‘Armour of God: Ultimatum’ Begins Filming in Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region
World.content:
ALMATY – Production has officially begun on the international feature film “Armour of God: Ultimatum” in Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region on July 18, with globally renowned actor Jackie Chan and director Robert Kun launching filming during a ceremonial event.

Following a long-standing filmmaking tradition, Chan and Kun broke a ceremonial film slate to mark the official start of production. The film’s principal photography will take place at the Bozzhyra tract, one of Mangystau’s most recognizable natural landmarks. The international production team is expected to film large-scale scenes showcasing the region’s distinctive landscapes to audiences worldwide.

The project is expected to boost Kazakhstan’s film industry and strengthen the country’s position as an attractive destination for international productions, while promoting its natural and cultural heritage on the global stage.

Filming began days after Jackie Chan arrived in the Mangystau Region, where he met with regional governor Nurdaulet Kilybay. During the meeting, Chan praised Mangystau’s landscapes for their unique cinematic potential, while local authorities said hosting the production would create new opportunities for tourism, investment and the region’s international visibility.

World.title: ‘Police violence in Georgia has become part of everyday life,’ says Social Justice Center
World.content:
Police violence in Georgia

According to the Social Justice Center, physical violence, ill-treatment and abuse of power by law enforcement officers in Georgia have gone beyond isolated cases of police misconduct and become a routine feature of the system.

The organisation says recent information points to the normalisation of inhuman treatment of detainees, describing the trend as deeply alarming.

The organisation says police violence is driven by several factors, including a lack of political will, weak institutional oversight, a culture of impunity and political influence over the police.

It argues that the cases reported by the media represent only a fraction of the true scale of the violence.

According to the organisation, most victims choose not to speak out against law enforcement for fear of retaliation, fabricated evidence, new criminal charges or being falsely accused of drug offences.

High-profile cases: Torture, coma and death

The Social Justice Center highlights several serious cases that have recently received widespread media attention.

The case of Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili

Friends Alan Kakitashvili and Irakli Tatunashvili were arrested at a police station in Tbilisi last year following a fight at a restaurant in the city of Gori.

Kakitashvili says that he and Tatunashvili were severely beaten inside the police station. After being questioned at the Gldani-Nadzaladevi police station, Tatunashvili was taken to hospital in a coma. He died on 9 June 2025.

Alan Kakitashvili himself spent nine months in prison before being fully acquitted by two courts.

Although an investigation into the alleged police violence has been launched, Tatunashvili has yet to be granted victim status and has not been questioned by investigators.

Violence at Dusheti police station

The Georgian broadcaster Pirveli recently aired a report in which Aleksandre Gogochuri said he had been beaten by around 15 employees of the Dusheti municipal administration.

According to the Social Justice Center, prosecutors dropped the criminal investigation against the alleged perpetrator but instead charged Gogochuri with giving false testimony, avoiding the question of possible police accountability.

Gori: Dozens of police officers accused of assaulting two men

On 27 May 2026, the news outlet Kartlis Ambebi published video footage appearing to show more than 10 police officers beating two men.

These are only a small number of the high-profile cases reported in recent months.

The Social Justice Center says it has documented hundreds of cases of violence during the dispersal of protests and the arrest of demonstrators over the past two years.

The organisation also cites findings by the Public Defender, which indicate that the number of people reporting ill-treatment after arrest has continued to rise.

According to the report, 30.2% of those detained during the 20–21 June 2019 protests said they had been subjected to ill-treatment. That figure rose to 79.5% among those detained between 29 November and 2 December 2024, and to 88% for arrests made between 2 and 3 February 2025.

Despite the scale of the violence, the organisation says no adequate legal response has been taken to date.

What needs to change?

The Social Justice Center says preventing police violence requires:

Independent and impartial investigations into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased;

into alleged crimes committed by police officers that are timely, effective and unbiased; Appropriate legal classification of ill-treatment under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, rather than general offences related to abuse of office;

of ill-treatment under the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, rather than general offences related to abuse of office; Investigations extending beyond direct perpetrators to include senior officials who may bear responsibility;

to include senior officials who may bear responsibility; Stronger protections for victims , shielding them from retaliation, renewed prosecution, new criminal charges or fabricated evidence;

, shielding them from retaliation, renewed prosecution, new criminal charges or fabricated evidence; Mandatory video and audio recording for all law enforcement officers, not only patrol police;

for all law enforcement officers, not only patrol police; Institutional reform, including depoliticising the police and strengthening public and legal oversight of the force.
