World.title: Fears for koala habitat as Dreamworld development approved
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandEndangered species Fears for koala habitat as Dreamworld development approved Tom Wark July 21, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Construction of an ecotourism hub adjacent to one of Australia’s biggest theme parks could fast track koala extinction in a key habitat, conservationists warn. The Queensland government has come under fire for using special powers to approve a major Dreamworld development on the Gold Coast that will clear land for the 55.3 hectare masterplan. The Coomera area has been identified as a key koala habitat, and conservationists have warned the project could be disastrous for the local population. Dreamworld chief Greg Yong said the project’s approval was a “watershed moment” for the theme park. Getty In 2025, surveys confirmed 68 koalas were within a two-kilometre radius of the area and further development would directly threaten their survival.



“This Dreamworld expansion is a nightmare for our iconic koalas, who are suffering death by a thousand cuts in south-east Queensland,” Queensland Conservation Council acting director Anthony Gough said on Tuesday. “We ... call on the federal government to intervene and ensure this project is properly assessed under Commonwealth law.” The footprint of the new Dreamworld development. Under the masterplan approved on Monday, ecotourism attractions such as boardwalks, viewing platforms and guided tours will be offered on land adjacent to the Dreamworld and WhiteWater World theme parks. Approval for a new high-density resort, a $200 million hotel, and housing developments on the site was also granted after the Queensland government used its ministerial powers to “call in” Dreamworld’s 2023 application.



It gave Infrastructure and Planning Minister Jarrod Bleijie the power to make a final decision on the proposal. Conservationists said approving the destruction of the koala habitat under the guise of expanding sustainable tourism was not a suitable use of the minister’s power. A render of the new development at Dreamworld. “Minister Bleijie and the Crisafulli government have put Coomera koalas on a fast track to local extinction,” said Coomera Conservation Group’s Karina Waterman. “While we encourage sustainable development and genuine ecotourism, this proposal is in direct conflict with endangered koalas.”



Conservationist groups said they would keep fighting to protect the local koala population, but conceded the community had no right of appeal over the minister’s decision. Dreamworld chief executive Greg Yong said the project’s approval was a “watershed moment” for the theme park, and was critical for the state’s infrastructure in the lead-up to the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. “With a shortage of quality hotel accommodation between the northern Gold Coast and Brisbane, and momentum building towards the 2032 Games, we’re well placed to help close that gap,” he said. World.title: ‘If you’re out there, Bobby’: McRae’s public plea to premiership star
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Craig McRae has opened up about premiership-winning small forward Bobby Hill.

Tony Modra has taken to social media to thank the doctors and paramedics who saved his life.

Laura Kane has defended the AFL’s call to host the Australia v Ireland women’s clash at North Sydney Oval.

Chris Scott has heaped praise on assistant coach Nathan Buckley, who lost out on the Tasmania Devils coaching role to Ken Hinkley. ‘A lot of love and care’: McRae’s heartfelt message to premiership star Jon Pierik An emotional Craig McRae says Bobby Hill will forever be a beloved Magpie, as Collingwood and the Norm Smith medallist prepare to split. McRae said on Tuesday he had not seen Hill for some time, the star small forward and father of three dealing with personal issues.



Happier days: Bobby Hill embraces teammate Nick Daicos during a Collingwood training session. Eddie Jim Hill has spent significant time away from the club over the past year, managing only three VFL games this season, and appears certain to part ways with the club. “[I] haven’t seen Bobby in the building for a while, which it’s always something, as a coach, you go, ‘[I] hope the young lad’s going OK ’,” McRae said, his eyes almost welling up. Hill and Craig McRae speak to the media after their side’s famous 2023 premiership win. AFL Photos “If you’re out there, Bobby, we’ve got a lot of love and care for you, and still do, and [we] never, never change, [and] never waver in our love and support for the young man.



“We’re always trying to remain connected, and sometimes [it’s] a bit harder than other times.” Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Buckley at a ‘fork in the road’ after Tassie’s AFL coach call on Hinkley Hill is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal worth about $750,000 per season, league sources say. McRae said he had attempted to contact Hill, who has played 108 games across eight seasons with GWS and the Magpies. “There is an emotion attached to it ... there’s the playing part, the high performance of what he’s capable of doing for our team and for our supporter base, and then there’s the other personal part of, as a father, [you] get emotional thinking about a young man with three kids,” McRae said.



“We want the best for all our players [who have] come into our environment, [to] be good humans, and be a good father and a good husband. Those things that we’re trying to instil , but yeah, environments change and shift, and so [we’ve got] lots of love and care for them [Hill and his family].” The eighth-placed Magpies head to Adelaide for Thursday night’s clash against the Crows on a roll, having won five straight in a stretch of games they had targeted. Now comes a refresh with a new theme, but the Magpies may be without Scott Pendlebury, who could be rested. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making “Howey’s [Jeremy Howe is] back and someone has to go out – [there are] lots of [players in] good form, and players deserve to keep their spot ... I anticipate that ‘Pendles’ plays. That’s probably where it’s going to land,” McRae said. Josh Daicos (ankle) did not train on Tuesday, McRae adding a final call on his fitness could be as late as game time. Howe, the premiership backman, trained strongly and will return. Fellow defender Isaac Quaynor, who had a minor wrist issue in the last quarter against Carlton, is also expected to play.



The Magpies will celebrate Jordan De Goey’s 200th game, McRae saying the robust midfielder was in the best form he had been in during his coaching tenure. De Goey, pushing for All-Australian selection, is contracted until the end of 2027, and is keen on a multi-year extension, league sources say. The Crows, without the suspended Izak Rankine, won by 14 points when the two clubs met at the MCG in round one. Modra ‘humbled’ by support after near-fatal accident Andrew Wu Adelaide goal-kicking great Tony Modra has thanked the doctors and paramedics who saved his life, in a heartfelt social media post.



Modra took to Instagram on Tuesday to express his gratitude to those who wished him well in the immediate aftermath to his near-fatal accident last month. The former Crows superstar revealed he had several titanium plates inserted into his face to “put me back together” during extensive facial surgery after the truck he was driving crashed into a tree that had fallen across the road. Tony Modra has posted a photo of himself and family after recovering from a truck accident in June. Instagram Former teammate Mark Ricciuto had quipped Modra, a glamour forward in the 1990s, may not retain his model looks after the accident, but he showed few visible signs of his injuries in a picture he shared on social media of him with his wife Erica and their two children, Luke and Hayley.



“Still as handsome as ever,” former Crows captain Rory Sloane wrote. There were grave fears for Tony Modra after a truck accident in June. Instagram Modra paid tribute to the SA Ambulance Service, the South Coast District Hospital and the Flinders Medical Centre for saving his life. “I’m getting out and about a bit now, and slowly catching up on everything I missed over the last month,” Modra wrote. “I’m so humbled to learn how many people were cheering these incredible medical teams on … and our family too. I’ll never be able to thank everyone enough.” Loading



The football world was in shock when news broke of Modra’s accident during the telecast of the game between one of his former clubs, Fremantle, and Geelong about five weeks ago. Renowned for his high-flying marks, Modra was one of the biggest stars of the game in the 1990s when forwards ruled. He burst onto the scene in 1993 when he booted 129 goals in 23 games, including finals, but was beaten for the Coleman Medal by Geelong great Gary Ablett, who kicked 124 goals in the home-and-away season. Modra finished with 588 goals from 165 games with Adelaide and Fremantle, and sits second on the Crows’ all-time goals list with 440, behind Taylor Walker. AFLW players Georgie Prespakis, Taylah Gatt, Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw and Sophie McKay. AFL Photos



Why pubs and Irish expats are behind the call not to move sold-out clash Danny Russell AFLW boss Laura Kane has defended a decision not to shift the competition’s looming international match to a bigger stadium, despite the game’s boutique venue, North Sydney Oval, selling out. The league has come under fire from fans and past players for not opening up the first-ever Irish-Australia women’s clash on August 1 to a larger live audience by relocating it to the SCG. The intimate North Sydney Oval holds fewer than 10,000 people.



But Kane said the league had monitored ticket sales and waiting lists to inform their decision. Related Article AFLW ‘Something in the water’: The massive footy boom Ireland didn’t see coming “When we announced this game, we wanted to create an amazing atmosphere, and so a sellout is incredible,” Kane said on Tuesday. “Do I want to be, you know, in future talking about the MCG, the SCG or Marvel Stadium? Absolutely, I do, and we will get there. “But for now, our priority is making sure that we have a packed-out stadium, and we are going to get that with North Sydney Oval.



“It’s such a great place to play footy, and really, it comes down to the data. What does the data tell us around what our fans want to do? When it tells us that we can fill the SCG, we’ll play there.” Laura Kane at the AFLW season launch. AFL Photos Instead of seeking a bigger venue, the league opted to work with Sydney pubs to set up fan zones for the city’s large Irish ex-pat community to watch the game. There are no AFL matches fixtured in Sydney that weekend. Former Carlton and Brisbane Lions star Lauren Arnell called the decision “baffling”.



“You’re already telling people two weeks out, ‘You can’t come’,” the former Port Adelaide coach told the ABC. “I just feel like you are limiting the game.” But Kane, the AFL’s executive general manager of AFLW, health and football operations said the league had turned its attention towards attracting a larger TV audience once the stadium sold out. “We want people watching it in their lounge rooms. We want people watching it at restaurants, at pubs, at venues all over the country – not just in Sydney,” she said. The AFLW season starts on August 9 when St Kilda and Carlton clash as part of an AFL double-header at Marvel Stadium, which coincides with ‘Spud’s Game’, held in memory of Saints great Danny Frawley and to raise money for and awareness of mental health.



Kane said the AFL was continually looking to reduce the number of AFLW venues, having already cut ground numbers from 38 to 27, and had done away with computer chips for ball-tracking technology. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Ben Long ban slashed to one-match for heavy Maynard bump; New video review system for AFLW “We want to make sure that we have the best technology available for both of our competitions, AFL and AFLW … and we felt that the time was right to evolve to vision and video review,” she said. “Both Greg Swann and I are looking at, ‘What does optical tracking look like?’, in the context of all venues that we play at, notwithstanding that there’s a few extra W venues that we play footy at. “What is the long-term solution? At the moment, the best technology that we feel [is] available for score review is video and the video review system, but it’s always something that we’re looking at improving.”



‘He would have been a great Tasmanian coach’: Scott’s praise for Buckley Danny Russell Chris Scott says his decorated assistant Nathan Buckley will escape any negative perception that is usually associated with applicants missing out on senior coaching jobs. Buckley joined the Geelong coaching panel at the start of this season to enhance his chances of landing the Tasmania Devils role. Nathan Buckley missed out to Ken Hinkley on the Tasmania Devils coaching job. Getty Images



But the fledgling club announced this week it had overlooked the Collingwood great for Ken Hinkley. “I suspect if Tassie get the opportunity to talk publicly about him, they would say similar things to me, ‘He was an outstanding candidate and would have been a great Tasmanian coach, but the fit wasn’t quite as good as the other guy’, who just happens to be one who coached for 15 years in the AFL, or thereabouts” Scott said. “There’s no shame in running, I don’t know whether he ran second, but let’s assume he ran second to Ken Hinkley – there’s no shame in that.” Loading The Geelong coach said Buckley’s willingness to publicly announce his interest in the Tasmanian position spoke to “how secure he is in his ability, and his position in the game”.



“It seems to me that it is quite rare that a coach puts their hand up and says, ‘This is something that I want, and I’m prepared to go through the process’,” Scott said. “He didn’t only go through the process, he went back to work, which, obviously, has been a real positive for us. “I suspect it won’t happen that much, so if you like his way of going about it, make the most of it now because I don’t think you will see it too often.” Scott said it was less likely younger candidates would put themselves on the line in the same manner as Buckley. Loading



“The likelihood for all the candidates for these positions is that you are probably going to miss, irrespective of how good a job you do,” he said. “Inevitably, the kind of perception could be, ‘Well, there must have been a good reason why someone didn’t get the job’. “I think the reality is more likely that you could actually be a fantastic candidate, you are just not the right fit for that point in time. “But again, the perception of that can hurt, in particular young coaches. In that context, I am certain that the negative perception won’t apply to ‘Bucks’.” Buckley, who coached Collingwood to the 2018 grand final, said missing out on the Tasmanian gig had left him at a “fork in the road”.



He has all but ruled out applying for the vacant Carlton and Essendon roles. “I haven’t really reflected on where those roles sit and I don’t think I would enter those processes,” Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night. “I’m absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out. I was committed to that [Tasmania job], and that ended a day ago. “The future there [at the Cats] for me will inform my next step in footy. I probably wouldn’t have come back [to AFL coaching] in unless I’d looked at Tassie, so it’s a fork in the road. “I’m really grateful for where I’m at, rather than maybe just being on the couch, [having spent] five years in media, without really knowing what I was doing with footy.



“But now that I’m back in a club, I don’t know what’s next.” Buckley said Devils CEO Brendon Gale informed him of their decision to appoint Hinkley on Sunday afternoon. “I think it’s taken me a little bit of time to reflect because I was really keen on it. I was in on it,” he said. “I texted back [to Gale] that, ‘I’m disappointed, but thanks for letting me know’. “I’ll come back around and touch base in time [with Tasmania, for some feedback] because it’s obviously a busy time for the Devils.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Family rejects coroner’s finding that newborn’s death was unpreventable
World.content:
NationalQueenslandInquest Family rejects coroner’s finding that newborn’s death was unpreventable Rex Martinich July 21, 2026 — 5:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A family whose daughter died hours after her birth from an undiagnosed heart defect has rejected a coroner’s finding that her death was unpreventable. Thea Flaskett died on the morning of September 11, 2023, a little more than four hours after she was born at a Queensland hospital. Her inquest was told the newborn suffered from a congenital defect called transposition of the great arteries, which affects blood flow through the heart. Thea’s parents, Meg and James Flaskett, sought an inquest but say they have been left with unanswered questions. AAP Thea’s mother, Meg Flaskett, had a routine morphology scan at 20 weeks of her pregnancy in May 2023 that did not detect the defect.



“The weight of the evidence supports a finding that Thea’s death was not preventable, her transposition of the great arteries not having been detected [before birth],” Queensland Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher said in her findings on Monday. Related Article Inquest Parents’ emotional plea after newborn’s hospital death Thea’s heart defect was “not uncommon” to be missed during pregnancy, regardless of the quality of the scans, Gallagher found. Thea’s mother and partner James Flaskett had sought an inquest into her death, with hearings in Brisbane last year. In a statement that criticised the inquest’s findings, Mrs Flaskett said the family was “devastated, but not surprised, by the outcome”.



“Had Thea’s condition been diagnosed before birth, her labour, delivery and immediate management would have been fundamentally different,” she said. She disputed that Thea’s heart defect was the only major contributor to her death at Redcliffe Hospital, north of Brisbane. “Although these findings bring the coronial process to an end, they do not bring us peace, nor do they answer the questions that have driven us for almost three years,” she said. Queensland Health supervising sonographer Craig John Collins testified during the inquest that he performed about 150 ultrasounds per year and had only once discovered a case of transposition from a scan. In her findings, Gallagher said: “Ideally, Thea’s [heart defect] would have been suspected during Mrs Flaskett’s morphology scan and gone on to be diagnosed by a materno-fetal medicine specialist or paediatric cardiologist soon thereafter.”



Related Article Courts Newborn’s fatal heart defect mistaken for lung disease Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital senior staff neonatologist Pieter Koorts testified that even if Thea’s heart defect had been detected and she was born at a major city hospital and received immediate surgery, her survival was “not assured”. Gallagher said Redcliffe Hospital staff did everything they could with the resources they had. “Despite resuscitating Thea to a high standard, her outcome was determined by her underlying congenital cardiac abnormality, not the standard of her post-delivery care,” she said. Gallagher recommended Metro North Health consider adopting the bedside live-streaming services and neonatal retrieval processes used in NSW. AAP

World.title: Accused Brighton cocaine dealer identified as De La Salle student, son of gangland-linked lawyer
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Accused Brighton cocaine dealer identified as De La Salle student, son of gangland-linked lawyer Carla Jaeger Updated July 21, 2026 — 5:51pm ,first published 4:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The estranged son of gangland-connected lawyer Victor Doree is facing potential time behind bars after a police raid on his Brighton East home allegedly uncovered bricks of cocaine with a total estimated street value of $100,000. A month-long investigation into the suspected circulation of illicit drugs in the elite bayside suburb led detectives to the North Road home on Monday morning. Accused Brighton cocaine trafficker Jesse Doree was denied bail on Tuesday. Jesse Doree, 28, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday after he was arrested on charges of cocaine trafficking, drug possession, and possessing proceeds of crime. Doree, who briefly attended Malvern private school De La Salle, was supported in court by his partner, brothers and mother Fiona.



Senior Constable Jack Wills told the court that during the raid police seized two mobile phones, $45,000 in cash, various drugs – including ketamine – as well as the bricks of cocaine. “We believe one phone is used as a clean phone, and the second phone is used for trafficking drugs,” Wills said. The drugs were stashed in the kitchen range hood, bedroom nightstand and pantry cupboard, according to the police summary. A wad of cash was also discovered hidden behind the home’s venetian blinds, as well as $1560 in the cutlery drawer, $450 in a sock drawer, $560 in a Mercedes-Benz and $600 in the bedroom drawer, the summary stated. Loading



A text message sent from one phone allegedly contained a list of names alongside money owed, with individual debts recorded at $35,000, $42,000, and as high as $50,000, the court heard. “Then [there] was an address sent with a screenshot from Google Maps of a picture of a house, and he’s asking someone to go and collect that debt for him,” Wills said. Doree allegedly told the arresting officers he doesn’t use cocaine, and self-prescribes sedatives as he “doesn’t trust doctors”. Jesse Doree The court heard the 28-year-old claimed he was unemployed, aside from a business he’s starting focused on “finding lawyers online” and cash-in-hand roofing jobs.



Wills told the court he believed Doree would continue drug trafficking if granted bail. “He’s developed a lifestyle based on selling drugs, and it would be extremely difficult for him to give that up,” he said. “We’ve seized a lot of cash from his house, so he’s going to have to try and make that up somehow.” Wills told the court there was a risk an “outside party” would chase up the alleged debts owed that “could result in violence”. Victor Doree, principal lawyer at Kingsford Lawyers. Kingsford Lawyers Doree’s estranged father, Victor, has had longstanding business ties to the underworld, including with Finks bikie club president Mark Basille and gangland figure Mick Gatto.



Victor made headlines in May when his Spotswood warehouse – housing three law firms, including his own – was torched under suspicious circumstances. Doree’s mother, Fiona, told the court her son had not seen his father for over a decade. “Jesse’s father left [us] in 2012. He had an extramarital affair with one of the women from the office, which was rubbed in all of our faces for a long time.” She told the court her son struggles “tremendously” with post-traumatic stress, after witnessing and being subjected to emotional abuse and physical violence at the hands of his father. “He’s a really, really good kid. He has a really good heart,” Fiona said. “His dad leaving was probably the start of him lashing out and ... just making really silly choices.” The court heard Doree had a limited criminal history, including a trafficking charge that did not result in a conviction.



However, the magistrate denied bail, saying he was not satisfied Doree would not reoffend despite the clear support of his family. Doree was remanded until his next court date in October. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Group let out ‘war cry’ before stabbing schoolboy with knives and swords
World.content:
A teenage boy has been hospitalised with serious injuries after being attacked by a group of youths after school in Melbourne’s south-eastern suburbs on Monday. Police said three boys were walking home near Cranbourne North’s Alkira Secondary College at 3.20pm when they turned around and saw three hooded youths, aged between 16 and 20, charging at them with a “variety” of weapons including “knives” and “swords”. A shopping strip in Cranbourne North, in the same suburb as the park attack. Detective Inspector Mark Patrick said the three offenders, who remain on the run, let out a collective scream before attacking in Sabel Drive. “It was similar to a war cry when you go into battle and that’s what it appeared to be to get their attention to create fear into their intended victims,” he told a press conference.



Patrick said officers suspect the 15-year-old victim, a student of the college, was directly targeted. He suffered multiple injuries in the back, arms and hands and is currently undergoing surgery in an inner-city hospital. Patrick said his parents were “shocked and concerned about the welfare of their son”. “They are concerned about retribution and motivation associated to why their son was attacked,” he said. Police were on Tuesday morning still searching for multiple people involved, after the group fled the scene on foot.



The offenders were not believed to be students from the school. Investigators do not have a motive but confirmed they were investigating whether any of the offenders had links to known gangs. Police have appealed to the community in the Sabel Reserve and Moss Street areas of Cranbourne North to review their CCTV footage and are calling on the attackers to hand themselves in to authorities. “It’s frustrating for us to see continual knife-related assaults and offences and items, knives, are readily available. If you look at your kitchen drawer you pull out a knife,” Patrick said. “There’s certainly a bit more numerous weapons there than anything that’s been surrendered.”



Related Article Courts AFL legend Mick Malthouse says accused home invaders were ‘a bunch of cockatoos’ Ambulance Victoria’s Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance and Advanced Life Support paramedics treated the teenager on Monday. An Ambulance Victoria spokesperson said the boy was transported to hospital in a serious condition after sustaining injuries to his upper body. Alkira Secondary College was on Tuesday providing wellbeing support to those involved in the incident. An Education Department spokesperson said the assault occurred outside the school and after school hours. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tuakau residents evacuated after hazardous chemical enters drains
World.content:
Residents in the north Waikato town of Tuakau are being evacuated and others are being advised to stay indoors after a large amount of an unknown chemical entered drains near the water treatment plant.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said fire-fighters had responded to the "hazardous substances incident", which was reported at 4pm.

In a statement, FENZ said residents have been evacuated from houses in the vicinity of Kowhai St and Matipo Drive.

"Other people in the area are advised to stay inside with doors and windows closed to avoid possible exposure to fumes. Other members of the public should stay away from the area until further notice."

Police have assisted FENZ with the evacuations.

Specialist advice has been sought from the Queensland Fire Department to help identify the substance and FENZ was working with the Waikato District Council and Watercare to develop a plan to flush the drains safely.

World.title: Scrapping council/iwi agreements 'only takes things backwards'
World.content:
Plans to scrap iwi involvement in councils under the Resource Management Act (RMA) will take away a seat at the decision making table for Māori, says the chair of a Northland iwi.

But the minister in charge of RMA reform says the reforms will allow iwi to participate in statutory processes and activities like the identification of significant sites.

The environment select committee has recommended a raft of changes to the proposed RMA reforms, including scrapping agreements dictating the role of iwi in council decision making - called Mana Whakahono a Rōhe agreements.

Northland iwi Ngāti Hine signed a Mana Whakahono a Rōhe agreement in 2024 with the Northland Regional Council. Ngāti Hine chair Rowena Tana told RNZ there were two more applications with the Far North Regional and Whangārei District councils.

Tana said the agreement gave Ngāti Hine a "seat at the table" to talk with the council as "rangatira to rangatira".

"It also ensured that any resource consents, any developments, anything like that, we were being notified and our view [was] given effect to."

She said that relationship was "really important for our people".

"We do a lot of monitoring, a lot of implementation, and that's to preserve taiao and our way of life for our future generations.... our mana is derived from the whenua."

Tana told RNZ she was "very surprised, but not surprised" by the announcement.

"It's yet another example of modern-day control and oppression, marginalisation of our iwi, our people - another example of that behaviour."

Northland Regional Council chair Pita Tipene - whose council has an agreement with Ngāti Hine - told RNZ he learned about the changes on Monday.

He said the reforms were "despicable".

"I think it's absolutely despicable on one hand, and I think it's also cowardly. I think it's getting quite desperate, given that the runway into the general elections is quite short now."

Tipene said his council had three agreements in place and a hard position of honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

He said Northland's Māori population was about 40 percent and as high as 90 percent in some places.

"If we are to truly improve the circumstances of our communities and our regions, we've got to embrace each other, we've got to develop relationships that are proactive and progressive.

"This only takes things backwards," he said.

Speaking to Midday Report, Māori environmental expert Tina Porou gave an example of how the agreement worked for her own hapu.

"We have shared discussions over which trees will be cut down in the Tūrangi township... now I know that would scare people having a Māori help decide that, but that is some of the conversations we have around the table."

Porou said the changes would ultimately cost councils more in the long run.

"What I do know after 30 years in this business is that investing in a relationship at the beginning - creating good outcomes - is much cheaper than trying to manage a long-term, bad relationship with iwi and hapū."

She told Midday Report the conversations around the reforms had a "racist lens" and "ignored the evidence", something RMA reform Minister Chris Bishop denied.

"It's not racist at all," Bishop said.

"We're making provision in the legislation for iwi participation agreements, which are an important mechanism to make sure that councils and iwi can work out exactly how they relate to each other when it comes to identification of sites, for example," he said.

Bishop said the legislation was "relatively clear" and iwi would help with spatial planning and identifying sites of significance which "most people would regard as really important".

"The iwi participation agreements are about devising a mechanism to give effect to those roles and we've got a commitment to upholding Treaty settlements as well. Again, the iwi participation agreements are a way of essentially putting in place a mechanism for how treaty settlement obligations are given effect to," he said.

Asked if there would be a distinction for iwi who had and had not settled, Bishop said the new agreements would apply to iwi who had settled and a "wider level in relation to the role of mana whenua when it comes to a local council".

The reform is supported by Federated Farmers who, in a statement, said decision-making powers should remain with elected and accountable representatives.

Spokesperson Mark Hooper said the agreements had raised concern among farmers who had worries around accountability.

"While there is absolutely a place for relationship agreements between councils and iwi, they need appropriate safeguards.

"The new guardrails announced by the government are an important step in ensuring that." he said.

RNZ contacted two councils - Whangārei District (WDC) and Waikato Regional (WRC) - to ask what they thought of the reforms.

In a statement, a spokesperson for WDC said its role was to work within the framework set by central government and ensure local communities were served.

"Our interest is in having clear, practical and effective mechanisms that support constructive engagement with hapū, regardless of the legislative model adopted."

WDC has an existing Mana Whakahono a Rōhe agreement with Patuharakeke and Takahiwai hapū - signed in 2020 - but recently declined an application from Ngā Hapū o Whangārei to get one.

The spokesperson said while elected members acknowledged the "importance of strong relationships" with hapū, the request was declined because the resource management system and local government itself was undergoing significant changes.

"The decision also recognised that council already has long-standing arrangements in place through Te Kārearea, our strategic partnership committee established in 2012, Te Huinga, the collective forum that brings brings hapū and council together, and direct engagement with hapū across a range of council activities," the spokesperson said.

In another statement to RNZ, a spokesperson from Waikato Regional Council said the council had not yet had the opportunity to "formally consider" the proposed changes.

"Waikato Regional Council is currently involved in a number of Mana Whakahono ā Rohe processes. Over the past 14 months, the council has received 11 initiations, which are at varying stages of progression from early engagement through to active negotiation.

World.title: Big demand for cycle workshop practically giving bikes away
World.content:
Christchurch bike fix up seeing high demand Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

A Christchurch workshop that is practically giving bikes away is seeing record high demand.

Volunteer organisation Aranui Bike Fix-up repairs or refurbishes hundreds of bikes every year, with a team of 10 volunteers getting the donated bicycles ready for their new riders.

Demand is high right now, despite winter usually being a quieter time.

Aranui Bike Fixup founder Steven Muir told Checkpoint that the workshop was "quite steady" at the moment.

"With higher petrol prices, people have been more motivated to switch to more active transport, which has a lot of wins for their health and their pocket and for the whole roading network, really."

He said it was very rewarding to see people of all ages get on to a bike that had been given a second life.

"We get people who come in and have just got a job and they start at three in the morning or something and can't get a bus there - it's just life-changing for some people, being able to bike somewhere.

"A lot of people go out the gate with smiles all over their faces and it's very satisfying role to be playing in the community."

He said when someone came in their gate, they were pointed to a container where there was a stockpile of bikes that had been donated, and the new rider would choose one that suited their size and need, and the workshop team would fix it up for them, and off they went.

Muir said sometimes these new riders would give the workshop a donation - and sometimes they did not.

"Often it's just a few loose coins in the bottom of their pocket, because they don't have much to spare, but other people can afford to be a bit more generous. And that's really helpful, it helps us buy the parts we can't get second hand from other bikes like brakes and hand grips."

Many of the donated bicycles were old bikes that had been sitting in the garage for years, while others came from similar organisations.

Muir said the crew working on the bikes were largely "enthusiastic amateurs".

"Some have working in the bike industry for many years and others like myself just like tinkering on bikes. Most repairs are oiling chains, fixing punctures and the odd cable replacement, that's 90 percent of the repairs that need doing on the bikes, you don't need extensive skills to help out.

"We have one guy who just strips bikes and takes the useful parts off them, and that's a really useful role that we need more of as well."

World.title: Auckland Council votes in favour of intensified housing plan
World.content:
Auckland Council has voted in favour of a plan that could see more intensified housing in the city.

It is a response to a government requirement for the council to allow for more than 1.4 million homes to be built in Auckland.

The plan put to councillors today was a compromise between two options that have been sent to local boards for consultation.

One option would have met only the minimum requirements set by the government. The other would have seen further intensification in the city, particularly around town centres and transport hubs.

Councillors voted in favour of the hybrid plan by 17 votes to five. There is a further opportunity for public consultation on Plan Change 120.

The plan keeps six-storey zoning for all areas within walking distance of rapid transit and town centres.

Building heights would also lift to 10-15-storeys around most train stations on all lines within 10km of the city centre, not just specific Western line stations specified in law.

World.title: Lower Hutt mayor backs plan for Wellington super-city merger
World.content:
A proposal to merge at least nine councils in the Wellington region into one super-city has the backing of Lower Hutt's mayor.

Mayors are considering a plan from consultants MartinJenkins that could involve merging Wellington city, Porirua, Kāpiti, two Hutt Valley and three Wairarapa councils, and Greater Wellington regional council.

Horowhenua District Council might also be involved.

The unitary Wairarapa-Wellington council would be headed by a regional mayor and consist of unitary councillors and community council chairs.

It would be in charge of regional responsibilities such as transport, emergency management, rates, large-scale planning and environmental protection.

Community councils, which have not existed before, could oversee pools, libraries and grants. The idea is that people could vote for the councillors on the five community councils.

Ken Laban told Morning Report the layer of community councils would protect local voice.

The MartinJenkins proposal involves five community councils, which could represent Wairarapa, Kāpiti Coast/Horowhenua, Porirua, Hutt Valley and Wellington.

Laban said the current MartinJenkins proposal was a "very good one".

"Our community have been very strong in the establishment of community councils, with locally elected leaders - be they mayors or chairs - tasked with the responsibility of ... protecting those assets ... clearly libraries, swimming pools, other local assets and projects are a significant part of it."

Lower Hutt City Council had also produced its own suggestion for amalgamation that involved combining nine councils, without Horowhenua, made up of 19 members and with six community councils sitting beneath that.

Laban said both models were similar and there were a range of views between mayors and councillors throughout the region.

"I can't speak on behalf of the other mayors. We're all dealing with multiple personalities on our councils who all have their own views, and I think our Lower Hutt City Council we have some that are in support, some that are ambivalent, and some that are opposed because they want the status quo to continue."

He doubted amalgamation would immediately lower rates, although he thought it would ultimately result in a "leaner" operation.

Wellington deputy mayor Ben McNulty previously told RNZ no decisions had been made on the MartinJenkins proposal and exactly which regions were a part of it was still being discussed.

South Wairarapa mayor Dame Fran Wilde said the three Wairarapa councils were still considering their options about whether to join in with Wellington or go it alone with their own amalgamated council.

World.title: Hawke's Bay runner fundraises for children living with disabilities
World.content:
An ultra marathon runner is going the distance fundraising for children living with disabilities so they can hopefully move more freely.

Hawke's Bay runner Andrew McCrory is raising money for a Rotorua centre that specialises in intensive therapy for children with neurological disabilities and disorders, including cerebral palsy.

Ultra-marathon runner fundraising for children with disabilities Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

The Centre of Movement aims to improve essential motor skills like rolling, sitting, crawling and walking, but courses can cost thousands of dollars.

Andrew McCrory has been fundraising for children needing surgery or therapy for several years now, after he injured his own back and needed spinal surgery in 2018.

His next big run is the 320-kilometre Great Naseby Water Race in August.

Andrew McCrory (right) was inspired to start fundraising after he injured his own back and needed spinal surgery in 2018. Andrew McCrory

McCrory told Checkpoint it was his own back injury that inspired him to begin his fundraising journey.

"I was scrolling Facebook and I found a wee girl that needed some help. She had cerebral palsy and so I just jumped in and helped her out. She had surgery in America; I had surgery in New Zealand.

"I took up running after I had my spine fused in 2018 and sort of haven't stopped."

The money McCrory is currently raising is going straight to the kids at the Centre of Movement, which has centres in Rotorua and Christchurch.

"The therapy and stuff that they need costs a lot of money and so every single cent that I raise just pays for their therapy."

McCrory said he had the opportunity to visit the centre on Saturday and squeezed in an 80km training run while he was at it.

Andrew McCrory's next big run is the 320-kilometre Great Naseby Water Race in August. Andrew McCrory

Before the centre opened locations in New Zealand, McCrory had fundraised to send kids to the centre in the Gold Coast.

He said having the service available here was making an unbelievable difference.

"It's the little things that we take for granted, sitting, standing, even walking, using the toilet.

"All the therapy can help and it's not just helping the kids out, it's helping the families as well... they do amazing stuff."

McCrory said his own experience had made him appreciate movement so much more.

"With my back, I could barely walk, I couldn't sit on my bum, I had to lie on my left side.

"So having my surgery and doing my rehab and getting back into moving and all of that gives me an appreciation big time, seeing the struggles that these kids have."

In his years of fundraising so far McCrory estimates he has been able to donate around $125,000.

Without putting a figure on it, he said he would like to fundraise as much as possible for his upcoming 320km Great Naseby Water Race.

The gruelling race will be McCrory's longest yet, a whopping 80km further than his current record, a 240km journey through the Karangahake Gorge Rail Tunnel last year.

In order to get in shape for the challenge, McCrory runs six days a week, dedicating Saturday and Sunday to longer runs.

For the mental side of getting through such a long journey, his training schedule is less rigourous.

"Mentally, I don't know, we'll deal with that after 200 kilometres."

World.title: Health NZ spend on locum doctors hits a new high, at $220 million
World.content:
The amount of money spent on temporary doctors to plug gaps in the health system has hit a new high, topping $200 million for the third year in a row.

Health NZ says it's working hard to recruit permanent specialists and has even cut the budget for locums for the next financial year.

But, others in the health sector say more drastic action is needed to bring the spend under control and incentivise doctors to stay on our shores.

Locums have a place

Dr James Irwin recently resigned as the last full-time permanent gastro specialist at Palmerston North Hospital, a service now staffed by locums and fill-ins from other districts.

He's seen the positive and negative side of using locums.

"In a a department, where you've got a full department and then someone is sick or goes away for a period of time, getting a locum is great because it helps fill holes and helps get work done.

"You have an expectation that you're going to have a full department going forward to deal with all of the long-term stuff and all of the departmental planning, and so forth."

Dr James Irwin. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Reliance on them, however, was less satisfactory when it became more of a medium-term arrangement, or longer.

"As a longer-term employee you're then the one that's dealing with all of the chronic disease management and planning for the department."

This happened to Irwin.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Health NZ spent about $220m on locums, up from about $208m in 2024-25 and $209m in 2023-24. The bill was $168m in 2022-23, Health NZ's first year of operation.

Irwin said constantly changing faces had an effect on continuity of care for patients too.

"It's a consequence of the transactional model of healthcare.

"If you employ a locum and pay them money to do something for six weeks, they come and do that, but they're not going to want to take on additional responsibility that continues after they finish," Irwin said.

"You need to be employing people in a situation where it's clear that they're going to be providing long-term care. That requires a long-tern appointment."

He said that's why permanent appointments were needed.

Budget trimmed after spend increases

Health NZ national director of people, culture, health and safety, Robyn Shearer, said the organisation was recruiting overseas and working with medical schools to get more doctors long term.

"It's a global challenge. It is hard to get all the doctors we need," she said.

"Locums play a really important role for us in maintaining continuity of care and staffing, particularly in specialities and regions which are harder for us to staff.

"They're an important part of how we fill and manage short-term gaps in our rosters and provide cover for our permanent doctors, in particular, to take a break."

New Zealand was competing against other countries for specialists, so Health NZ worked hard to promote the country as a great destination.

"We are in a competitive market, there's no doubt about it, and we have to be prudent financially," Shearer said.

"There is always a balance around what we offer, but we do look at, certainly, what New Zealand has to offer, and you'll have probably seen we've had an influx of doctors in the South Island from America who are promoting New Zealand as a great place to work and live."

She said health authorities had always used locums, but more were required as the demand for health services increased, putting pressure on the workforce.

However, Health NZ was looking to bring the cost under control, cutting the budget for the 2026-27 year to $179m.

"We are deliberately looking to have a decrease in our spend. What we are supporting districts and regions with is how we can given them information so they have more awareness of locum use and spend."

Shearer said Health NZ regions could look at alternatives, drive recruitment and look at "alternate workforce ways of working" such as using nurse practitioners.

Minister orders reliance to end

Executive director of senior doctors' union, the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists, Sarah Dalton, said locums did quality work, but permanent staff provided better value.

"When you're relying on locums to help run a service, anything from the complete collapse of the gastroenterology service in Palmerston North through to another service in another part of the country that needs locums on a regular basis to fill gaps in rosters, it is a cost to patients and to colleagues."

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists' Sarah Dalton. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Patient Voice Aotearoa's Malcolm Mulholland had another idea to try to hold on to doctors, rather than use more expensive locums.

"I do not for the life of me know what Health NZ aren't coming up with a better plan - something along the lines of getting our best and brightest when they graduate from med school and bonding them in hard-to-staff areas.

"[Health NZ] could say as part of that bonding, 'We're also going to take care of your student loan.'

"To my mind it would still be a cheaper option than looking to employ locums left, right and centre."

Simeon Brown. RNZ / Louis Dunham

Health minister Simeon Brown has written to Health NZ's chairperson, saying he expects the organisation to move away from depending on locums.

"As a priority I expect you to monitor and prioritise shifting away from dependence on locums to recruiting permanent senior medical officers to vacancies - with an initial focus on regions that have high dependency on locums," he wrote.

The minister's office told RNZ locums would always play a role, as the minister's priority was to make sure patients received the care they needed, when and where they needed it.

World.title: Nicola Willis blames 'Trump spike' for high inflation
World.content:
The Finance Minister says US President Donald Trump is to blame for New Zealand's rising inflation.

StatsNZ figures released on Tuesday showed annual inflation lifted to 4.1 percent, the highest level in more than two years as fuel prices surged due to the US-Iran war.

Nicola Willis said the figures reflected the international oil shock, which the government could not control.

"What they show was the Trump spike in inflation, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices," she said.

"New Zealanders have already experienced this at the pump, and we know that it's been a very difficult period for many."

Willis said without higher fuel prices, inflation would have been within the target band, at 2.9 percent.

"That is an encouraging sign that the underlying factors driving inflation are being better controlled by our government," she said.

However, it was not only fuel prices driving inflation. There were also annual jumps in electricity prices (12 percent) and rates (9 percent).

Willis said the government was doing everything it could to keep costs down for New Zealanders, including introducing rates caps.

"We do not accept that the level of rate increases that New Zealanders have had to put up with in recent years is acceptable, and we are acting to prevent that happening in future," she said.

On electricity, Willis said the government was consenting more renewable generation, which would bring down households' prices in future.

Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds blasted Willis for pinning high inflation on uncontrollable factors.

"She just continues to blame everybody else but take no responsibility for some of those other underlying costs, such as government costs, that has increased by 21 percent over the last two years," Edmonds said.

"GP fees have also gone up by over 20 percent. Those are all factors that she could have looked at in the last two years but decided to pass those costs on to everyday New Zealanders."

Edmonds said she was holding Willis to the same standard as Willis held former Labour finance minister Grant Robertson to.

"Which is, you can't just blame everything on overseas factors, you've got to take some work yourself."

Power rises

Meanwhile, an economist is raising questions about the lack of savings being passed on to households by power companies.

The latest figures showed power prices are up 12 percent annually and in the last nine months electricity prices increased at the fastest rate since 1989.

Tim Hazeldine from the University of Auckland told Checkpoint that New Zealand produced most of its own electricity.

He said much of that was hydropower, which was relatively cheap.

But Hazeldine said wholesale electricity was largely priced on the cost of thermal generation, which was more expensive.

"Everybody has to pay the higher price and the electricity retailers pocket a big, windfall gain on that and that is worth a bit more government attention."

World.title: How this Champions League winner aims to ignite Stingers
World.content:
Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, are no strangers to success.

Winning a silver medal at the Paris Olympics, the best performance by any Australian team at those Games, put the Stingers right in the upper echelons of their field.

It's what makes the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup finals, being hosted in Australia from July 22-26 at the Sydney Aquatics Centre at Homebush, so exciting.

But the fact the Stingers are challenging at the top of the world rankings is no accident.

The entire team is packed with genuine superstars, playing in some of Europe's biggest clubs in the biggest competitions in the world.

Abby Andrews has proven herself to be one of the very best.

Abby Andrews's first major trophy was the biggest in club water polo. (Supplied: Instagram)

The 25-year-old left-handed shooter won the LEN European Champions League title with Greek giants Olympiacos earlier this year.

Not only that, but the Brisbane native was named the most valuable player in the Final Four tournament, scoring four goals in the semifinal and a fabulous five in the final.

"It was definitely an out-of-body experience," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport ahead of this week's World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney.

"I mean, as an Australian, we always look and we watch the Champions League finals every year and we always think, 'Oh, how cool would it be to be in that, let alone win?'

"I said to some of my [Stingers] teammates here in Australia when I got back, I don't think I've ever won anything.

"Actually being able to lift a cup and just the feeling of euphoria with that, and the celebrations and our massive fan base in Europe is insane …

"That was probably one of the coolest moments of my life. It was awesome."

Abby Andrews scored nine goals across the semifinal and final. (Supplied: LEN European Aquatics)

Andrews's Olympiacos side beat Barcelona-based CN Mataró, featuring Stingers teammate Tilly Kearns, 14-12 in the semifinal, before downing Hungarian giants Ferencvárosi TC in the final by a score of 17-14.

"As the season went on, our team was really gaining strength," Andrews said.

"The semifinal was tough, but I think it was a great stepping stone for us.

"And then the final was brutal. We had lots of momentum swings but honestly, until the very end, we just completely stuck together."

The Final Four, held on the Mediterranean island of Malta, was an enormous occasion, the first time the men's and women's competitions were held at the same venue at the same time.

That allowed the women's teams to truly benefit from the enormous and fanatical support of their ultras.

Loading Instagram content

"It's insane," Andrews admitted of the enormous support.

"I mean, certain games that we play will have flares. They'll have this massive police presence and you just never know like what the crowd's going to do; when they're going to start chanting, if they'll go quiet for a bit.

"It's just something we don't experience here.

"I think what's so cool about the European multi-sport organisations is that they're just fanatics, like, they are absolutely mad, but ultimately their presence is so lifting and we love playing in front of them.

"It's just such a different experience.

"And for women's water polo to get that kind of attention as well, both our men's and women's teams were in the Final Four and the men unfortunately lost the semi, so all the attention shifted to us and the fans just went, 'you know what, let's give [the support] to the women'."

Abby Andrews has been a mainstay in the Stingers team. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

Andrews joined Olympiacos, the enormous multi-sport club based in the Piraeus region of Athens better known for its football team, soon after winning Olympic silver in 2024.

Having already played overseas in the American college system and in Italy, Andrews has been exposed to the very best of the best for her entire career.

Being able to cap her second season by winning the biggest prize in club water polo underlines the fact that she is on the right track personally.

"I think each experience teaches you something different," Andrews said.

"Having that exposure against the European powerhouses and just playing them regularly, having camps with them is honestly so invaluable and it's been a huge addition to my game.

"I love bringing the new techniques that they have, because obviously some Europeans are different in size, strength, skill and you kind of just adopt new methods as you see them. So it's really fun.

"I think my latest one in Olympiacos, it being my second year, I was able to establish myself more in the systems that the Greek teams play and really settle into that, as well as just realising that I can also step up and have a really big attacking presence.

"It's just such a cool environment to be in and I love like learning about myself in those environments and how I can step up."

Abby Andrews is expecting pressure at her first-ever home World Cup finals. (Getty Images: DeFodi Images/Marcel ter Bals)

Andrews did accept that playing at such a huge club comes with enormous pressure, but that it was "kind of a good extra pressure to have".

Extra pressure is something that Andrews is hoping to embrace over the next week, as the Stingers look to show off their status as genuine world challengers in the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup, starting in Sydney on Wednesday.

The world's top eight men's and women's national water polo teams will all compete at the event at the Sydney Aquatic Centre, the first time the city has hosted a major global water polo competition since the 2000 Olympics.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Sydney has twice hosted the World Cup finals before: the men's edition in 1999, won by Hungary; and the women's in 1995, won by the Aussies.

The Women's World Cup has also been hosted in Brisbane (1981) and Perth (2002).

But as much as the overall goal is to win the title in Sydney, emulating the Australian women's water polo team that won gold in the same Sydney Olympic Pool at the Sydney Games of 2000, filling the stands and inspiring others to follow in the Stingers' wake is just as important.

"I think this new generation coming through is so eager, I've never seen this kind of excitement from the younger kids coming through," Andrews said.

"I think it's already got such a good momentum and I think if we can really build on that and just fill the stands, get everyone there.

"You're going to be seeing some high-quality water polo from every team around the world, and being able to have this at home, who knows when we'll have this again, maybe not until Brisbane [2032].

"So while we've got this, let's use it. Everyone come down. I just think it's going to be such a spectacle."

World.title: Vaughters says night tests would have saved cycling '25 years of drama'
World.content:
Former professional cyclist and Cannondale-EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters has weighed in on the row over pre-dawn doping tests at the Tour de France, arguing such controls ​could have exposed cycling's blood-doping era decades earlier had they existed at the time.

Riders including race leader Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for unannounced doping checks ahead of ​the 15th stage, prompting ‌complaints that the disruption to sleep was unfair and potentially dangerous.

Vaughters, who rode professionally through the late 1990s and early 2000s, defended the practice.

"2am testing is one of the very effective ways ‌to prevent peptide (EPO, hGH) and testosterone micro dosing," Vaughters wrote on social media.

"If ⁠UCI [Union Cycliste Inter]ationale) had tested us in 2001 at 2am? We'd all have ‌been suspended and saved the sport ​25 years of drama."

His comments ‌carry particular weight given his own history with doping.

Jonathan Vaughters (right) was teammates with Lance Armstrong (left) on the US Postal team. (Getty Images: Graham Watson)

Vaughters was a teammate of Lance Armstrong on the US Postal Service team and later admitted using performance-enhancing drugs, including EPO, during his career.

When Lance met Oprah Lance Armstrong had successfully doped for years. But when the evidence backed him into a corner, he took control of the narrative and confessed live on Oprah's couch, martyring himself to cycling's EPO era.

He subsequently testified in the US Anti-Doping Agency's (USADA) investigation into ​Armstrong, ‌who was stripped of his seven Tour titles in 2012 after the agency concluded he ran what it called the most sophisticated doping program the sport had seen.

Vaughters ⁠went on to found the team now ‌known as Cannondale-EF, positioning it as ‌an advocate for clean racing.

His remarks come as riders pushed back on the timing of ‌Sunday's tests.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Vingegaard, tested at 2 am, said the visit cost him about 40 minutes of sleep before a mountain stage on which he later ‌crashed ​and broke his collarbone.

Pogačar, ⁠tested at 5 am, said he managed only four hours of sleep. Stage winner Remco Evenepoel called the practice "inhuman".

The International Testing Agency, which oversees doping controls for the UCI, said it was "conscious that night-time testing may be disruptive ⁠to riders' rest and recovery" but that effective testing must, "in limited and justified circumstances," occur outside daytime hours.

Micro-dosing of substances ‌such as EPO ‌and human growth hormone, which can clear the body within ​hours, has long concerned anti-doping authorities, who say predictable daytime-only testing makes such practices easier to evade.

Reuters

World.title: Weatherald retains Australian Test spot despite middling Ashes returns
World.content:
Opening batsman Jake Weatherald has retained his spot in Australia's Test squad for the looming series against Bangladesh.

Despite a middling Ashes campaign last summer, Weatherald is among a 13-man squad bolstered by the return of a trio of big guns.

Captain Pat Cummins, paceman Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon all return after recovering from injury.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They have worked extremely hard, individually and with the [fitness] teams, over the past few months to return from their respective injuries," Australia's chairman of selectors George Bailey said.

"While this is a 13-player squad, we have players prepared and available should any adjustments be required in the lead-up to these matches.

"The volume of cricket and schedule across the next 12 months are likely to present further opportunities across all formats for many players."

Missing from Australia's squad for the final Test against England last January are Usman Khawaja (retired), Michael Neser, Todd Murphy and Brendan Doggett.

The Australians host Bangladesh in Darwin from August 13-17 and Mackay from August 22-26, the start of a gruelling 12 months featuring 20 Test matches.

Weatherald will resume his opening batting partnership with Travis Head after playing all five Tests last summer against England.

The Darwin-born left-hander made only 201 runs at an average of 22.33 but has been given another chance to enhance his Test credentials.

AAP

World.title: Buckley opts out of Dons, Blues coaching races after Tasmania snub
World.content:
A disappointed Nathan Buckley is ruling out bidding for other vacant AFL head coaching jobs after being overlooked by the Tasmania Devils.

While Buckley, who openly coveted the Tasmanian post that went to Ken Hinkley, says he wants to be a head coach again, he is unlikely to pitch for the vacant positions at Essendon and Carlton.

"I haven't really reflected on where those roles sit, and I don't think I would enter those processes," Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night.

Loading...

Buckley said his most likely outcome next year was to remain at Geelong, where he is an assistant to Chris Scott.

"I am absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out," he said.

"I will take some time to reassess what is after that."

Buckley was committed to winning the Devils job that instead was given to former Port Adelaide boss Hinkley.

"I went home, kicked the dog, threw the toys out of the cot … because I was really keen on it," he said.

"If you're going to go for a job, you have got to decide if you're absolutely all in on it — and I was.

"And I absolutely respect the process that the Devils have run, and I respect their decision with Ken as well. I am glad they have found their man, and they're really clear that Kenny is the guy for them."

However, the former Collingwood boss said the Devils' decision was a personal "fork in the road".

"I was really deliberate in getting back into Geelong, and that was as much to give myself the very best chance to be ready to go for the Tasmania role," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Now that is off the table, so I will be absolutely committed to what is going on at Geelong. I have got an option for next year there and that is probably the most likely outcome.

"There are no guarantees in this, and you have got to put yourself out there, and you have got to have a crack.

"So there's disappointment."

Asked if he remained steadfast in wanting to be a head coach again, Buckley replied: "Yeah. I determined that about 12 months ago.

"That is what I believe I am capable of doing. It's what I want to do."

AAP

World.title: Millions greet Spain's WC heroes as FIFA probes ugly post-match fights
World.content:
Spain's World Cup-winning team has been met with an estimated two million fans at a raucous championship parade through the streets of Madrid.

The 26 players and their coaching staff met with the country's royals, and then with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after arriving in the Spanish capital a day after beating Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey.

"Thank you to the coaches and players for the style of play, the effort and the victory," Sánchez said. "We have truly enjoyed watching you play."

Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars As some of football's biggest names lit up the World Cup, Spain flew under the radar all the way to hoisting the trophy on its final day.

The squad then boarded an open-top bus for a raucous parade through central Madrid. "Stars shine together" was written on the bus, which also carried photos of the footballers.

Players — carrying the World Cup trophy and wearing shirts with the words Somos Campeones (We Are Champions) — danced and interacted with the fans along the route.

"It's been an emotional and proud experience to represent a wonderful country with such passionate and devoted fans," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said before the parade started. "We are filled with joy."

The squad travelled down Madrid's historic avenues from near Moncloa Palace, the prime minister's official residence, to Cibeles Square, where authorities told local media that some 120,000 people were on hand for a ceremony.

Players were introduced one by one before entering the stage set up at the square. Each picked the song to be played when they came in. Álex Baena, celebrating his 25th birthday, entered with the World Cup trophy.

Coach De la Fuente was thrust into the air by his players after being introduced. The coach was among those who sang along to the song being played for them.

Striker Borja Iglesias featured as a DJ at one point, with his teammates dancing on the stage.

Singers Aitana, Ana Mena and Lola Índigo were among those entertaining the crowd and the players.

Thousands of Spanish fans gathered around the Cibeles Fountain (Fuente de Cibeles) in Madrid to celebrate their World Cup win. (Ruben Albarran/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The ceremony ended with the whole Spain squad lifting the trophy again, just like at the awards ceremony on Sunday, but now in front of the local crowd.

Groups of fans had begun securing their spots near Cibeles late Monday morning local time ahead of the team's arrival, bringing umbrellas to protect against the sun and temperatures of up to 35 degrees Celsius.

The square is where previous Spain teams and their supporters have typically gathered to celebrate. It is also the traditional celebration spot for Real Madrid when it wins titles.

FIFA launches investigation into ugly post-game fracas

Argentina's Leandro Paredes was given a red card after fighting Spain's Gavi following the final whistle. (Getty Images: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

FIFA opened an investigation Monday after Spain's celebrations on beating Argentina in the World Cup final took an ugly turn when players briefly clashed on the field.

Video replays showed several players involved in a scuffle, including Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes.

He appeared to shove Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat. When Spain substitute Gavi jumped in to intervene, Paredes pushed him to the ground.

Spain captain Rodri also seemed to be hit in the stomach by Argentina defender Nahuel Molina as he ran past to join teammates celebrating the title win.

Molina later crowded Rodri, who was the target of a verbal confrontation by his former Manchester City teammate Nicolas Otamendi.

Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni and other players rushed in to de-escalate the situation.

FIFA said in a statement its "disciplinary committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the [FIFA disciplinary code] with regard to the post-match incidents".

The brief statement gave no timetable for an investigation and did not name Paredes, who was not shown a red card after the game yet could face a suspension.

Spain needed extra time to win Sunday's final 1-0 after Argentina was reduced to 10 men. Enzo Fernandez was sent off with a second yellow card in stoppage time at the end of 90 minutes.

The Argentina players stood facing their fans, with their backs to the podium, when Spain's squad lifted the trophy. It was an unusual show of disrespect to the new champions, who had given their opponents a guard of honour to collect their medals.

AP

World.title: Aussie world champs name new rugby sevens coach for LA Olympics
World.content:
Reg Tayler has been named head coach of the world champion Australian women's rugby sevens team, as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics loom on the horizon.

The decision completes a succession plan following Tim Walsh's departure from the position after Australia clinched the World Championship in France last month.

Tayler was an assistant coach to Walsh, who has since become Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance.

New Australia coach Reg Tayler (right) pictured with Tim Walsh. (Rugby Australia)

Tayler will guide Australia through its two-year build-up to the Olympics.

"The squad is determined for continued success through to the Olympics in Los Angeles," Tayler said in an RA statement.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

"Our players are professional and dedicated to achieving a gold medal, and I am confident we will have the squad capable of that in 2028."

Tayler, who joined the Australian sevens program last year, has big shoes to fill.

Walsh not only led Australia to its recent World Championship victory but was also in charge when it won the inaugural Olympic gold in women's rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Games.

It is the only time Australia has won Olympic gold in the sport.

Australia won the first women's Olympic rugby sevens gold on offer in 2016. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

Walsh, who coached Australia across two stints, will still have input through his newly created role as part of RA's strategy to align the sevens and Wallaroos programs.

He is confident Tayler will leave his mark as head coach, describing the appointment as a "seamless acquisition" for the squad.

"Reg is highly knowledgeable of the World Series circuit and has worked with many of our players coming through the pathways system," Walsh said.

"He's not going in cold, he completely understands the game and his expertise is going to be fully utilised by the program.

"It's a privilege and honour to retain Reg."

Tayler has previously coached the Australia A women's sevens team.

He also spent time working with Ireland's women's and men's squads between 2023-25.

Australia claimed the World Championship with victories in the final two legs of the series in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

World.title: Football world 'devastated' by death of English icon Keegan
World.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died aged 75.

Keegan's family and Newcastle United revealed in January that the two-time European Footballer of the Year was undergoing cancer treatment, without disclosing details of his illness. His death was confirmed by Newcastle overnight.

Last month, Keegan, who was nicknamed "King Kev" and "Mighty Mouse" and was one of the most influential figures of his generation in English football, revealed he had stage four cancer.

Fans lay flowers at St James' Park, Newcastle United's home ground, in memory of Keegan after his death. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history," Newcastle said in a statement.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an entertainer."

Glittering career as player and manager

Keegan became one of English football's biggest superstars in his time with Liverpool from 1971-77. (Getty Images: Harry Ormesher)

Keegan began his career at Scunthorpe United before joining Liverpool in 1971.

He made 323 appearances for Liverpool in all competitions, scoring 100 goals over six seasons. He won three First Division titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups and the 1977 European Cup during a glittering spell at Anfield.

After moving to Hamburg, Keegan was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979, becoming the only British player to win the Ballon d'Or twice. He later returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984 at the age of 33.

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the side 31 times.

He moved into management at Newcastle in 1992, guiding the club into the Premier League and transforming it into one of England's most entertaining sides.

Keegan's team came agonisingly close to winning the 1995-96 Premier League title before they were overtaken by Manchester United.

Although the title race did not go Keegan's way, his rant aimed at United manager Sir Alex Ferguson in the heat of the race went down in football folklore.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, he had a brief spell at Fulham before taking charge of England in 1999 following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

He resigned after Euro 2000 and a defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, famously saying he was "not good enough" to do the job, at a media conference. He won seven of his 18 matches in charge.

Keegan later managed Manchester City before leaving the club in March 2005 and initially announcing his retirement from football. He made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, though his second spell at the club lasted only eight months.

A lasting legacy

A statement from Keegan's family, quoted by British media, said on Monday: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

Tributes poured in for Keegan, with Liverpool saying in a statement: "Our 'Mighty Mouse', his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history."

England Football wrote on X: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away," while former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer wrote: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss".

Reuters

World.title: PM backs bid for future NT AFL team, no promises on funding
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed the prospect of an AFL team in the Northern Territory, but has stayed tight-lipped on whether his government would help fund it to get off the ground.

With a 20th AFL licence up for grabs, the NT has been touted as one of the top options to take it home, with Western Australia and the ACT also billed as possible contenders.

It comes as Tasmania prepares to enter the AFL with the Devils in 2028, bringing the competition a step closer to becoming truly representative of each state and territory.

This year's Tiwi Islands grand final marks the first time a sitting PM has ever attended the iconic match. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Despite being known as a breeding ground for some of the competition's most exciting talent, from regions like Gove and the Tiwi Islands, the NT has never had a top-tier team.

Mr Albanese visited the Tiwi Islands on Sunday, the first time a prime minister has travelled to the islands north of Darwin in more than 25 years, where he voiced his support for an NT team.

"I'd love to see a team here in the territory, as I'm sure all Territorians would," he said.

"It's a while off, [but] we'll continue to talk and engage with the AFL as well."

Anthony Albanese met with local players at the Tiwi Islands grand final on the weekend. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)
